articles.title: Concurrent electrical and mechanical adaptations of forearm muscles across graded handgrip intensities: Evidence from EMG and myotonometry.
articles.authors: Abdurrahman Tanhan, Merve Tunçdemir, Tülay Çevik Saldıran
articles.abstract: Grip force production depends on coordinated neural activation and intrinsic muscle mechanical properties; however, their concurrent behavior across graded contraction intensities and potential sex-related differences remains insufficiently characterized. This study examined simultaneous changes in surface EMG (sEMG) activity and myotonometry-derived mechanical properties of the flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) and extensor digitorum (ED) muscles during graded handgrip contractions. Twenty healthy adults (10 women, 10 men) performed isometric grips at rest and at 40 %, 60 %, 80 %, and 100 % of maximal voluntary contraction (MVC). Muscle activation was recorded via surface EMG (RMS), while tone, stiffness, and logarithmic decrement (LD, an inverse index of elasticity) were concurrently assessed using MyotonPRO. Contraction intensity effects were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA, and sex-based comparisons were conducted at each force level. sEMG amplitudes increased progressively with contraction intensity (p < 0.001). Muscle tone and stiffness showed parallel intensity-dependent increases (p < 0.001), whereas LD remained relatively stable. Sex-related differences were limited in sEMG but more evident in mechanical parameters, with males demonstrating higher FDS tone and stiffness and lower LD in the ED muscle (p < 0.05). Increasing grip force induces coordinated neuromuscular activation and mechanical stiffening with parameter-specific responses. Combined sEMG-myotonometric assessment provides an integrated framework for sex-sensitive evaluation of muscle function.

articles.title: Postural control differences in children who are deaf or hard of hearing: A systematic review and meta-analysis of postural sway outcomes.
articles.authors: Hannah Ray, Maddie Gose, Nikolina Djumic et al.
articles.abstract: Children who are deaf and hard of hearing (DHH) may exhibit altered postural control due to differences in sensory inputs contributing to balance regulation. Quantitative synthesis of posturographic outcomes can clarify the magnitude and consistency of these differences while identifying methodological factors that limit comparability across studies. This review evaluated postural sway outcomes in DHH children relative to typically hearing peers. Following PRISMA guidelines, five databases were searched for studies employing static posturography in pediatric DHH populations. Twenty-five studies satisfied inclusion criteria for the systematic review and 12 studies were included in the meta-analysis. Standardized mean differences were calculated for anterior-posterior (AP) and medial-lateral (ML) sway metrics. Between-study heterogeneity was examined with attention to task conditions and measurement approaches. Pooled estimates indicated altered sway in DHH children, with AP and ML variability consistently differentiating groups. However, heterogeneity was high across tasks, and limited reporting of protocol features constrained evaluation of how postural difficulty, sensory conditions, and analysis choices influenced outcomes. Posturographic evidence supports meaningful differences in postural control between DHH and typically hearing children, but substantial heterogeneity of findings limits interpretability and cross-study comparison. Given the need for greater standardization in task design, outcome selection, and reporting to advance mechanistic understanding for pediatric balance assessment, we provide methodological recommendations for future investigations to inform the development of standardized assessment protocols.

articles.title: Temporal Eating Patterns Show Inconsistent Associations With Cancer Incidence and Mortality: Systematic Review of Prospective Studies.
articles.authors: Sihan Song, Tuo Lan, Seho Park et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Temporal eating patterns, such as eating time, frequency, and regularity, may be associated with cancer outcomes through circadian and metabolic pathways, but evidence remains limited. OBJECTIVES: We aimed to systematically review prospective studies examining associations between temporal eating patterns and cancer incidence or mortality. METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed and Embase were searched from inception to September 2, 2026. Eligible studies included prospective cohorts of adults assessing eating or fasting duration, nighttime eating, breakfast frequency or timing, meal regularity, or eating frequency in relation to cancer incidence or mortality. Meta-analyses were conducted when ≥3 studies examined comparable exposure-outcome pairs, and the quality of meta-evidence was evaluated using the NutriGrade scoring system. Risk of bias was assessed using the Risk of Bias for Nutrition Observational Studies tool. RESULTS: Seventeen prospective cohort studies were included. Findings for eating or fasting duration and nighttime eating varied across studies for both cancer incidence and mortality. Lower breakfast frequency was associated with higher cancer mortality and colorectal cancer incidence in some studies, but not with breast cancer incidence. Greater eating-time variability and unrestrained eating were associated with higher cancer mortality, with unrestrained eating also associated with higher colorectal cancer incidence. Associations between eating frequency and cancer outcomes varied across studies and cancer sites. A meta-analysis of three studies showed a non-significant inverse association between eating frequency and colorectal cancer incidence in both categorical (HR = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.64-1.03) and dose-response analyses (HR per 1 time/day increase = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.89-1.01), with very low-quality meta-evidence. Risk of bias varied across domains, with common concerns related to confounding and exposure changes over follow-up. CONCLUSIONS: Findings from cohort studies suggest potential associations between temporal eating patterns and cancer outcomes, but the evidence remains limited and heterogeneous, underscoring the need for further investigation. PROSPERO REGISTRATION: CRD420251246423.

articles.title: Antenatal multiple micronutrients versus iron-folic acid supplementation and infant neurodevelopment: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Jitender Nagpal, Sarika Tyagi, Swapnil Rawat et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Antenatal multiple micronutrient (MMN) supplementation reduces the risk of low birth weight and small-for-gestational-age birth compared with iron and folic acid (IFA), but whether the benefits extend to neurodevelopment remains uncertain. OBJECTIVES: To estimate the effect of antenatal MMN compared with IFA on infant cognitive, motor, and language development up to 24 months of age. METHODS: We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Google Scholar, OpenGrey, Wiley Online Library, and trial registers through June 10, 2026 for randomized controlled trials comparing antenatal MMN with IFA and reporting infant neurodevelopment. Two reviewers independently screened and extracted data; risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 and certainty with GRADE. Hedges g estimates were pooled with a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model and Knapp-Hartung adjustment; cluster-trial variances were inflated by the design effect. RESULTS: Of 2,943 records, seven trials (8 reports; 5,331 infants for the cognitive comparison) were included. MMN and IFA did not differ in cognitive development (g = +0.02; 95% CI -0.06, +0.10; P = 0.53; I2 = 13%) or motor development (g = -0.02; 95% CI -0.09, +0.05; P = 0.49; I2 = 0%). Language showed a small, non-significant advantage for MMN that was not robust across sensitivity analyses (g = +0.07; 95% CI -0.00, +0.14; P = 0.06; I2 = 0%). All pooled point estimates were below the conventional threshold for a small, standardized effect of 0.2. Certainty was moderate for cognitive and motor outcomes and low for language. CONCLUSIONS: Antenatal MMN supplementation was associated with little to no difference in infant cognitive or motor development compared with IFA up to 24 months of age. The small language difference was not statistically significant, was not robust across sensitivity analyses, and is unlikely to be clinically important. PROTOCOL AND REGISTRATION: PROSPERO CRD420261392389. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261392389.

articles.title: Dietary threonine requirement of healthy older adults >60y stratified by age and sex in a repeated measures design1.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Alyssa Paoletti, Wala Naeem, Paul B Pencharz et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Current dietary guidelines for most of the world recommend increased plant protein consumption to improve health and support environmental sustainability. Threonine is an indispensable AA required for protein and mucin synthesis which is present in low concentrations in plant proteins. Threonine requirement is needed to guide dietary planning and assessment of protein adequacy particularly in those consuming predominantly plant-based protein diets. However, no data exist on dietary threonine requirement in older adults. OBJECTIVES: 1) Determine the threonine requirement in older adults using the indicator amino acid oxidation (IAAO) method in a repeated measures design. 2) compare the derived estimates based on age: 60-69y and 70-79y and sex. METHODS: The threonine requirement was determined using the IAAO method with L-[1-13C] phenylalanine as the indicator. Twenty-two older adults >60 y (n = 10 males and n = 12 females) were randomly assigned to receive up to 7 threonine intakes (5 to 35 mg/kg/d). The mean threonine requirement was determined from oxidation of L-[1-13C] phenylalanine (F13CO2) using a two-phase linear mixed effect model. The 95% CI was calculated using parametric bootstrap. The overlap of the 95% CI between the 2 age groups were used to compare the requirement estimates. The null hypothesis was accepted if the interval contained zero. RESULTS: There was no effect of sex on the threonine requirement. However, the threonine requirement for adults 60-69y and 70-79y were 11 mg/kg/d (R2m = 0.10, R2c = 0.81; 7.70, 14.30 mg/kg/d) and 17.9 mg/kg/d (R2m = 0.44, R2c = 0.64; 13.23, 22.57 mg/kg/d) respectively with those 70-79y having a higher requirement than those 60-69y ( -1.18, -12.62). CONCLUSIONS: The result of the current study demonstrates that AA needs among older adults change within decades of age. This should be integrated into future AA recommendations for accurate planning and assessment of protein nutrition in the elderly. The trial was registered at Clinical Trials Registry: # NCT02008955, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06225648.

articles.title: Beyond imbalance: an elasticity framework for the distance-averaged force-velocity relationship in vertical jump.
articles.authors: Zhaoqian Li, Mingyu Li, Xing Zhang et al.
articles.abstract: This study aimed to (1) establish the distance‑averaged F‑V relationship framework and (2) develop elasticity metrics that quantify how F‑V relationship variables govern jump height and inform training decisions. Theoretical derivation and experimental validation across 108 F-V relationship models derived from 1578 jumps (countermovement jump and squat jump at three knee angles; 20 well-trained subjects) yielded a systematic error of - 2.1% and a strong linear association (r = 0.96, 95% CI [0.93; 0.97]) between measured and predicted jump height. Four elasticity metrics were formulated: force elasticity ([Formula: see text]), the elasticity of jump height to maximal force ([Formula: see text]); velocity elasticity ([Formula: see text]), the elasticity of jump height to maximal velocity ([Formula: see text]); the force-velocity elasticity norm [Formula: see text], reflecting the overall sensitivity of jump height to changes in F-V relationship variables; and the force-velocity elasticity ratio [Formula: see text]), indicating which variable dominates the jump height response. Simulations and experiments revealed that [Formula: see text] bore an inverse relationship to [Formula: see text], and [Formula: see text] was inversely related to [Formula: see text], reflecting diminishing marginal returns. At a fixed jump height, simulations showed [Formula: see text] and [Formula: see text] displayed a U-shaped relationship; a balanced profile ([Formula: see text] = 1) did not always correspond to the lowest [Formula: see text]. The distance-averaged F-V elasticity framework offers a physically grounded and quantitative tool for linking F-V relationship variables directly to jump performance, providing a basis for informing individualized training decisions.

articles.title: Visual external focus of attention modulates corticospinal excitation-inhibition balance after acute exercise.
articles.authors: Philipp Bauer, João H Oliveira, João S Gomes et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Individuals are frequently instructed to adopt an internal focus during exercise, such as concentrating on a specific muscle, which may inadvertently lead to online conscious motor processing and constrain automatic motor control. In contrast, an external focus, particularly with distant visual feedback, is thought to benefit corticospinal modulation, enhancing automaticity and movement complexity. Nonetheless, the effective integration of attentional focus into evidence-based exercise prescription requires a mechanistic understanding of its neurophysiological basis. Therefore, this study investigated whether a single exercise bout performed with visual external, external or internal focus differentially modulates corticospinal excitation-inhibition balance (Corticospinal Excitability/Silent Period ratio), short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), intracortical facilitation (ICF) and torque complexity. METHODS: Thirty-seven healthy young adults were randomised to internal (12), external (12), or visual external focus (13) groups, completing a seated calf-raise bout to failure under the respective focus of attention instruction. Neurophysiological outcomes were assessed using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and analysed in a linear mixed-effects model. RESULTS: Corticospinal excitation-inhibition balance was enhanced after an exercise bout carried out with a visual external focus (increase 1.40 ± 0.42 mV/s, p = 0.005), while no changes were detected with an external or internal focus (all p ≥ 0.05). SICI, ICF and torque complexity showed no significant effect regarding attentional focus. CONCLUSION: The present study contributes to the neurophysiological basis for using goal-oriented visual feedback cues to increase corticospinal drive, offering a targeted intervention strategy which has potential to optimize motor performance in elite athletes and accelerate functional recovery in clinical populations. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: The present study was registered under NCT06538766 on 26/07/2024.

articles.title: New decompression gas CF₄/O₂: reducing DCS risk and ameliorating injuries in male rats.
articles.authors: Jiaqi Li, Hong Chen, Zhi Li et al.
articles.abstract: Decompression sickness (DCS) remains a major risk in diving. Prolonging decompression reduces inert gas load but increases operation time and underwater exposure. We tested a carbon tetrafluoride-oxygen mixture (CF₄/O₂) as a decompression gas in two rat decompression protocols: 6 ATA compressed air and 9 ATA helium-oxygen (heliox). Switching to CF₄/O₂ 10 min before decompression significantly reduced DCS incidence in both protocols: air, 68% (19/28) to 11% (3/28); heliox, 68% (15/22) to 18% (4/22). Mortality was significantly reduced in the compressed-air protocol (29% [8/28] to 0 [0/28], P = 0.004) but not in the heliox protocol (14% [3/22] to 0 [0/22], P = 0.233). Echocardiography showed fewer or no intracardiac bubbles after CF₄/O₂. In the heliox protocol, CF₄/O₂ significantly modulated some pulmonary function parameters; in the compressed-air protocol, pulmonary function changes were time-dependent and did not differ significantly between groups. CF₄/O₂ also reduced lung inflammation, endothelial injury, and histological damage in both protocols. In a 28-day repeated hyperbaric exposure protocol assessing selected serum biochemical endpoints, CF₄/O₂ did not increase serum alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, creatinine or urea; however, this protocol did not include post-exposure histopathology or haematology, so safety conclusions are limited to the measured endpoints. These findings support the tested CF₄/O₂ gas-switching strategy under the specific conditions used. Shorter decompression protocols were not tested, and shortening decompression time remains a potential application rather than a demonstrated outcome.

articles.title: Neuromechanical associations in vertical jump adaptation after plyometric training: a multivariate meta-analysis.
articles.authors: Lin Xie, Jing Dai, BingHong Gao et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Plyometric training (PT) is widely used to enhance vertical-jump performance, but the associations between muscle-tendon mechanical adaptation, lower-limb sEMG amplitude, and" performance across jump tasks with different neuromechanical demands remain incompletely understood. In particular, whether stiffness adaptations are uniformly beneficial across Stretch-Shortening Cycle(SSC)-dependent and predominantly concentric jump tasks remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: This study employed a multivariate meta-analysis to quantify associations between changes in vertical stiffness (Kvert), Achilles tendon stiffness (Ktendon), knee-extensor and plantar-flexor sEMG amplitude, and vertical-jump adaptation, while examining whether these associations differed according to jump type and intervention duration. METHODS: In strict accordance with PRISMA guidelines, seven major databases were searched for randomized controlled trials from inception to December 2025. Multivariate random-effects models were constructed using the metaSEM package in R, supplemented by Pearson correlation analysis. The GRADE framework was utilized to assess the certainty of evidence. RESULTS: Twenty-nine randomized controlled trials were included. Plyometric training significantly improved vertical jump outcomes (all p < 0.05; standardized mean differences(SMD) > 0.40), vertical stiffness (SMD = 0.37; 95% CI, 0.07-0.67), and Achilles tendon stiffness (SMD = 0.43). Descriptive Kvert-VJ correlations were positive for CMJ (r = 0.51) and negative for DJ (r = - 0.72). Formal moderator analysis supported differences in the Kvert-VJ association across jump types (LRT = 11.33, df = 2, p = 0.003) but not across intervention-duration categories (LRT = 2.05, df = 2, p = 0.358). Formal moderation by jump type or intervention duration was not observed for Ktendon or the sEMG outcomes, although these analyses were based on relatively few studies. CONCLUSION: Plyometric-training adaptations showed formal evidence of task-specific Kvert-VJ associations, whereas duration-specific moderation was not supported. Associations involving Ktendon and sEMG amplitude were less consistent and should be regarded as exploratory.

articles.title: Aerobic exercise preconditioning enhances skeletal muscle resistance and recovery after contusion: involvement of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis.
articles.authors: Wei Wang, Zhao Tian, Peijin Li et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Compared with passive recovery after injury, exercise preconditioning may provide an active strategy for improving the subsequent response of skeletal muscle to injury. This study aimed to investigate the effects of aerobic exercise preconditioning (AEP) on skeletal muscle injury (SMI) and post-injury repair, with particular focus on the involvement of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis and changes in PGC-1α acetylation. METHODS: This study initially investigated the effects of continuous aerobic exercise on skeletal muscle in healthy mice. Subsequently, the influence of AEP on injury severity and regenerative repair of the gastrocnemius muscle was examined in mice with SMI. Western blotting was used to determine the expression levels of SIRT1 and PGC-1α proteins, immunoprecipitation was performed to assess the acetylation status of PGC-1α, and qRT-PCR was used to analyze the expression of genes associated with mitochondrial biogenesis-related markers and muscle regeneration. Finally, the involvement of SIRT1 signaling in the AEP-associated response to SMI was further examined using the pharmacological SIRT1 inhibitor EX527. RESULTS: Continuous aerobic exercise was associated with increased SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling and changes in mitochondrial biogenesis-related markers in the gastrocnemius muscle of healthy mice. AEP was associated with reduced injury-related changes and an improved post-injury repair profile in mice with SMI. During the early stage after injury, AEP was accompanied by sustained SIRT1/ PGC-1α signaling and reduced PGC-1α acetylation. Pharmacological inhibition of SIRT1 with EX527 partially attenuated the AEP-associated protective and reparative effects on the injured gastrocnemius muscle. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that AEP establishes an adaptive state in skeletal muscle that is associated with reduced injury-related damage and an enhanced post-injury reparative response. The SIRT1/PGC-1α axis and altered PGC-1α acetylation may contribute to these AEP-associated effects.

articles.title: Neural, contractile, and muscular determinants associated with lower strength in recreationally active older men: a cross-sectional study.
articles.authors: Ronan Sherman, Mathias Forsberg Brobakken, Ole Kristian Berg et al.
articles.abstract: Skeletal muscle strength declines with age. However, the relative contributions of various neuromuscular factors to this decline appear to not be fully understood. Thus, we compared relative attenuations in key neural and muscular strength determinants with age, in vivo and in vitro, recruiting 22 old (75 ± 1 years) and 18 young (25 ± 1 years) recreationally active men. Leg extension maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), early (0-100 ms) and late (0-200 ms) rate of force development (RFD), were reduced by - 39%, - 55%, and - 49%, respectively, in the old (all p < 0.001); however, estimated thigh cross-sectional area (CSA) was not different between groups. In contrast, efferent neural drive assessed by evoked recordings (m.soleus normalized V-waves; V/Msup), largely dependent on corticospinal factors, revealed a - 72% age-related reduction (p < 0.001). A - 51% reduction was also observed in peripheral motoneuron excitability, measured as Hmax/Mmax at 10% MVC (p < 0.001). The neural age-related decline was confirmed applying peak electromyography (EMG; - 14%), early (- 31%), and late (- 30%; all p < 0.05) rate of EMG rise, during leg extension MVC. While voluntary activation was unaltered with age, quadriceps contractility was reduced (resting twitch: peak force, - 41%; RFD, - 43%; delay, +39%; time-to-relaxation, +56%; all p < 0.01). Biopsies from m.vastus lateralis showed an age-related decrease in proportion, - 16% (type II: 43% (old) vs. 51% (young); p < 0.001), but not size, of fast twitch fibers. Concomitantly, slow twitch fibers were 12% larger in old vs. young (p < 0.05). Collectively, these findings showed that age-related reductions in muscle strength were accompanied by pronounced alterations in neural function alongside changes in muscle phenotype, despite preserved thigh CSA.

articles.title: Longitudinal transcriptomic monitoring of erythropoietic adaptations in endurance athletes: a prospective study protocol.
articles.authors: Sushmita Kumari, T K Sanjith, Jayaseelan Murgaiyan et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Understanding systemic molecular adaptations to endurance training and environmental hypoxia is important for advancing physiological monitoring in athletes. Transcriptomic profiling of peripheral blood mononuclear cells offers a promising approach to characterising erythropoiesis-related biological responses, yet longitudinal data under real-world training conditions remain limited. This protocol describes the rationale and design of a prospective longitudinal study aimed at investigating erythropoiesis-related transcriptomic adaptations to variations in training load and hypoxic exposure in endurance athletes. METHODS: A total of 60 trained endurance athletes will be followed over a 12-month period, encompassing baseline conditioning, intensified training phases, competition, recovery, and altitude exposure, where applicable. Training load will be quantified using daily session logs and wearable-derived metrics. Peripheral blood samples will be collected at baseline and monthly intervals, with additional sampling during key physiological phases. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells will undergo transcriptomic profiling using high-throughput gene-expression platforms, with pathway-focused analysis targeting hypoxia signalling, erythroid differentiation, iron metabolism, and angiogenic regulation. Longitudinal statistical modelling will be employed to evaluate adaptation trajectories, intra-individual variability, and associations between transcriptomic responses and quantified training exposures. EXPECTED RESULTS: The study is expected to identify phase-dependent modulation of erythropoiesis-related transcriptional pathways and to enable estimation of physiological ranges of molecular variability across training cycles. Repeated within-individual assessment may provide insight into the persistence and magnitude of transcriptional responses to training stress and hypoxic stimuli. CONCLUSION: This longitudinal framework is anticipated to generate foundational evidence supporting the feasibility of transcriptomic monitoring in athletic populations and to inform future development of advanced biological surveillance strategies in sport.

articles.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence or Telerehabilitation on Consumer Ratings in Physical Therapy: An Online Randomized Experiment.
articles.authors: Megan H Ross, Joshua Simmich, Daniela Berg et al.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into health care delivery, but its influence on consumer perceptions of physical therapist services remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: The objective was to examine how the use of AI influences consumer perceptions of in-person and telerehabilitation physical therapist services. DESIGN: This study used a randomized 2 × 2 factorial experimental design comparing AI use and delivery mode. SETTING: The experiment was conducted online in Australia. PARTICIPANTS: The study included 710 Australian adults recruited through a paid panel. EXPOSURE: Participants were randomized to 1 of 4 hypothetical physical therapist consultation scenarios (in-person vs telerehabilitation; AI used vs not used). MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Perceived warmth; competence; safety; provider trust; emotional trust; relational and functional service quality; working alliance; and intention to use were measured on 7-point Likert-scales. Composite mean scores were analyzed using ordinary least squares regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. RESULTS: Mean scores in the no-AI, in-person condition ranged from 4.8 to 5.8. Among in-person scenarios, described AI use was associated with lower ratings across all outcomes, including warmth (b = -0.3, 95% CI = -0.5 to -0.1), competence (-0.4, -0.6 to -0.2) and safety (-0.8, -1.1 to -0.6), provider trust (-0.5, -0.7 to -0.3) and intention to use (-0.8, -1.0 to -0.5). Without AI, telerehabilitation also reduced ratings by 0.2 to 0.7 points across outcomes. Positive interaction effects indicated attenuation of AI-related reductions in telerehabilitation for relational (interaction b = 0.4, 95% CI = 0.1 to 0.8) and functional service quality (0.36, 0.02 to 0.70), intention to use (0.6, 0.1 to 1.0), and perceived safety (0.5, 0.1 to 0.9). CONCLUSIONS: Hypothetical in-person consultations described as involving AI were associated with poorer consumer perceptions of physical therapists and services. Telerehabilitation was also perceived less favorably than in-person care. RELEVANCE: Future studies should test whether transparency and reassurance mitigate the effects of AI-use on consumer perceptions of physical therapy.

articles.title: Graft integration in autologous costal cartilage transplantation: a long-term study using chondrocyte-laden fibrin gel.
articles.authors: A D Kurenkova, S A Sheleg, Y M Efremov et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Mosaicplasty of articular cartilage can be performed using costal cartilage due to its structural similarity. This method has been successfully applied in clinical practice for small joints; however, its use in large joints is limited, partly due to graft displacement. In this study, we used chondrocyte-laden fibrin gel to improve integration in a rat model of autologous costal cartilage transplantation into a knee joint defect and assessed long-term outcomes. METHODS: Costal cartilage was characterized histologically, immunohistochemically, and biomechanically. Autologous grafts were harvested from the tenth rib and implanted into knee defects pretreated with chondrocyte-laden fibrin gel. Controls included cell-free fibrin gel, defect-only control, and sham-operated animals. Graft integration, subchondral bone resorption, and graft composition were analyzed at 1, 6, and 12 months using micro-CT, histology, and immunostaining. RESULTS: Costal cartilage demonstrated histological and biomechanical properties comparable to articular cartilage. Chondrocyte-laden fibrin gel did not significantly improve integration but reduced subchondral bone resorption, a preliminary finding consistent with an anti-inflammatory effect. Retained grafts restored joint congruity, integrated with host tissue, and showed no resorption or loss of hyaline cartilage markers over 12 months, despite age-related osteoarthritis changes in surrounding tissue. CONCLUSIONS: Although chondrocyte-laden fibrin gel did not enhance graft integration, this study demonstrates long-term structural preservation of costal cartilage grafts in a rat knee defect model. Further studies in larger animals are needed to optimize integration strategies and support translation into clinical practice, potentially expanding treatment options for patients with limited donor tissue.

articles.title: Fatty infiltration of the lumbar paravertebral muscles is related to functional limitations in patients with adult spinal deformity.
articles.authors: Nabil Nassim, Ayman Assi, Elio Mekhael et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Adult spinal deformity (ASD) is associated with reduced quality of life and functional impairment. Fatty infiltration of paravertebral muscles, quantified on MRI, has been linked to global malalignment and postoperative complications, but requires time-consuming analysis and specific protocols. The simpler qualitative Goutallier classification remains underexplored in ASD. This study aimed to assess the relationship between paravertebral muscle fatty infiltration, functional and radiographic parameters, and quality-of-life scores using the Goutallier method. METHODS: Sixty-four ASD patients underwent full-body biplanar X-rays and completed the ODI questionnaire. 3D gait analysis was performed to calculate joint kinematics, spatiotemporal parameters, and the Gait Deviation Index (GDI: 0-100; decreases with severity). Lumbar MRIs were used to assess paravertebral muscle fatty infiltration with the Goutallier classification. Patients were grouped as High-Infiltration (Goutallier grades 3-4) or Low-Mod-Infiltration (Goutallier grades 0-2). Radiographic, kinematic parameters and quality-of-life scores were compared, and correlations with Goutallier grade were calculated. RESULTS: Patients were divided into 33 High-Infiltration and 31 Low-Mod-Infiltration. The High-Infiltration group had increased SVA (76 vs 22mm) and PI-LL mismatch (19 vs 3°; all p < 0.05). During gait, they showed decreased GDI (80 vs 91), walking speed (0.7 vs 0.9 m/s) and increased thorax flexion (13 vs 4°; all p < 0.05). They also had increased ODI scores (47 vs 36, p = 0.02). Goutallier grades correlated with SVA (ρ = 0.43), PI-LL mismatch (ρ = 0.44) and walking speed (ρ = -0.43; all p < 0.05). CONCLUSION: The Goutallier classification, a simple method using routine MRI, is associated with malalignment severity and functional impairment in ASD. High grades may help identify patients who could benefit from targeted interventions, such as muscle strengthening to optimize outcomes.

articles.title: Diffuse adverse coronary hemodynamics associated with type 2 diabetes: A CCTA-CFD phenotyping study.
articles.authors: Yue Qiu, Pei-Lun Han, Si-Quan Cheng et al.
articles.abstract: Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) have a disproportionately high risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, which is not fully explained by the degree of coronary stenosis alone. In this retrospective study, patient-specific computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models were reconstructed from coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) data obtained from 53 individuals (26 non-T2DM and 27 T2DM). Time-averaged wall shear stress (TAWSS), oscillatory shear index (OSI), and relative residence time (RRT) were calculated to characterize the hemodynamic environment. Plaque composition and cardiac chamber dimensions were also analyzed. Results show patients with T2DM had significantly greater proportions of coronary surface area meeting the prespecified criteria for low TAWSS, high OSI, and high RRT than patients without T2DM (all P < 0.05) despite similar percent diameter stenosis. In plaque-level mixed-effects analyses accounting for within-patient clustering and clinical covariates, T2DM remained associated with lower TAWSS across all plaques (all P < 0.05). In plaque-type-stratified analyses, the most consistent adjusted differences were observed in non-calcified plaques. Longer diabetes duration was significantly associated with higher RRT (β = 0.0738, 95% CI: 0.0153 to 0.1324, P = 0.0135). These findings suggest that under standardized CCTA-CFD modeling assumptions, T2DM was associated with a greater patient-level burden of adverse simulated coronary hemodynamic regions. Plaque-level associations varied according to plaque composition and remained most evident in non-calcified plaques after multivariable adjustment. These findings suggest that CFD-derived hemodynamic assessment may provide information complementary to conventional anatomical measurements.

articles.title: Is Large Language Model a New Hope for the Global South? A Rapid Bibliometric Synthesis of Artificial Intelligence in Anatomy Education.
articles.authors: Yue Lin, Yusi Huang, Junming Zhou et al.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), especially the recent proliferation of generative Large Language Models (LLMs), is transforming traditional anatomy education by introducing new teaching tools. However, the adoption of these cutting-edge technologies raises questions about global educational equity. It remains unclear whether AI will serve as a digital equalizer or further exacerbate marginalization. This rapid bibliometric synthesis aims to provide a comprehensive, data-driven overview of the "Application of Artificial Intelligence in Anatomy Education" (AAAE). We seek to map the intellectual landscape, detect structural and technological shifts, evaluate the geopolitical disparities, and provide corresponding references. A total of 85 consolidated records were retrieved from Web of Science and Scopus. These data constituted the whole panorama of AAAE. Bibliometrix and CiteSpace were utilized for static and dynamic mapping. A multidisciplinary expert panel validated the thematic clusters using Gwet's AC1 and the Normalized Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI). Publications surged following ChatGPT's release, indicating a shift from specialized computer vision to the application of general-purpose LLMs. While high-income countries maintain leadership, AI could exert a "democratizing effect" on upper-middle-income countries, doubling their odds of publication compared to traditional anatomy. Six research frontiers and three research trajectories were captured, and corresponding implications for future researchers in the global south and north were presented. AAAE could be conducted using a stratified strategy: different expansions of AI technologies for pedagogy; leveraging commercial APIs to bypass infrastructure bottlenecks; and validating open-source models. Global equity critically demands cross-border collaboration and inclusive datasets.

articles.title: The So-Called "Vastus Lateralis Obliquus" is the Most Distal Part of the Vastus Intermedius.
articles.authors: Takafumi Ono, Mio Imai, Yuto Kawasaki et al.
articles.abstract: The vastus lateralis (VL) has long been described as comprising a longitudinal part (vastus lateralis longus, VLL) and an oblique part (vastus lateralis obliquus, VLO), the latter inserting onto the superolateral border of the patella and traditionally regarded as a component of the VL that stabilizes the patella laterally. However, the anatomical relationship between the VLO and the remainder of the VL has never been rigorously defined, and electromyographic studies have independently regarded the muscle belly emerging at the distolateral thigh as the "superficial region of the vastus intermedius (VI)." To address this discrepancy, we re-examined the structure and innervation of the VLO in five thighs from five embalmed cadavers by gross dissection. The belly conventionally identified as the VLO was present in all specimens and inserted onto the superolateral patella. When the VLL was reflected, this belly was continuous with the VI, which arose broadly from the anterior surface of the femoral shaft; thus, the VLO was the most distal portion of the VI protruding lateral to the lateral border of the VL. Consistently, this region was supplied by the terminal twigs of the lateral branch of the VI (femoral nerve), whereas the branch to the VL did not reach it. We conclude that the so-called VLO is not part of the VL but the distal part of the VI. This reinterpretation reconciles the anatomical convention with electromyographic findings and has implications for anatomical nomenclature, interpretation of VI surface electromyography, and understanding the traction source in painful bipartite patella.

articles.title: Conservation of a synaptic blueprint across the animal kingdom.
articles.authors: Aiden J Houcek, Ege T Kavalali
articles.abstract: Chemical synapses are fundamental computational units of the nervous system that enable rapid and precise information transfer through the nanoscale organization of presynaptic and postsynaptic components. Despite hundreds of millions of years of animal evolution and extraordinary diversity in nervous system architectures, the core physiological principles of chemical synaptic transmission remain remarkably conserved. Studies across Drosophila melanogaster, zebrafish, Caenorhabditis elegans, frogs and mammals reveal recurring principles governing active-zone organization, synaptic vesicle exocytosis, calcium signalling and postsynaptic specialization. Here, we examine the evolution of chemical synapses across the animal kingdom, focusing on the relationship between molecular diversification, nanoscale organization and functional conservation. We propose that the evolutionary stability of synapses reflects, in part, a stringent biophysical constraint imposed by the requirements for rapid chemical communication. We further consider how these conserved synaptic operations are assembled into neural circuits of dramatically different complexities, as well as the ctenophore nervous system as a critical test case for distinguishing molecular conservation from architectural and functional convergence. Across species, the emerging picture is that evolution has adhered to conserving the geometry and organizational principles of chemical synapses more stringently than a precise molecular composition. Synapses thus represent stable yet adaptable information-processing architectures in which conserved nanoscale constraints coexist with molecular flexibility and extensive diversification of neural circuits.

articles.title: When intestinal protection does not improve performance: Biological effect vs. functional effect - why this discrepancy?
articles.authors: Regina Eloina Dos Santos Pereira, Michelle Barbosa Rosário, Isabelle Zanata Fabiane

articles.title: Food as Biological Information: A Testable Dietome Framework for Precision Nutrition and Whole-Food Meal Design.
articles.authors: Mohammad Nazrul Islam Bhuiyan
articles.abstract: Nutrition science has established the importance of energy, essential nutrients, dietary patterns, and food matrices, yet researchers often study these dimensions separately from the biological systems that transform and interpret a meal. This Perspective proposed the Dietome as a testable, systems-level description of food-derived inputs and the Informational Nutrition Framework (INF), comprising encoding, transmission, decoding, execution, and biological memory. The framework integrates sensory perception and eating behaviour with digestion, microbial metabolism, host signalling, and context-dependent responses. Its novelty is not the claim that food contains a literal code, but the proposal to connect food composition and structure to measurable, falsifiable predictions about meal-level responses. Evidence from personalized postprandial prediction, foodome network analysis, microbial short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-associated chromatin regulation, and computational diet modelling illustrates both opportunity and limitations. A worked meal example shows how to evaluate minimally processed foods and their combinations before considering engineered formulations. The Perspective also identifies sustainability, developmental nutrition, and food-allergy prevention as domains requiring cautious, evidence-specific application. Dietary microRNAs and long-term nutritional memory remain less established than conventional nutrient and microbial-metabolite pathways. The framework should therefore be judged by prospective validation, causal evidence, clinical utility, cultural acceptability, and environmental performance, not by terminology alone.
