The use of individually-calibrated Actiheart algorithms improved estimation of EEE during Bath University Rugby Union Shuttle Test (mean bias 4.5 ± 60.4 kcal) compared with individually-calibrated GENEActiv algorithms (mean bias 69.5 ± 86.6 kcal), and equivalence with indirect calorimetry was achieved, although substantial individual error remained (95% limits of agreement -113.9 to 122.8 kcal and intraclass correlation coefficients, .62 [.34 to .80]). Individualized Actiheart algorithms provided equivalent group-level estimates of EEE during intermittent high-intensity exercise, whereas neither Actiheart nor GENEActiv demonstrated acceptable validity or equivalence against the reference method for resistance training, suggesting Metabolic Equivalents of Task may be a more practical method of estimating EEE.

articles.title: Axial Complex of Deep-Sea Acorn Worm Quatuoralisia malakhovi (Hemichordata, Enteropneusta, Torquaratoridae).
articles.authors: Olga V Ezhova, Anastasiya I Lukinykh, Vladimir V Malakhov
articles.abstract: The axial complex (proboscis complex or heart-kidney) is well-studied for the shallow-living enteropneusts that burrow into the sediment and use the muscular proboscis as the primary locomotor organ. However, the deep-sea enteropneusts in the family Torquaratoridae are epibenthic surface-dwellers with a dispersed, poorly developed proboscis musculature. There is little data on the structure of their axial complex (AC). We have studied in detail the microscopic anatomy of the AC of three specimens of torquaratorid Quatuoralisia malakhovi Ezhova et Lukinykh, 2022. The proboscis of Q. malakhovi is widely fused with the collar along the entire dorsal side rather than being connected by a narrow stalk. The AC includes the buccal diverticulum (stomochord), pericardium, glomerulus (axial organ) and associated blood vessels, perihaemal coeloms, and proboscis skeletal elements. The latter are two separate symmetrical plates supporting the buccal diverticulum laterally. The buccal diverticulum is elongated in transverse direction and packed with large, vacuolated cells without a lumen. It is completely separated from the main course of the gut. The pericardium lies on the dorsal side of the buccal diverticulum. The heart is absent. The glomerulus consists of two symmetrical extensions separated by the confluence of the dorsal blood vessel. The latter is accompanied by the perihaemal coeloms and splits into several branches resembling the mouth of a river, which then flow into the glomerulus. Two buccal blood vessels with folded walls run from the sides of the glomerulus to the ventral blood vessel. A protocoelomic coelomopore is absent, however we found a pair of mesocoelomic coelomoducts and coelomopores. The torquaratorid AC demonstrates varying degrees of reduction. None of the previously studied species of Torquaratoridae possesses a complete set of AC components characteristic of shallow-living enteropneusts. Torquaratoridae are derived in terms of structure and composition of the AC compared to non-torquaratorid hemichordates.

articles.title: Biological Insights From the Osteohistology of a Nile Crocodile.
articles.authors: Ayanda Buso, Maria Eugenia Pereyra, Anusuya Chinsamy
articles.abstract: While long bones are mostly utlised for skeletochronology of extant and extinct vertebrates, among crocodilians, dermal bones have also been studied. However, there is a lack of a systematic and comprehensive study of the variation in osteohistology and skeletochronology of limb, axial, and dermal bones of extant crocodilians. Here, we undertake a comprehensive assessment of the histology of multiple postcranial elements of a single, captive adult Crocodylus niloticus (with approximately known age) to assess their utility for skeletochronology. We document the intraskeletal histological variability in the skeleton and show that despite the gastralia recording the highest number of growth rings, the radius, ulna, and fibula are more reliable for skeletochronology. We show substantial variation in the histology of the osteoderms depending on the plane of sectioning, as well as their location on the body of the crocodile. Additionally, we report that anteriorly sectioned dorsal osteoderms preserved the highest number of growth marks. Our study provides important information regarding intraskeletal variation in osteohistology and presents key information regarding the choice of skeletal elements for reliable life history reconstruction of C. niloticus.

articles.title: Functional Adaptations for Load-Bearing in a Dermal Bone: The Pectoral Fin Spine of the Russian Sturgeon (Huso Gueldenstaedtii).
articles.authors: Esteban Marroquín-Arroyave, Joshua Milgram
articles.abstract: Dermal bone, which forms a variety of skeletal structures and persists in a wide range of extant vertebrates, evolved prior to endochondral bone which forms all mammalian load-bearing long bones. Sturgeons (Acipenseriformes) are an early-diverging extant lineage of actinopterygians that retain prominent post-cranial dermal skeletal elements. They retain a long robust spine at the leading edge of the pectoral fin, called the pectoral fin spines (PFS). PFS are bone elements that are present in many extinct and extant species of non-tetrapod jawed fish. In this study, we characterize the structure (light, polarized, micro-computed tomography and scanning electron microscopy), composition (FTIR, TGA, BMD), and mechanical properties (3-point bending and microindentation) of the PFS of the Russian sturgeon (Huso gueldenstaedtii). The microstructure of the PFS is highly organized as it is formed by dermal osteonal bone and parallel fibered bone. Its microarchitecture, along with high material toughness, anisotropy, and substantial ash content, enables the PFS to bear loads and function in both locomotion and protection. In addition, we show an interconnected network of neurovascular canals and ornamentations, features also found in PFS of other non-tetrapod jawed fish. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that dermal bone can form structurally organized, mechanically competent load-bearing elements and provide new insights into PFSs in ray-finned fish.

articles.title: General Morphology and Neurite Projection Patterns of Supramedullary Neurons in the Cunner, Tautogolabrus adspersus.
articles.authors: Nick Hiza, Jun Liu, Tina Wong et al.
articles.abstract: Supramedullary neurons (SMNs) are located on the dorsal surface of the hindbrain and spinal cord in many adults of teleost fishes. Comparative morphological studies have revealed differences in SMN size, number and distribution among fishes. However, little information exists on the projection patterns of SMN neurites within the central nervous system. We focus on a single species of adult teleost fish, the cunner, Tautogolabrus adspersus, a fish that has 25-46 SMN somata aligned dorsally along the midline in the hindbrain and rostral third of the spinal cord. Light and transmission electron microscopic techniques provide new information on the general morphology of SMNs and Lucifer yellow filled SMNs reveal that these neurons are not morphologically homogeneous. Rather, four different morphotypes can be identified based on projection patterns of major neurites in the hindbrain and spinal cord wholemounts. The morphological variations suggest that some SMNs exit the brain exclusively through the first dorsal root while others exit the central nervous system through a dorsal root and the trigeminal nerve. Despite the remarkable size and accessibility of SMNs, their function(s) remains unknown. One proposed role of these cells is eliciting mucous secretion in response to skin abrasion from predation. Variation in projection patterns in the cunner provides a morphological framework from which to design electrophysiological studies to help reveal SMN function.

articles.title: The Evolutionary History of Early Ray-Finned Fishes (Pan-Actinopterygii).
articles.authors: Jack Stack
articles.abstract: One out of every two vertebrate species is a ray-finned fish (Actinopterygii). The ~380-million-year fossil record of ray-finned fishes provides a window into the evolutionary history of actinopterygian diversity in deep time. The actinopterygian fossil record shows that the ray-finned fish crown group (Actinopterygii) lived alongside speciose members of now extinct lineages, collectively referred to as early actinopterygians. I review the evolutionary history of early actinopterygians through deep time, including morphology, taxonomy, phylogeny, and the fossil record itself, to form a foundation for future research. Early actinopterygians are a paraphyletic assemblage of ~600 extinct species divided between ~22 named clades and the "palaeoniscoids," a taxonomic wastebasket comprised of hundreds of species. Although nearly a decade of phylogenetic research indicates that most early actinopterygians branch off the ray-finned fish stem group, their interrelationships are largely unresolved. Notable gaps in the record of early actinopterygians, which ranges from the Early Devonian to the Early Cretaceous, include a nearly non-existent Early Devonian record, an almost complete lack of Pennsylvanian-Middle Permian marine assemblages, a gap in the Middle Triassic record obscuring the start of a decline in early actinopterygian diversity, and a sparsely documented Jurassic record. We are poised to build a reliable systematic framework for early actinopterygians via novel methods for phylogenetic analysis, fossil imaging, and the increased connectivity of paleoichthyologyists around the globe. The promise of a reliable systematic framework for early actinopterygians is to better describe the entire history of Actinopterygii and actinopterygian macroevolution in deep time.

articles.title: Effectiveness of Neuromuscular Training and Training Load Management Interventions for Reducing Injury and Attrition in Tactical Recruits: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis.
articles.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
articles.authors: James R Mckee, Bruna M Tessarin, Vanessa Sutton et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To estimate the effectiveness of neuromuscular training and training load management interventions for reducing injury and attrition in tactical personnel (military, law enforcement, and other first responder organizations) during recruit training. DESIGN: Intervention systematic review with meta-analysis. LITERATURE SEARCH: PubMed, CINAHL Plus with full text, EMBASE, CENTRAL, Web of Science, and SPORTDiscus were searched from January 1, 2000, to March 14, 2025. STUDY SELECTION CRITERIA: Studies were included if they were quasi-experimental and randomized controlled trials examining neuromuscular training interventions conducted during or before commencing recruit training, or with training load management interventions, on medical-attention and time-loss injuries and attrition in tactical recruits aged at least 16 years. DATA SYNTHESIS: Inverse-variance, random-effects meta-analyses provided log odds ratio (Log OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). RESULTS: Thirty-three studies (n = 49,062 participants) were included, and outcomes were of very low-certainty. Neuromuscular training interventions delivered during recruit training reduced medical-attention injuries (Log OR = 0.520, 95% CI = 0.226 to 0.815), but not attrition (Log OR = 0.525, 95% CI = -0.292 to 1.342). Neuromuscular training interventions delivered before commencing recruit training did not reduce medical-attention injuries (Log OR = 0.487, 95% CI = -2.216 to 3.190) but could have significantly increased attrition (Log OR = -0.982, 95% CI = -1.874 to -0.090). Training load management interventions did not reduce medical-attention injuries (Log OR = 0.286, 95% CI = -0.183 to 0.755). CONCLUSION: Neuromuscular training interventions during recruit training may reduce medical-attention injury probability without increasing attrition. The lack of specificity and progressive overload for included interventions may have limited further protective effects against injury. Delivering neuromuscular training interventions before commencing recruit training may increase attrition during recruit training without affecting injury probability. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(10):642-656. Epub 18 August 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.14272.

articles.title: Portable Dynamometry Is Reliable for Measuring Knee and Ankle Strength in Daily Practice: Results From a Systematic Review With Meta-analysis and Evidence Gap Map Using the COSMIN Methodology.
articles.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
articles.authors: Rubén Gajardo-Burgos, Teresa Jaque de la Barra, Rodrigo Ramírez-Campillo et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To estimate the reliability and criterion validity of knee and ankle muscle strength measured using portable dynamometers. DESIGN: Systematic review with meta-analysis and evidence gap map. LITERATURE SEARCH: Systematic search of MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science from inception to April 2025. STUDY SELECTION CRITERIA: We included studies that evaluated reliability or criterion validity of portable dynamometers for measuring knee extensor/flexor or ankle dorsiflexor/plantarflexor/invertor/evertor isometric strength in uninjured people or people with a lower-limb musculoskeletal condition. DATA SYNTHESIS: We performed meta-analyses for each muscle group, position, and fixation method. Methodological quality was assessed using the COSMIN (COnsensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement INstruments) Risk of Bias tool. Certainty of evidence was graded using a modified GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluations) approach. RESULTS: We included 123 studies (n = 5042 participants); 113 studies were included in the meta-analysis. There was moderate- to high-certainty evidence of sufficient reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient ≥ 0.70) across most muscle groups, positions, and fixation methods. High-certainty evidence supported external fixation for assessing knee extensors/flexors and ankle plantarflexors. Evidence for criterion validity was sparse, and the certainty of evidence ranged from very low to high. There was high-certainty evidence of sufficient validity for knee extensor and flexor strength with external fixation in seated positions (r = 0.82-0.90). CONCLUSION: Portable dynamometers were sufficiently reliable for measuring isometric knee and ankle strength in clinical practice. The evidence for criterion validity was limited. Portable dynamometers should not yet be considered direct substitutes for isokinetic dynamometry. Reliability and validity estimates were consistent across uninjured and clinical populations. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(10):657-671. Epub 7 Jul 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.14091.

articles.title: Is Reduced Spinal Range of Motion a Prognostic Factor for Pain Intensity, Disability, and Global Recovery in People With Specific or Nonspecific Spinal Pain? A Systematic Review.
articles.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
articles.authors: Daniel Feller, Michela Bortoli, Adriano Rigo et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To determine if a reduced range of motion (ROM) of the spine was a prognostic factor for pain intensity, disability, and global recovery outcomes in patients with specific or nonspecific spinal pain. DESIGN: Prognostic factor systematic review. LITERATURE SEARCH: PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL were searched from inception to February 10, 2026. We also performed forward and backward citation tracking. STUDY SELECTION CRITERIA: Studies of adults with spinal pain where ROM was assessed as a prognostic factor were included. DATA SYNTHESIS: Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality in Prognostic Studies (QUIPS) tool. The certainty of evidence was evaluated with the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. Given heterogeneity in the results, a narrative synthesis was conducted. RESULTS: Thirty-seven studies were included: 11 of nonspecific acute low back pain (LBP), 11 of nonspecific chronic or unspecified-duration LBP, four of nonspecific chronic neck pain, two of lumbar spinal stenosis, eight of whiplash-associated disorders (WAD), and one of cervical myelopathy. All studies were rated as high risk of bias. Across conditions and follow-ups, findings were inconsistent. Most studies of acute and chronic LBP reported no clear association between reduced ROM and outcomes. Similar inconsistencies were observed for chronic neck pain, lumbar stenosis, WAD, and cervical myelopathy. When associations were found, they were often unadjusted and based on low-quality analyses. The certainty of the evidence was consistently very low. CONCLUSION: Due to the very low certainty of evidence, it is unclear whether reduced spinal ROM independently predicts pain, disability, and/or global recovery in people with spinal pain. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(10):672-688. Epub 6 Aug 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.13872.

articles.title: Not Just Faster Horses: Telerehabilitation as a Necessary Evolution in Physical Therapy.
articles.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
articles.authors: Miguel Farraj, Julien Lebleu, Bruno Bonnechère et al.
articles.abstract: SYNOPSIS: This editorial draws an analogy between the transition from "faster horses" to automobiles and the digital transition facing musculoskeletal physical therapy. Musculoskeletal rehabilitation has long emphasized face-to-face sessions; digital solutions such as telerehabilitation have often been perceived as alternatives to conventional care. However, increasing rehabilitation demands, persistent gaps between sessions, and the need for long-term patient support highlight the importance of rethinking how physical therapists deliver care. We argue that telerehabilitation should not replace physical therapists but rather extend their role through facilitating continuous monitoring, communication, education, and patient engagement. Successful implementation requires more than simply adopting new technologies-it requires clinicians to develop new skills, adapt professional habits, and integrate digital tools while preserving therapeutic relationships and patient-centered care. Just as innovation required moving beyond faster horses, the future of musculoskeletal physical therapy may depend on embracing new models of care rather than simply iterating on traditional approaches. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(10):624-626. Epub 28 Aug 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.14510.

articles.title: Female Soccer Players at High Risk of Injury Maintained Improved Knee Abduction Load 6 Months After Neuromuscular Training Program.
articles.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
articles.authors: Jeffrey B Taylor, Thomas J Hockenjos, Anh-Dung Nguyen et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To estimate immediate and long-term (retention) improvements in knee abduction moment (KAM) following a neuromuscular training (NMT) program with augmented biofeedback in individuals at high and low risk for injury. DESIGN: Secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial. METHODS: One hundred fifty adolescent female soccer players were enrolled in a 6-week NMT program and randomized to biofeedback training groups: NMT + Hip-focus (NMT+H), NMT + Knee-focus (NMT+K), or NMT with a sham biofeedback. NMT was completed 3 times each week with augmented biofeedback delivered once per week. Standard 3-dimensional motion analysis of a drop vertical jump over artificial turf with embedded force platforms was performed at baseline (PRE), immediately following training (POST), and 6 months post training (RET). Baseline measures of KAM were used to stratify participants into low- (n = 87, 12.7 ± 2.2 years, 153.0 ± 11.4 cm, 47.2 ± 11.8 kg) and high-risk (n = 44, 14.0 ± 1.8 years, 161.6 ± 5.8 cm, 53.5 ± 9.2 kg) groups, based on a previously determined cut point. A mixed-design analysis of variance with between-group factors of risk (high, low) and training group (NMT+H, NMT+K, NMT), and a repeated within-group factor of session (PRE, POST, RET) were used for the analysis. RESULTS: A significant interaction was identified between risk and session (P < .001). Within training groups, the high-risk group had a significant reduction in KAM from baseline to posttest, and from baseline to 6 months (PRE: -37.5 ± 9.0 N m; POST: -25.2 ± 11.4 N m; RET: -29.4 ± 14.5 N m). There were no changes in the low-risk group (PRE: -12.2 ± 6.2 N m; POST: -12.2 ± 7.6 N m; RET: -12.9 ± 8.7 N m). CONCLUSION: Female soccer players with knee biomechanics that put them at high risk for anterior cruciate ligament injury had improved KAM following an NMT program. The changes in KAM remained at 6 months after training. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(10):689-698. Epub 28 Aug 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.14125.

articles.title: Correction to 'Peripheral cholecystokinin promotes thermogenesis via vagal afferent signalling, hypothalamic oxytocin and sympathetic outflow to brown adipose tissue'.
Insights into Channelopathies and Sport: The Genotype-Positive/Phenotype-Negative Athlete from Molecular Diagnosis to Management.
articles.authors: Isabel Diebold, Franziska Hahn, Eimo Martens et al.
articles.abstract: Channelopathies, diseases with ion channel perturbations, are a major cause of sudden cardiac death in athletes. Advances in genetic testing have identified a growing population of athletes carrying (likely) pathogenic variants in cardiac ion channel genes who remain phenotypically silent. These genotype-positive/phenotype-negative (G+/P-) individuals present a distinct clinical challenge. Standard preparticipation screening, designed around phenotypic findings, provides little guidance for their management. A critical gap exists in providing prognostic guidance based on the involved gene, specific variants, and its molecular consequences. Beyond a critical review of existing literature, we provide a mechanistically anchored framework for variant-specific arrhythmic risk stratification across the major channelopathy genes. For each gene, we translate molecular pathophysiology into clinically actionable risk profiles and examine how exercise-specific triggers, including adrenergic surge, electrolyte shifts, and sympathovagal imbalance, interact with the underlying molecular substrate to modulate arrhythmic vulnerability. Standard diagnostic tools ranging from electro- and echocardiography, exercise stress testing, and pharmacological provocation to emerging modalities such as electroanatomic mapping and magnetocardiography are evaluated for their capacity to unmask subclinical disease and refine sports eligibility decisions. The case for an interdisciplinary sports-cardio-genetic board is made alongside a call for international collaborative registries, as existing evidence in G+/P- athletes is largely absent. The integration of artificial intelligence and telemonitoring into longitudinal athletic surveillance is discussed as a pragmatic strategy for early phenotype detection. Ultimately, guidance for the G+/P- athlete rests on a thorough understanding of the causative genetic variant and its pathophysiological consequences.

articles.title: How Effective is Stretching for Injury Prevention? A Large-Scale Systematic Review with Meta-analysis.
articles.authors: José Afonso, Ricardo Martins, Rohit K Thapa et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sports injuries can impact athletes' availability, threaten their career, and have substantial financial impact. Stretching is commonly used as a prevention strategy. However, controversial evidence, methodological shortcomings, and substantial time elapsed since previous key data syntheses justify performing an updated systematic review. OBJECTIVE: Our goal was to assess the effects of stretching interventions on injury risk. METHODS: We followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. Eligible studies included humans performing stretching and at least one comparator group; sports-related injury data were required. Studies were identified from six electronic databases (CINAHL Complete, Embase, PubMed, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science), reference lists, citation tracking, and consultation with external experts. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane tools. Raw injury data were used to assess odds ratios (OR), with OR < 1 meaning a preventive effect for stretching. Results were presented with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and prediction intervals (PIs). An inverse-variance random-effects model was employed using the DerSimonian and Laird estimator. Certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. RESULTS: Over 300,000 records were screened, with 19 studies fulfilling the eligibility criteria (> 9000 participants, > 80% male, age range 14-59 years), of which 15 were used for the meta-analyses. Interventions lasted 4-24 weeks and mostly implemented static unassisted stretching with varying volumes. Half the studies used passive controls, and half used diverse active comparators. Risk of bias was high for ~90% of randomized trials and serious for all non-randomized trials. No injury prevention effect was detected for stretching versus all other comparators (k = 15, n = 9,002; OR = 0.945, p = 0.396, 95% CI 0.828-1.078, 95% PI 0.773-1.155), passive controls (k = 10, n = 6273; OR = 0.923, p = 0.209, 95% CI 0.814-1.046, 95% PI 0.796-1.069), or active controls (k = 6, n = 2744; OR = 1.190, p = 0.312, 95% CI 0.849-1.667, 95% PI 0.738-1.919). Likewise, no injury prevention effect was found for muscle, tendon, and ligament/joint capsule injury risk, or across 19 sensitivity analyses, 3 subgroup analyses, and 3 secondary analyses. GRADE denoted very low certainty of evidence for all outcomes except bone injury risk (low certainty). CONCLUSIONS: Despite the very low to low certainty of evidence as per GRADE judgments, the data consistently showed no chronic effect of stretching on injury risk across multiple analyses. No study assessed the acute effects of stretching on injury risk. Given the studied samples, these conclusions apply mostly to male participants aged 14-60 years performing static unassisted stretching, with little to no information about other populations or interventions. There is virtually no research using sport-specific stretching exercises. Several other caveats are discussed, as well as implications for practice, policy-making and future research. REGISTRATION: PROSPERO: CRD42024616532. OSF project ( https://osf.io/umj8h/ ) and registration ( https://osf.io/ybdvw ).

articles.title: Force and Power Testing in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Literature: A Scoping Review.
articles.authors: Alessandro Compagnin, Francesco Della Villa, Stefano Di Paolo et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Force and power testing has been recognised as a key aspect of anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) rehabilitation. However, a literature synthesis is required to examine how these physical characteristics have been assessed due to pronounced heterogeneity in the methods used. OBJECTIVES: To synthesise and describe the existing literature on force and power testing post-ACLR. METHODS: A scoping review of the electronic databases MEDLINE (PubMed), SPORTDiscus, Cochrane Library and PEDro was conducted including studies adopting at least one force or power test in patients post-ACLR. The search methodology followed the Joanna Briggs Institute Manual for evidence synthesis and included the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). RESULTS: In total, 1625 studies fulfilled the inclusion criteria. Seven main device categories were identified, with different rates of implementation over the years (1981-2023) and throughout the recovery process: (1) isokinetic dynamometry (IKD; 64.9%), (2) jump (without force platform; 32.2%), (3) force platform (28.0%), (4) traditional gym equipment and bodyweight exercises (6.2%), (5) hand-held dynamometry (4.0%), (6) manual muscle testing (1.5%) and (7) other devices (5.5%). Studies used 1.42 ± 0.62 devices, with 45 different combinations recorded. Various tests were conducted using different devices, ranging from 8 to 72 recorded tests per category. Only force plate assessments showed a linear increment in implementation from the surgical procedure (r = 0.86, p = 0.012). CONCLUSIONS: Significant heterogeneity in assessment device selection, metrics analysed, test implementation and protocols was observed. Most studies included a single device category to examine force and power characteristics of patients post-ACLR. The IKD remains the most adopted testing device in research, but current assessment practices are more varied than in the past.

articles.title: Evaluating the effects of changes in minute ventilation and the partial pressure of end-tidal carbon dioxide on the diaphragm electromyogram during voluntary hyperpnoea.
articles.authors: Jack R Dunsford, Leah M Mann, Paolo B Dominelli et al.
articles.abstract: The diaphragm electromyogram (EMGDIA) is commonly used as a proxy for inspiratory neural drive (IND) based on correlative evidence; however, robust experimental evidence supporting its use is lacking. To determine the effects of independent changes in minute ventilation ( V ̇ E ) and the partial pressure of end-tidal carbon dioxide ( P ETC O 2 ) on EMGDIA. n = 10 healthy adults (20-40 years; n = 5 males, n = 5 females) completed spirometry, a 10-min rest period and a series of hyperpnoea trials at three standardized levels of V ̇ E by having participants breathe according to tidal volume (VT) and breathing frequency (FB) targets. Within each level of V ̇ E , P ETC O 2 was set to -5, +0 or +5 mmHg relative to resting P ETC O 2 using dynamic end-tidal forcing. Trials were performed in a quasi-randomized, single-blind manner. EMGDIA was assessed using an intraoesophageal catheter, standard ventilatory and gas exchange variables were collected, and the perception of dyspnoea intensity was assessed using the Borg category-ratio 0-10 scale. EMGDIA increased significantly with V ̇ E (P < 0.001) but was unaffected by changes in P ETC O 2 (P = 0.320). Moreover, EMGDIA was significantly associated with V ̇ E , the work of breathing, and the pressure-time product of the diaphragm (R2 = 0.762-0.824; all P < 0.001), but not P ETC O 2 (R2 = 0.529; P = 0.947). Dyspnoea perception increased significantly with V ̇ E (P < 0.001) and P ETC O 2 (P < 0.001). During voluntary hyperpnoea involving manipulations of P ETC O 2 across a physiological range observed with exercise (i.e., 5 mmHg below and above resting P ETC O 2 ), EMGDIA reflects the mechanical ventilatory output of IND rather than changes in the drive to breathe due to variations in P ETC O 2 .

articles.title: CetaSpiroX12: An ultrasonic spirometer to investigate respiratory physiology and mechanics in cetaceans.
articles.authors: Elmar Ottiger, Christian Buess, Felix Daners et al.
articles.abstract: Understanding respiratory physiology in species with exceptionally high respiratory flow, such as cetaceans, requires accurate tools capable of capturing rapid and turbulent airflow. Traditional methods, including Fleisch-type pneumotachographs, are limited by dependence on laminar flow within the flow sensor, sensitivity to environmental conditions, water droplets and restricted measurement ranges, leaving gaps in our knowledge of comparative respiratory mechanics. To address this, we developed and validated a novel ultrasonic spirometer, the CetaSpiroX12, which integrates 12 commercially available human spirometry sensors into a radial manifold to extend the measurable flow range. Bench tests confirmed individual sensor performance to 16 L s-1 and accurate summation of the 12 sensors during assembled-system testing at total flows up to 90 L s-1. The parallel sensor configuration provides a theoretical combined measurement capacity of 192 L s-1, provided that flow through each individual sensor remains within its validated range. Together, these results indicate that the CetaSpiroX12 provides accurate flow measurements across a wide range of respiratory flows, overcoming long-standing limitations of previous approaches. Beyond advancing our understanding of cetacean ventilatory physiology and mechanics, this technology has broader applications for both clinical health assessment in managed populations and non-invasive respiratory studies in the wild. Moreover, the modular manifold design can be adapted to other large marine and terrestrial mammals, enabling comparative investigations into respiratory strategies across species with high ventilatory demands.

articles.title: Deciphering the role of brainstem vestibular-related inhibitory networks in shaping postural reflexes in the Xenopus tadpole.
articles.authors: Léandre Lavenu, Mathilde Pain, Gabriel Barrios et al.
articles.abstract: Brainstem vestibulospinal (VS) nuclei generate excitatory commands in response to multi-modality sensory inputs, to activate specific spinal networks and generate adapted postural reflexes. Comparably organized in all species, bilaterally-distributed excitatory VS nuclei with both ipsi- and contralateral projections alone fail to explain the mostly unilateral reflex responses typically observed. Consequently, we investigated the role of central vestibular inhibitory circuits in the functional organization of vestibular-driven postural reflexes. Then, using a larval Xenopus brainstem/spinal cord in vitro preparation, we show that the spinal responses evoked by galvanic vestibular stimulation are shaped by both commissural and local inhibitory brainstem networks. We further show that a complex interaction between GABAergic and glycinergic inhibitory networks regulate VS neuron excitability and, consequently, the expression of the spinal response. Our data reveal that, although excitatory VS neurons execute the neural score, inhibitory neurons in the central vestibular system co-ordinate and modulate the overall performance. KEY POINTS: Excitatory vestibulospinal (VS) pathways alone fail to explain reflex postural adjustments. VS neurons receive massive GABA and glycine inputs, both from local and commissural vestibular-related brainstem neurons. Perturbing either inhibitory influence specifically modulates vestibular-evoked spinal reflexes, and commissural integrity is mandatory for proper VS-evoked reflex expression. Both local and commissural neurons regulate VS excitability via complex inhibitory interactions. Our study demonstrates the critical role of brainstem vestibular-related inhibitory circuits in shaping spinal postural responses.

articles.title: Sex and respiratory muscle efficiency are associated with costal diaphragm perfusion relative to respiratory work during exercise hyperpnoea.
articles.authors: Madison M Coyle, Megan L Lance, Madison J Gorsline et al.
articles.abstract: Females experience greater work of breathing (WOB) and oxygen cost of respiration ( V ̇ O 2 RM) than males at moderate-to-high ventilations, primarily due to smaller airways and lungs. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) provides an index of relative costal diaphragm microvascular perfusion ( Q ̇ di), allowing the examination of whether the Q ̇ di-WOB relationship differs by sex and is associated with estimated respiratory muscle efficiency (EffRM). We hypothesized that the Q ̇ di-WOB relationship would be steeper in females, and that individual Q ̇ di-WOB slopes would be inversely associated with estimated EffRM. Seventeen healthy adults (27 ± 5 years; 9 females) completed an incremental maximal cycle exercise test and, on a separate day, voluntary hyperpnoea at 45%, 60%, 75% and 100% of maximum exercise ventilation. Exercise-derived breathing patterns and respiratory mechanics were replicated. Oesophageal pressure-volume loops quantified WOB. V ̇ O 2 RM was estimated from whole-body oxygen uptake, and EffRM was calculated as WOB divided by estimated respiratory metabolic energy expenditure. Relative microvascular perfusion within the sampled costal diaphragm region was estimated using CEUS. The relationships between the CEUS-derived Q ̇ di (min-1) and inspiratory work and WOB (kJ min-1) were steeper in females by +83 ± 37 kJ-1 (P = 0.0367) and +63 ± 25 kJ-1 (P = 0.0203), respectively. The Q ̇ di- V ̇ O 2 RM relationship did not differ by sex (P = 0.581). Individual Q ̇ di-WOB slopes were inversely associated with estimated EffRM (slope: -12.6 ± 5.8 kJ-1%-1, r = -0.49, P = 0.0476). Thus, relative costal diaphragm perfusion increased with respiratory mechanical demand, and the perfusion-work relationship differed by sex and was associated with estimated EffRM. KEY POINTS: Females exhibit a greater work of breathing and oxygen cost of breathing than males during moderate-to-high ventilatory exercise, but whether this is accompanied by differences in human costal diaphragm perfusion was unknown. We used contrast-enhanced ultrasound to estimate relative microvascular perfusion within the medial costal diaphragm during voluntary hyperpnoea that closely replicated breathing patterns attained during exercise. Costal diaphragm perfusion increased proportionally with respiratory muscle work, indicating that perfusion of the sampled diaphragm increased in relation to the overall mechanical demand of ventilation. Females exhibited a steeper costal diaphragm perfusion-work of breathing relationship than males. Across participants, a steeper perfusion-work relationship was associated with lower estimated respiratory muscle efficiency. These findings provide new insight into the associations of sex and estimated respiratory muscle efficiency with costal diaphragm perfusion during high ventilatory demand.

articles.title: Effects of High-Intensity Interval Training Combined With Mango Leaf Extract Supplementation on Inflammatory Biomarkers in Overweight and Obese Men: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.journal: International journal of sport nutrition and exercise metabolism
articles.authors: Fatemeh Omidali, Fatemeh Shabkhiz, Ali Akbarnejad
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Chronic low-grade inflammation is a key factor in obesity-related metabolic disorders. This study examined the effects of an 8-week whole-body high-intensity interval training program combined with mango leaf extract (ME) supplementation on inflammatory biomarkers in sedentary overweight and obese men. METHODS: Forty sedentary men (age 25-40 years; body mass index ≥ 25 kg/m2) were randomly assigned to control, exercise plus placebo, ME, or exercise plus ME. WB-HIIT was performed three times weekly for 8 weeks. The ME and placebo groups received 500 mg twice daily (1,000 mg/day). Fasting blood samples were collected pre- and postintervention, and serum interleukin-6, interleukin-13, calprotectin, and interleukin-1 receptor antagonist were analyzed using ELISA. Data were analyzed using analysis of covariance adjusted for baseline values (p < .05). RESULTS: Significant between-group differences were observed for interleukin-6 and calprotectin (p < .001), with the exercise plus ME group showing the greatest reductions compared with all other groups. No significant difference was found for interleukin-13 (p = .073). Interleukin-1 receptor antagonist showed a significant Time × Group interaction, although no significant pairwise differences were detected. Body weight, body mass index, and waist circumference improved significantly in both exercise groups compared with control (p < .05), whereas no changes were observed in the ME group. CONCLUSION: Whole-body high-intensity interval training combined with mango leaf extract supplementation may enhance anti-inflammatory adaptations in overweight and obese men. This combination may represent a promising nonpharmacological strategy for attenuating obesity-related low-grade inflammation.

articles.title: Ten Years of Training in a Male World-Class 800-1500 m Swimmer.
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: Espen Tønnessen, Ivar Idsøe Flaten, Øyvind Sandbakk et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To investigate the training process of a world-class 800- to 1500-m swimmer and identify key characteristics and differences between successful and less successful competitive seasons. METHODS: A mixed-methods case study design was used to capture quantitative and qualitative aspects of the training process. Data were collected through (1) 10 years of training logs (ages 19-28); (2) in-depth semistructured interviews with the swimmer, his club coach, and national team head coach; and (3) systematic quality assurance through negotiation among researchers and key informants. RESULTS: Performance improved gradually until 23 to 24 years of age before slightly declining. Annual training volume ranged from ∼1000 to ∼1380 hours per year, with swimming accounting for ∼80% of total training time in most seasons (2700-3700 km·y-1), including extensive long-course, stroke-specific training. The swimmer followed a traditional periodization model with 3 macrocycles annually, characterized by high volumes of low-intensity training during preparation and increased intensity with reduced volume approaching competition. A later shift toward more zone 2 training at the expense of zone 1 and reduced long-course exposure coincided with the performance decline in his mid-twenties. Successful seasons were characterized by high quality in the holistic training process, including strong motivation and structured recovery, whereas less successful seasons were marked by slightly weaker recovery habits, and declining motivation and self-confidence. CONCLUSION: This study provides novel information regarding the training process for a world-class long-distance swimmer, including differences between successful and less successful seasons. These data may serve as a framework for practitioners aiming to optimize long-term performance development.

articles.title: Context-Dependent Mechanisms of Striated Muscle Dysfunction.
articles.authors: Orlando Laitano, Aneesha Dasgupta, Tyler J Kirby et al.

articles.title: Evolution of cranial architecture and inter-element articulations in salamanders of the family Salamandridae.
articles.authors: Ana Ivanović, Aleksandar Urošević, Tijana Vučić et al.
articles.abstract: Mobility of skull elements relative to the braincase is a widespread vertebrate trait with major consequences for feeding performance, though its macroevolutionary dynamics remain poorly understood in amphibians. Using high-resolution micro-CT data from 277 specimens representing 54 species across 18 salamandrid genera (family Salamandridae), we quantified variation in 10 cranial articulations over four skull regions and constructed a composite cranial articulation index. The articulation index varied substantially across species, ranging from largely separated (open) to fully consolidated (fused) articulations. Comparative analyses revealed that articulations of the snout and the skull roof evolved as an integrated module, whereas palatal and suspensorial articulations followed independent evolutionary trajectories, indicating a mosaic pattern of evolution in cranial articulation. Most articulations and the composite articulation index were best explained by Ornstein-Uhlenbeck models, consistent with evolution toward constrained or lineage-specific optima. We tested relationships between cranial articulation and skull size, skull robustness (bone thickness), and ecological preferences (length of the aquatic period). Contrary to expectations, our results indicate that cranial articulation in Salamandridae evolved as a modular system independent of these traits. These findings suggest that salamandrid cranial architecture is maintained near a structural optimum within a wider spectrum presumably governed by the complex synergy of developmental, phylogenetic, and ecological constraints.

articles.title: Always stay close to your mom.
articles.authors: Tim D Smith

articles.title: Association of Mediterranean-DASH intervention for neurodegenerative delay (MIND) diet with cognition and total and cardiovascular mortality: results from the HAPIEE cohort.
articles.authors: Martin Ming Him Wong, Yim Ching Yau, Magda Kozela et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay (MIND) dietary pattern, developed to slow cognitive decline, has been linked to cardiometabolic benefits and lower mortality. Its associations with cognition and mortality have not been studied in Eastern European populations. This study aimed to assess the relationship between MIND diet, cognition and mortality in Eastern European adults. METHODS: Data from 15,427 adults aged 45-69 years at baseline in the Czech and Polish cohorts of the Health, Alcohol and Psychosocial factors in Eastern Europe prospective cohort were analyzed. Baseline MIND diet scores (range 0-15), derived from validated food frequency questionnaires, were classified into three groups: low (<6), moderate (6-7), and high (>7). Trained nurses assessed cognitive domains at baseline. Deaths were ascertained via national registries. Multivariable regressions estimated the MIND diet-mortality and MIND diet-cognition associations, adjusting for sociodemographic and lifestyle characteristics. RESULTS: Over about 20 years of follow-up, 3,792 deaths occurred. After controlling for age and sex, MIND diet adherence was associated with lower total and CVD mortality and better cognitive outcomes. However, after full adjustment, the associations were no longer significant (high vs low adherence for all-cause mortality: HR = 1.01, 95%CI:0.93-1.10; for CVD mortality: HR = 1.01, 95%CI:0.88-1.16), and only the positive association with verbal fluency remained significant (high vs low: coefficient 0.058, SE 0.024, p = 0.015). CONCLUSION: This study of MIND diet in Central and Eastern European cohort did not find clear evidence on mortality, but the results on cognition, particularly verbal fluency, were generally consistent with the literature.

articles.title: Cyanocobalamin supplementation strategies in patients with Crohn's disease and terminal ileal resection in clinical practice.
articles.authors: Anna Pèlach, Margalida Calafat, Sofia Dall'Oglio et al.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Vitamin B12 (B12) is absorbed at the terminal ileum. Patients with Crohn's disease (CD) resection of the terminal ileum (RTI) are at risk of B12 deficiency. No standard recommendations on the monitoring and supplementation of B12 after non-extensive RTI are available. Our aims were to describe B12 supplementation modalities in clinical practice in patients with CD and RTI and to identify potential factors associated with B12 deficiency in this population. METHODS: Retrospective, single-centre study that included patients with CD who underwent RTI between January 2008 and October 2022. B12 levels, supplementation, indication and route of administration after RTI were recorded. RESULTS: One hundred and ninety-seven patients were included. Thirteen (7%) patients were on B12 supplementation prior to RTI. Seventy-nine patients (40%) were not supplemented and did not develop B12 deficiency. B12 supplementation was prescribed for 60% of patients during follow-up (6% of whom were already supplemented before surgery), 53% preventively after surgery and 47% after B12 deficiency. Intramuscular administration was the most common (97%, mainly monthly), and oral administration was limited (11%, mainly weekly). During follow-up, changes to the B12 supplementation occurred in 36% (mainly prolonging the interval of intramuscular administration). RTI length over 20 cm (OR 1.944, 95% CI 1.019-3.709; P = 0.042) was the only factor associated with developing B12 deficiency following surgery. CONCLUSIONS: B12 supplementation in patients with CD and RTI is heterogeneous. Preventive supplementation might be driven by ileal resection length, being recommended in those greater than 20 cm. Recommendations on supplementation and monitoring are needed to optimize clinical practice.

articles.title: A Digital Ultrasonic Height Measurement Device for Children Aged Under Five Years show high reliability yet variable accuracy.
articles.authors: Ms Shan Huang, Prof Caroline Se Homer, Dr Joel Conkle et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Accurate height measurement is essential for monitoring child growth. OBJECTIVE: Our aim was to assess the reliability and accuracy of a handheld ultrasonic measurement device compared with a standard measurement board METHODS: We used a cross-sectional methods-comparison study design with experts measuring n=57 children aged 0-5 years in metropolitan Melbourne, Australia. The ultrasonic device was our index test and the measurement board, our reference test. RESULTS: The ultrasonic device demonstrated a similar reliability to the board with a technical error of measurement (TEM) of 0.25cm (95%CI: 0.22, 0.28cm) and 0.19cm (95%CI: 0.17, 0.22) respectively, both within current standards. F-test ratios (ultrasonic vs. board) for intra-measurer TEMs were higher for children ≤2 years at 1.39 (95% CI: 1.03, 1.87; p=0.03) than children >2 years at 1.20 (95%CI: 0.94, 1.51; p=0.14). The ultrasonic device measured children slightly taller than the board (mean difference 0.20 cm; 95% CI: 0.02, 0.38; SD=0.67; p<0.01), with a larger difference in older children who were measured standing (0.35 cm; p=0.01). The Bland Altman 95% limits of agreement ranged from -1.13cm to 1.53cm, demonstrating variance in the measurements between the different tools. CONCLUSION: We found that the ultrasonic device showed high reliability for children under 5 years when compared to the board, though accuracy was variable, with greater bias found in older children. Further testing is required to identify the source of inaccuracies and also evaluate reliability in other contexts.

articles.title: US legal definitions of ultra-processed food depart from the research construct in different ways.
articles.authors: Jimmy Chun Yu Louie
articles.abstract: Definitions of ultra-processed food (UPF) are multiplying in US law and policy. California enacted a statutory definition in 2025, two Senate bills introduced in 2026 propose federal labeling triggers, and in August 2026 a white paper proposing a federal definition was submitted for interagency review. The white paper is a non-binding notice, and its text has not been released. It is nonetheless likely to become a reference point for states, retailers and researchers. Most evidence on UPF and health comes from studies in which trained coders assigned foods to Nova group 4 and exposure was expressed as the dietary share of those foods. A legal definition must instead classify individual products from ingredient lists, without case-by-case expert judgment. This Perspective proposes three tests for that translation. Construct preservation asks whether the legal rule selects the same products as the research classification. Dimensional consistency asks whether products leave the regulated category on the same basis on which they enter it. Evaluability asks whether changes in regulatory status can be read as changes in the exposure that the evidence links to health outcomes. The tests are applied to the two definitions that are fully specified in the public record. The operational definition recommended by the Healthy Eating Research expert panel appears to track Nova at the level of the food supply but lacks product-level validation, and its nutrient-based exemption fails the dimensional consistency test. California's definition satisfies dimensional consistency by design but defines a narrower category than the one examined in most UPF research. The tests do not presuppose any position on Nova and can be applied to the federal text once it is released.

articles.title: Motivational Interviewing for Nutrition Counseling among Athletes: A Systematic Review.
articles.authors: Bailee Cooper, Madison Lazirko
articles.abstract: Athletes can be placed into four unique categories, based on physical intensity. Athletic status impacts the amount time spent on the sport; everyone should be assessed for dietary intake. Registered dietitian nutritionists utilize a standard clinical practice to evaluate goals for athletes during counseling sessions. There are different types of nutrition counseling techniques which can be applied, but there is lacking evidence for Motivational Interviewing (MI). This systematic review explores how MI can impact sports nutrition and what evidence there is to support positive nutrition outcomes. A Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses method was performed in October 2026. The databases for the study included PubMed, Scopus, Science Direct, Cochrane Reviews and web-based search. Inclusion criteria was MI for nutrition counseling, athletes/recreational individuals, sports, for all ages and genders. There were an original search of 894 in total and then this was narrowed down to 9 studies by two researchers using Rayyan software. The RoB 2.0 was used to assess randomized clinical trial risk of bias and the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool was used to check quality of all the studies in the final review. While all the studies included MI during the nutrition intervention sessions, only one study used MI as the only counseling technique. The duration of the intervention was 4 weeks to 12 months. The most common quality of the studies were three stars and there were two studies which had a high risk of bias. MI as a counseling technique does illustrate promising results for positive nutrition outcomes, especially among athletes who struggle with an eating disorder and/or Relative Energy Deficiency Syndrome. Future studies with higher quality should focus on male team sports, (ie. contact and court sports) and randomized control trial design for MI as a technique for nutrition counseling. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: OSF, registration DOI Identifier 10.17605/OSF.IO/H63NV.

articles.title: Low-Carbohydrate, Animal-Centered Diets and Plant-Based Diets Exert Opposing Effects on Cardiometabolic Diseases.
articles.authors: Rami S Najjar
articles.abstract: Low-carbohydrate, animal-centered (LCAC) diets are promoted for the prevention and treatment of type 2 diabetes (T2D) and cardiovascular disease (CVD) because randomized trials have shown short-term reductions in select risk factors, such as body weight, triglycerides, and glycated hemoglobin. However, controlled feeding studies have shown increases in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), apolipoprotein B, and circulating free fatty acids with LCAC diets. Importantly, LCAC diets can also drive lipotoxicity and inflammation. These latter pathological biochemical effects directly act on pathways involved in the development of T2D and CVD. In contrast, high-carbohydrate, unrefined plant-based diets in these conditions reduce insulin requirements even without weight loss, lower blood pressure and medication use, and improve atherogenic lipoproteins and inflammation. Meta-analyses of randomized trials demonstrate reductions in LDL-C, apolipoprotein B, and glycated hemoglobin with vegetarian or vegan diets. Further, plant-based dietary interventions have also shown regression of coronary atherosclerosis and improvements in myocardial perfusion and cardiac function, an effect absent from LCAC diet literature. Thus, public health efforts aimed at the prevention and treatment of T2D and CVD should continue to focus on improving the quantity and quality of plant foods consumed rather than carbohydrate restriction alone.

articles.title: Fermented Foods Target Multiple Hallmarks of Aging to Promote Healthy Longevity.
articles.authors: Parijat Hazarika, Ipsah Akhtar, Mojibur R Khan
articles.abstract: Aging is associated with progressive physiological decline driven by chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, immune dysfunction, and gut microbial dysbiosis, and fermented foods contain probiotics and bioactive metabolites that may beneficially influence these processes. This narrative review summarizes evidence on fermented foods and mechanisms associated with healthy aging, particularly gut microbiota composition, immune function, oxidative stress, and inflammation, while explicitly distinguishing findings from cell-based (in vitro) systems, animal (in vivo) models, and human participants. Each finding is labeled by its evidence tier so the strength and translational relevance of the data can be judged transparently. In vitro studies using cultured cells, including senescent fibroblasts, immune cells, and cancer cell lines, show that fermentation-derived metabolites can activate antioxidant, autophagic, and anti-inflammatory signaling pathways, and studies in rodent models, principally aged mice, show that fermented foods and their metabolites can improve mitochondrial function, reduce inflammatory markers, and reshape the gut microbiota. Human observational and interventional studies indicate that regular consumption of fermented foods is associated with increased gut microbial diversity, reduced circulating inflammatory markers, and, in some cohorts, longer leukocyte telomere length, although direct human evidence for many of the mechanisms identified in cell-based and animal work remains limited, a gap highlighted throughout the review. Taken together, fermented foods show potential as accessible dietary interventions for promoting healthy aging, but mechanistic detail is derived largely from cell-based and animal studies, whereas human data remain mostly observational or limited to biomarker-level endpoints, and confirmation through well-controlled human trials is still needed. The reviewed literature does not establish a minimum effective daily intake for any fermented food, and questions of portion size, variety, cultural/geographic availability, and safety of sustained daily consumption (e.g., sodium and biogenic amine content) remain priorities for future research.

articles.title: Adding Locally Available Foods to SQ-LNS Increased Nutrient Intake but Not the Proportion of Infants Meeting Nutrient Requirements in Rural Zimbabwe: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.authors: Laura E Smith, Rachel Makasi, Alice Tengende et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) improve linear growth but may not close all nutrient gaps. Whether locally available foods can help meet these gaps remains uncertain. OBJECTIVE: Compare infant and young child feeding (IYCF) (ground maize+SQ-LNS) versus "IYCF-plus" (pro-vitamin A maize, SQ-LNS, moringa, egg and sugar beans) on the proportion of infants meeting nutrient requirements. METHODS: Infants in rural Zimbabwe were randomized to IYCF or IYCF-plus from age 6mo. The primary outcome was the proportion meeting energy requirements at age 9mo using 24-hour dietary recalls. Secondary outcomes were proportion of children meeting protein, iron, zinc, and folate intakes, plus anthropometric indices and hemoglobin concentration. Tertiary outcomes were protein-quality indicators. Analyses used intention-to-treat mixed-effects logistic and linear regression. RESULTS: Among 192 infants (95 IYCF; 97 IYCF-plus), 9 exited and 2 died. At 9 months, 92.2% (95% CI 87.2, 97.2) in the IYCF arm and 92.5% (95% CI 87.9, 97.0) in the IYCF-plus arm met energy requirements (adjusted OR 1.0; 95% CI 0.3, 3.3). Protein adequacy was 100.0% versus 99.3%; iron adequacy was 84.4% versus 88.8%; zinc adequacy was 87.0% versus 93.0%; and folate adequacy was 97.7% versus 96.0%. Anthropometry and haemoglobin concentration showed no evidence of differences: LAZ mean difference -0.0 (95% CI -0.3, 0.2); WAZ -0.1 (-0.4, 0.2); WLZ -0.2 (-0.5, 0.2); haemoglobin concentration -0.0 (-0.3, 0.3). Protein-quality indicators were higher in the IYCF-plus arm than in the IYCF arm, including available protein (mean difference 2.3 g/kg; 95% CI 1.8, 2.8), Digestible Indispensable Amino Acid Score (DIAAS) (mean difference 79.7; 95% CI 68.9, 90.5), and all available amino acids. CONCLUSIONS: IYCF-plus using locally available foods plus SQ-LNS did not improve the proportion of infants meeting nutrient requirements more than SQ-LNS+maize alone, but improved protein quality. TRIAL REGISTRATION: clinicaltrials.gov NCT04874688.

articles.title: Effects of Exercise on Symptom Burden During Cancer Treatment: Real-World Evidence from a Statewide Exercise Oncology Program.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Hao Luo, Robert U Newton, Dennis R Taaffe et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Cancer treatment often exacerbates symptoms such as fatigue, insomnia, and gastrointestinal disturbances. This study aimed to provide real-world evidence of exercise on symptom control in patients undergoing cancer treatment. METHODS: The analysis included patients undergoing cancer treatment, who participated in the three-month Life Now Exercise oncology program across 13 community-based sites in Western Australia. Individually tailored resistance, aerobic, and flexibility exercises at a moderate-to-high intensity were delivered twice per week in a group format, supervised by accredited exercise physiologists. Symptom burden was assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and six months post-intervention using the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality-of-Life Core module (EORTC QLQ-C30) and the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Fatigue scale (FACIT-F). RESULTS: Of 328 participants, 63% were aged under 65 years, 56% had breast cancer, 86% had localised disease, and 60% were undergoing hormonal therapy with/without additional radiotherapy and other systemic therapies. Improvements were observed at post-intervention in fatigue (EORTC: -3.3 [95% CI -5.5 to -1.1]; FACIT-F: 1.7 [95% CI 0.7 to 2.7]), insomnia (-3.6 [95% CI -6.9 to -0.3]), appetite loss (-3.2 [95% CI -5.9 to -0.5]), and financial difficulties (-2.8 [95% CI -5.5 to -0.1]), with most improvements sustained at six months post-intervention. Responses varied across breast, digestive, and genitourinary cancer subgroups and were associated with diverse demographic and clinical factors. However, meaningful improvements were consistently observed in patients with clinically relevant symptoms at baseline. CONCLUSIONS: Multimodal exercise at a moderate-to-high intensity is a promising non-pharmaceutical intervention for reducing symptom burden during cancer treatment. Similar exercise programs may be considered during cancer treatment for symptom control.

articles.title: Anatomical Handling Properties of Costal and Auricular Cartilage in Fresh-frozen Cadaveric Models for Revision Rhinoplasty.
articles.authors: Francesca Russo, Sebastiano Grimaldi, Giuseppe Esposito et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Revision rhinoplasty is among the most technically demanding procedures in facial surgery, requiring mastery of complex anatomy, advanced surgical skills, and proficiency in structural grafting. Cadaveric dissection remains a fundamental component of surgical training, yet the suitability of fresh-frozen anatomical specimens for simulating graft preparation has not been systematically assessed. This study evaluates the handling characteristics and graft-preparation feasibility of costal and auricular cartilage harvested from fresh-frozen cadavers used in structured revision rhinoplasty dissection. METHODS: Ten fresh-frozen cadaveric heads and two thoracic specimens were dissected. Costal cartilage was harvested bilaterally from ribs 5-8, and auricular cartilage bilaterally through a posterior conchal approach. Graft length, width, thickness, preparation time, carvability, laminar fragmentation, and suturability were assessed. Because multiple samples were obtained from the same donor, donor-level means were used for inferential comparisons. RESULTS: Costal cartilage was rigid and brittle, with macroscopic and handling characteristics consistent with calcification. Laminar thinning resulted in fragmentation in 85% of attempts, and intentionally thicker slices displayed macroscopically visible microfractures and fractured during suturing. No costal graft was suitable for spreader or septal extension graft simulation. Auricular cartilage maintained elasticity, allowed reproducible laminar carving, and withstood suturing without fracture. Preparation time differed significantly between graft types. CONCLUSION: In the specimens examined, costal cartilage was unsuitable for laminar graft-preparation simulation because of fragmentation and fracture, although rib harvesting remained valuable for thoracic-exposure training. Auricular cartilage was more consistently suitable for graft-shaping simulation. These findings describe distinct roles for the two cartilage sources within fresh-frozen cadaveric simulation of revision rhinoplasty.

articles.title: Branch-level anatomy and estimated portal injury risk during anterior ankle arthroscopy: a combined ultrasound and cadaveric study.
articles.authors: Hannes Platzgummer, Tobias Smodics, Veronika Vetchy et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To map the nerve branches at risk at the anterior ankle joint line with ultrasound, validate them by dissection, measure branch-specific distances to the anterolateral and anteromedial portals, and estimate per-branch injury probability. METHODS: Fourteen fresh-frozen ankles from 7 body donors were examined with high-resolution ultrasound (10-22 MHz). The intermediate (NCDI) and medial (NCDM) dorsal cutaneous nerves, the deep fibular nerve and the saphenous nerve were identified at the anterior joint line, dye-marked and verified by dissection. Distances to the portals were measured with digital calipers; injury probability was estimated with a normal distribution model and bootstrap confidence intervals. RESULTS: Dissection confirmed all sonographically identified branches (saphenous nerve 13/14 specimens, all others 14/14). The NCDI was single in 57% of specimens and split into two sub-branches in 43%. The single NCDI lay 3.6 ± 10.3 mm from the anterolateral portal (1-mm risk 3.6%, 4-mm risk 14.4%); each split sub-branch carried 5.6% and 22.1%, respectively. The saphenous nerve lay - 5.7 ± 5.2 mm from the anteromedial portal (1-mm risk 4.2%, 4-mm risk 17.0%). The NCDM and deep fibular nerve carried a 4-mm risk of 4.0% or less. The combined risk at either portal was 8.7% at 1-mm incision and 32.5% at 4-mm trocar width. CONCLUSIONS: Anterior ankle portal risk is branch-specific: in 43% of specimens, two NCDI sub-branches cross the anterolateral portal field. The combined 4-mm estimate reflects nerve contact rather than clinical injury and is an upper estimate. High-resolution ultrasound identified all sub-branches verified at dissection and may support preoperative portal planning.

articles.title: Bilateral asymmetric accessory iliopsoas musculature and variant relationships with the femoral nerve: an anatomical case report.
articles.authors: Caitlin Wetzel, Bailey Hall, Keirsten Templin et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Accessory musculature within the interval between the psoas major and iliacus may alter the expected course of the femoral nerve and complicate imaging or surgical exposure. This report describes a rare bilateral but asymmetric configuration of accessory iliopsoas musculature. METHODS: The posterior abdominal wall and iliopsoas regions of an 85-year-old male whole-body donor were dissected bilaterally. Accessory muscle origins, distal fusion patterns, dimensions, and relationships with the femoral nerve were documented. RESULTS: Two accessory muscular heads were identified on each side. On the left, both arose from the L4 costal process; on the right, the heads arose separately from the L2 and L3 costal processes. One head on each side fused to the native psoas major, and the other to the native iliacus. The femoral nerve passed between the native psoas major and accessory psoas-associated head on the left, but between the two accessory heads on the right. The heads differed in length and caliber between sides. CONCLUSION: In this donor, bilateral accessory iliopsoas heads had different origins and femoral nerve relationships. Recognition of unexpected intermuscular nerve intervals may aid anatomical interpretation and operative orientation, particularly in posterior abdominal wall or retroperitoneal exposures. No evidence of femoral neuropathy or altered biomechanical function was available.

articles.title: Does the morphology of the mandibular lingula affect the location of the mandibular foramen?
articles.authors: Atapol Yongvikul, Manop Khanijou, Nattharin Wongsirichat et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Accurate localization of the mandibular foramen (MF) is essential for successful inferior alveolar nerve block. The mandibular lingula (ML), a bony projection partially overlying the MF, is commonly used as an anatomical landmark; however, its morphology exhibits considerable variation. This study aimed to evaluate the relationship between ML morphology and the spatial position of the MF using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). METHODS: This retrospective CBCT-based study analyzed 288 scans (144 females; mean age 51.0 ± 19.4 years) acquired between March 2023 and March 2025. ML morphology was classified into truncated, nodular, assimilated, and other types. Vertical and horizontal relationships between the ML, MF, mandibular borders, and oblique ridges were measured using multiplanar reconstruction. MF dimensions and the presence of accessory mandibular canals were also assessed. Inter- and intra-examiner reliability were evaluated. Statistical analysis included one-way ANOVA and independent t-tests, with significance set at P < 0.05. RESULTS: The nodular ML was the most prevalent morphology (60.76%). ML type did not significantly influence the vertical position or dimensions of the MF (P > 0.05). However, significant differences were observed in horizontal localization, particularly relative to the internal oblique ridge, with the assimilated ML type demonstrating a more posteriorly positioned MF (P < 0.05). Accessory mandibular canals, present in 5.56% of cases, were associated with significantly reduced horizontal distances to the MF. CONCLUSION: ML morphology significantly influences its horizontal localization. Assimilated lingula and accessory mandibular canals may compromise the reliability of conventional landmarks.

articles.title: Morphological variability of the last denticulate ligament process: an anatomical study.
articles.authors: Loris Chaboissier, Ilona Baffaleuf, Hugo Lecot et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: The denticulate ligament plays a role in stabilizing the spinal cord. Its most distal extension, the last denticulate ligament process (LDLP), remains poorly described in the literature. This study aims to provide a comprehensive morphological characterization of the LDLP and its anatomical relationships. METHOD: Forty-four cadaveric dissections were performed, allowing analysis of 87 LDLPs. A posterior approach with intermyolaminar dissection between vertebral levels T10 and L4 was used. Morphological parameters and precise measurements, including distances between the LDLP and the apex of the conus medullaris, were recorded. The adjacent sensory rootlets were systematically documented. RESULTS: Five distinct LDLP morphologies were identified: long oblique, short oblique, horizontal, bifid, and atypical. The denticulate ligament terminated in a slender, pearly filament located cranial to the filum terminale. The LDLP was most frequently observed at the T12-L1 level (40.2%) and adjacent to L3 sensory rootlets (66.6%). The caudal spinal insertion of the LDLP was on average 4.34 cm from the apex of the conus medullaris. A notable positional trend was observed: on average, when the conus medullaris was located at vertebral level L1 or lower, the LDLP was positioned one vertebral level higher; specifically, when the conus medullaris was located at T12-L1, the LDLP was most frequently found at the T12 level. CONCLUSION: The LDLP displayed five morphological patterns and variable vertebral levels, with most insertions located around T12-L1. Its consistent relationships with the conus medullaris and sensory rootlets may provide useful anatomical landmarks for neurosurgical procedures.

articles.title: Distinguishing anatomical complexity from clinical risk in dual-origin lingual artery anatomy.
articles.authors: Santhiya Jayakumar

articles.title: The unexpected and previously discounted tale of muscle galactose uptake.
articles.authors: Joseph W Beals, Gordon I Smith

articles.title: Intermittent vagus nerve stimulation elicits spinal serotonin-dependent phrenic motor facilitation.
articles.authors: Alec L E Butenas, Gordon S Mitchell
articles.abstract: Intermittent vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) elicits a persistent increase in phrenic motor output, termed phrenic motor facilitation (pMF). However, prior studies demonstrating VNS-induced pMF used high-frequency stimulation (50 Hz), above the discharge frequencies of most afferent fibres. Here, we tested the hypothesis that 15, 1-min episodes of low-frequency (5 Hz; ∼6 V; 5 ms pulse width) VNS evoke pMF in urethane-anaesthetized, neuromuscularly blockaded and ventilated male rats; we also studied ∼4- vs. ∼16-month-old rats to assess the impact of advancing age. Low-frequency VNS elicited robust pMF for at least 90 min in young rats (n = 7); at 90 min post-stimulation, VNS increased integrated phrenic burst amplitude by 49% (±18% SD) vs. 17% (±15% SD) in time controls (n = 7; P = 0.004). We also tested whether VNS elicits long-term facilitation in renal sympathetic nerve activity; facilitation was not observed. We compared afferent vs. efferent VNS (cut nerves; each n = 7); afferent, not efferent, stimulation elicited pMF. Cervical intrathecal 5-HT2 receptor antagonism blocked VNS-induced pMF; neither 5-HT7 nor α1-adrenergic receptor antagonism had significant effects (n = 7 each). Since VNS activates slowly adapting pulmonary stretch receptors, we tested whether intermittent positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) evokes pMF. Intermittent PEEP elicited significant pMF (n = 7), implicating pulmonary stretch receptors as contributors to VNS-induced pMF. In ∼16-month-old rats (n = 5), neither phrenic nor renal sympathetic nerve facilitation was observed following intermittent VNS. Thus, low-frequency VNS is a robust stimulus to respiratory motor plasticity in young male rats. Slowly adapting pulmonary stretch receptors and spinal 5-HT2 receptors play important roles in its underlying mechanism.

articles.title: Mindless eating as a behavioural correlate of addictive-like eating symptoms in 10-12-year-old children: associations with disordered eating attitudes.
articles.authors: Meliha Çavdar, Nilüfer Özkan, Büşra Aslan Gönül et al.
articles.abstract: Middle childhood is a critical developmental period for the emergence of eating-related self-regulatory processes and maladaptive eating patterns. This cross-sectional study of 1060 children aged 10-12 years examined associations among disordered eating attitudes, mindful eating dimensions and addictive-like eating symptoms, focusing on the indirect role of mindless eating. Data were collected using a socio-demographic form, the Mindful Eating Questionnaire for Children (MEQ-C), the dimensional Yale Food Addiction Scale for Children 2.0, the Stunkard Pictogram and the Children's Eating Attitudes Test. Correlation analyses were conducted to examine associations among variables. Multiple linear regression was used to examine variables independently associated with addictive-like eating symptoms. An exploratory indirect-effect model tested whether mindless eating was involved in the statistical association between disordered eating attitudes and addictive-like eating symptoms. BMI category and meal skipping showed significant multivariate effects. In the regression model, MEQ-C-Mindless Eating showed the strongest independent association with addictive-like eating symptoms (β = 0·556, p < 0·001), followed by BMI z-score (β = 0·167, p < 0·001), disordered eating attitudes (β = 0·115, p < 0·001) and meal skipping (β = -0·105, p < 0·001). The indirect-effect model suggested that the association between disordered eating attitudes and addictive-like eating symptoms was statistically consistent with an indirect association involving mindless eating. Mindless eating may be an important behavioural correlate of addictive-like eating symptoms in middle childhood and may help contextualise their association with disordered eating attitudes. These findings highlight the relevance of eating-related self-regulation in children, although the conceptual overlap between mindless eating and addictive-like eating measures suggests findings should be interpreted with some caution.

articles.title: Associations of Countermovement Jump Performance and Body Composition With Baseball-Specific Base-Running Outcomes in Semiprofessional Position Players.
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: Tzu-Han Chan, Chieh-Ying Chiang, Chun-Yu Wang et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Linear sprint testing may not capture the spatial and technical demands of base running, and the associated physical characteristics remain unclear. This study examined associations of body composition and countermovement jump performance with outcomes across 3 distinct contexts: stealing bases (SB), running after hitting, and running between bases. METHODS: Male semiprofessional players (N = 35) completed bioelectrical impedance-derived body composition (body fat percentage, absolute muscle mass); countermovement jump (jump height, peak relative propulsive power, take-off velocity, peak velocity); and base-running (SB, running after hitting, running between bases total times) assessments. Base-running efficiency was also calculated. RESULTS: SB, running after hitting, and running between bases total times correlated positively (r = .61 to .84). Body fat percentage correlated positively with most time-based outcomes (r = .51 to .73), whereas absolute muscle mass showed trivial-to-small, nonsignificant associations. Jump height, PPrel, take-off velocity, and peak velocity correlated negatively with time-based outcomes (r = - .41 to -.78). SB movement time, but not SB reaction time, correlated with body fat percentage and all countermovement jump variables; base-running efficiency showed no significant associations. CONCLUSIONS: Base-running tasks share an acceleration-related component but remain task-specific. Within this sample, body fat percentage was more strongly related to running performance than absolute muscle mass. Jump height, PPrel, take-off velocity, and peak velocity showed broadly similar associations; their independent or incremental value was not tested. SB reaction time and base-running efficiency showed no significant associations, although measurement reliability and unmeasured technical or perceptual-motor factors limit interpretation of these findings.
