These findings support task-specific assessment of base running.

articles.title: "Train as You Play" or "Play as You Train"? Rethinking the Role of Match Data in Guiding Training Prescription.
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: Franck Brocherie, Yannis Irid, Jan G Bourgois et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: In contemporary high-performance team sports, the principle "train as you play" has become central to design sport-specific conditioning programs, aiming to replicate match demands in training to optimize player readiness. While wearable-based data have improved the understanding of match demands, an overreliance on these metrics for training prescription may lead to misinterpretation of players' needs and potentially contribute to detraining or increased injury risk. PURPOSE: This invited commentary critically evaluates the "train as you play" paradigm and propose an integrated framework that aligns match analysis with evidence-based training principles (ie, "play as you train" paradigm). EVIDENCE: Match-derived metrics represent the outcome of complex, context-dependent interactions including tactical decisions, opponent behavior, and psychological factors. Consequently, solely replicating match loads may overlook context-dependent individual variability and the nonlinear nature of physiological adaptation. Effective load monitoring should therefore integrate external workload indicators with concomitant internal responses, recovery markers, and neuromuscular assessments to better evaluate how players tolerate and adapt to training stress. CONCLUSION: The "train as you play" and "play as you train" paradigms are complementary rather than opposing, requiring coaches and practitioners to integrate match data with physiological, subjective, and contextual insights in an interpretative rather than imitative manner to best prepare players. Such a balanced approach can optimize adaptation, enhance performance, and reduce injury risk, ultimately fostering fatigue-resistant players who not only "train as they play" but also "play better because of how they train."

articles.title: Muscle coordination networks during human walking revealed by graphical LASSO analysis at individual and population levels.
articles.authors: Samuel A Acuña
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Understanding how the nervous system coordinates many muscles simultaneously during walking, and how that coordination breaks down in pathology, is a central challenge in gait biomechanics and rehabilitation. Existing approaches describe what muscles do individually or on average, but cannot reveal which muscles are directly coupled to one another at each moment of the stride. The purpose of this study was to establish the feasibility of graphical LASSO network analysis as a framework for characterizing muscle coordination at two complementary levels: stride-to-stride variation within a single representative participant, and between-subject variation across a healthy young adult population. METHODS: Surface EMG data were collected from six lower extremity muscles in twenty healthy young adults during treadmill walking at 1.0 m/s. Sparse partial correlation networks were estimated among the six muscles at each of 101 time-normalized gait cycle points at both the individual and population levels of analysis. RESULTS: Networks varied systematically across the gait cycle, recovering expected couplings including plantar flexor pairing during stance and quadriceps pairing during loading response and terminal swing. At the individual level, networks revealed which muscle relationships are stable features of that person's stride pattern and which vary across strides. At the population level, networks revealed which muscle relationships are common features of healthy young adult gait and which reflect individual differences in coordination strategy. Centrality metrics further identified muscles as coordinatively important at time points where their absolute activation was low. CONCLUSIONS: The graphical LASSO framework produces muscle coordination networks that are interpretable, biologically coherent, and sensitive to coordination structure at two clinically meaningful scales. By characterizing which muscles are directly couples at each moment of the stride and how that coupling structure evolves across the gait cycle, the approach offers a rich description of the neuromuscular organization of walking and a promising foundation for future clinical assessment of gait coordination.

articles.title: Optimal Wearing Position of Accelerometers for Monitoring Energy Expenditure in Tennis.
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: Linjie Shu, Hui Dong, Jiancai Chen et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Monitoring energy expenditure (EE) in tennis is complicated by its intermittent and technically variable movements. This study identified the optimal accelerometer wearing position for EE prediction and examined the contribution of additional covariates. METHODS: Thirty-eight right-handed national second-class tennis players (11 females, 27 males) performed 4 tennis-specific technical movements with accelerometers worn at 9 positions. Criterion EE was measured using Metamax3B portable metabolic analyzer. Associations of accelerometer-derived variables with criterion EE were examined through Pearson or Spearman correlation analyses. Candidate covariates were screened using Akaike information criterion-based backward selection. Three linear mixed-effects models were evaluated per position with participant as a random intercept. Variance inflation factors, leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, and Bland-Altman analyses assessed multicollinearity, predictive performance, and agreement, respectively. RESULTS: Lower-back and ankle positions showed more frequent significant correlations with criterion EE. Backward selection retained heart rate, basal metabolic rate, sex, and movement type across positions; all primary-model variance inflation factors were below 3. Across the 3 models, marginal Rm2 of lower back ranked first (.787) and of the dominant-side ankle second (.749). In primary models, lower back had the lowest cross-validated root mean square error (.810). Bland-Altman mean differences were close to zero in top-performing models, while proportional-bias slopes were significantly negative at all positions. CONCLUSIONS: Lower back represents the optimal accelerometer placement for model-based EE monitoring in tennis, and incorporating participant variables and movement type enhances prediction accuracy. These findings support sport-specific sensor placement and individualized calibration strategies to improve training load monitoring and nutritional planning.

articles.title: Modeling Career Attrition in Swimming Using Internal and External Age-Specific Performance Benchmarks.
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: Nur Adilah Masismadi, Minh Huynh, Matthew J Wylde et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This study examined whether absence of a recorded competitive appearance during event-specific normative peak performance age ranges (peakRange) could be predicted by medal history and performance times preceding peakRange. A secondary aim was to estimate the earliest statistically detectable differences in performance gaps between athletes with at least one competitive appearance during peakRange and those who did not. METHODS: World Aquatics race results up to 2019 were analyzed across 26 events for athletes whose peakRange fell entirely within the 2000-2019 window. Athletes were categorized into 5 career groups based on recorded appearance during peakRange and timing of first medal attainment relative to peakRange. Annual best times from age 13 to peakRange onset were evaluated against external benchmarks (global, continental, national) and internal benchmarks (debut year, prior year). Weighted penalized logistic regression models were fitted overall, and within early-medalist and nonmedalist subgroups. Post hoc analyses estimated divergence ages. RESULTS: Seventy of 78 classification tasks achieved a Matthews correlation coefficient >.10, indicating nonrandom predictive information. Divergence ages were detected across all 26 events in the overall sample, 5 events among early medalists, and 23 among nonmedalists. Divergence ages were generally earlier among women (15-16 y) than men (17-18 y). CONCLUSIONS: Performance-participation associations varied by medal history. Detected divergence ages more often corresponded to internal benchmarks among early medalists and to external benchmarks among nonmedalists. These findings concern recorded participation during peakRange, not the reasons for withdrawal from swimming.

articles.title: Female anatomies disguise ECG abnormalities following myocardial infarction: An artificial intelligence-enabled modelling and simulation study.
articles.authors: Hannah Joy Smith, Leto Luana Riebel, Ruben Doste et al.
articles.abstract: The ECG is modulated by torso-heart anatomy, challenging patients' diagnosis and risk stratification. This study aims to quantify how torso-heart anatomical factors affect sex differences in ECG biomarkers in acute and chronic myocardial infarction (MI). We exploit the perfect control of artificial intelligence (AI)-augmented multiscale modelling and simulation, using clinical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and ECGs for model construction and validation. A cohort of 1720 torso-ventricular anatomies (50% female) was constructed from MRIs of healthy and post-MI participants in the UK Biobank. A total of 8600 simulations were performed considering anatomical variability, three electrophysiological stages (healthy, ischaemic and infarcted) and two infarct locations (anteroseptal and inferolateral). Quantifying the effect of cardiac size, position and orientation on each ECG biomarker, we found that female anatomies had larger distances between infarct and ECG electrodes (relative to cardiac size) and larger angles between infarct normal and ECG lead axes, both primarily caused by their more superior cardiac position. This reduced ST elevation and amplitude of late depolarisation and repolarisation tails, ultimately shortening QRS duration (QRSd) and T-peak-to-end interval (TpTe). Overall, position and orientation of the heart impacted TpTe more severely than QRSd; our AI-enabled mechanistic modelling and simulation identified smaller ventricles, superior cardiac position and different ventricular orientation as key anatomical contributors of QRSd, TpTe and ST elevation being reduced in female versus male anatomies. Our framework provides a blueprint for quantifying the impact of anatomical sex differences on functional markers and enables future work in tailoring clinical guidelines considering unique patient anatomy to reduce biased outcomes. KEY POINTS: The ECG, important in diagnosing and managing treatment for myocardial infarction (heart attacks), is known to be impacted by the anatomy of the heart and torso. Women suffering myocardial infarction are underdiagnosed, and the effect of anatomical sex differences on the ECG in myocardial infarction is poorly understood. Our human computational modelling and simulation demonstrate that ST elevation in ischaemia was reduced in female anatomies, mainly as their hearts are higher in the torso than male anatomies. We show that ECG time intervals were affected differently by anatomy: the T-peak-to-end interval was more sensitive to cardiac positioning, whereas QRS duration was more sensitive to cardiac size. Our study demonstrates how computer simulations provide an efficient mechanistic tool to quantify the role of anatomical differences in clinical biomarkers and could ultimately support the inclusion of sex differences in clinical guidelines.

articles.title: Time-Restricted Eating and Caloric Restriction Impact Bone and the Gut Microbiota in Postmenopausal Women: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Brandon D McGuire, Shreya Ghosh, Yvette Schlussel et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Caloric restriction (CR) can reduce bone mineral density (BMD). Time-restricted eating (TRE) modulates circadian rhythms and gut microbiota, but its effects on bone when combined with CR are unknown. OBJECTIVES: This study examined the effects of TRE+CR on bone in postmenopausal females with overweight or obesity and whether it is associated with changes in the gut microbiota. METHODS: Forty-nine postmenopausal females (body mass index ≥25 kg/m2, 50-79 years) were randomized to 24-weeks of CR (-500 kcal/d) or TRE (<9-h eating)+CR. BMD and bone quality were assessed at weeks 0 and 24. Fecal samples were collected at weeks 0, 12, and 24, and blood samples at weeks 0 and 24. RESULTS: Participants (61±5 years, 33±4 kg/m2) had an eating window of 12.3±0.9 hours/day, which was maintained in the CR group (n=21) [+0.3h/day (0.0,0.68)], and reduced in the TRE+CR group (n=26) [-4.0h/day (-4.4,-3.6)] (P<0.001), with 88% and 94% adherence, respectively. Hip BMD decreased similarly in both groups over time [-0.010g/cm2 (-0.018, -0.002)] (P=0.001), without between-group differences (P=0.98). TRE+CR attenuated radius BMD loss compared to CR [0.009g/cm2 (-0.002, 0.021) vs. [-0.020g/cm2 (-0.033, -0.007); (P=0.001)]. Gut microbiota (beta-diversity) shifted within TRE+CR from baseline to week 24 (P<0.05), with increasing dissimilarity from the CR group emerging by week 12 (P<0.0001). Changes in microbial guild ratios were positively correlated with changes in radius BMD (P<0.05). Subgroup analysis indicated baseline microbial guilds predicted radius BMD preservation (AUC=0.73; 0.54, 0.92). Weight decreased [-6.8kg (-8.3, -5.4)] similarly between the groups (P=0.29), but visceral adiposity decreased more with TRE+CR (P=0.01). Serum bone turnover markers were unchanged, while glycemic indices improved (P<0.05) without between-group differences. CONCLUSIONS: TRE mitigated weight-loss-induced bone loss at a clinically relevant non-weight-bearing site, but not at the hip, and these effects may be associated with changes in the gut microbiota. Larger studies are needed to establish mechanisms and sustained health effects.

articles.title: Nutritional monitoring during spaceflight: tracking body composition and three-dimensional shape across a five-day research expedition.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Jonathan P Bennett, Michael C Wong, Nisa N Kelly et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Microgravity during spaceflight leads to rapid muscle loss and fluid shifts driven by skeletal unloading and dietary changes. Obtaining accurate measurements before, during, and after missions remains challenging due to the cost and feasibility limitations of traditional imaging and laboratory systems. OBJECTIVE: This study quantified changes in whole-body and regional body shape using three-dimensional optical imaging (3DO) and body composition using bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) before, during, and after a short-duration spaceflight. METHODS: Fat-free mass (FFM) and fat mass (FM) were estimated by combining 3DO-derived body volume (BV) and BIA-derived total body water (TBW) within a five-compartment (5C) model. Ground-based measurements were obtained immediately pre- and post-flight using clinically validated 3DO and BIA systems. In-flight assessments used smartphone-based 3DO and smartwatch-based BIA, calibrated to ground systems. Absolute and proportional changes in body mass, circumferences, and 5C body composition were characterized as the difference between post- and pre-flight values, with in-flight measures used to monitor longitudinal changes in TBW and body shape. RESULTS: Four astronauts completed the five-day research expedition. Body mass decreased by -2.27 ± 1.66 kg, driven primarily by FFM loss (-2.17 ± 1.22 kg), representing a -4.36 ± 2.76% proportional reduction (range: -1.12 to -7.76%). In-flight TBW reductions reached -3.0 L. Post-flight circumferences decreased across all regions, with the largest proportional changes in the legs and torso. The portable 5C approach demonstrated feasibility for in-mission monitoring, capturing rapid TBW loss confirmed by incomplete recovery upon landing. CONCLUSION: Alterations in diet, activity, and microgravity contributed to greater than 4% FFM loss over five days, with the greatest regional changes in the legs and torso. In-flight monitoring captured TBW loss that did not fully recover upon landing, demonstrating the feasibility of portable body composition monitoring for astronaut health management.

articles.title: Localized extracellular water responses to low-and high-load resistance exercise assessed by bioelectrical impedance spectroscopy.
articles.journal: Applied physiology, nutrition, and metabolism = Physiologie appliquee, nutrition et metabolisme
articles.authors: Masashi Taniguchi, Kazuki Umemura, Zimin Wang et al.
articles.abstract: This study evaluated extracellular water (ECW) responses measured using segmental bioelectrical impedance spectroscopy (S-BIS) across different measurement regions following resistance exercise (RE) and examined their associations with muscle thickness (MT) changes to assess the regional responsiveness of S-BIS to exercise-induced muscle swelling. Eighteen healthy young adults performed unilateral knee extension RE under two load conditions with matched total training volume on separate days (30% and 80% one-repetition maximum [1RM]). MT of the quadriceps femoris (QF) was assessed using ultrasonography, and ECW was estimated using S-BIS before and after each RE session. ECW was evaluated in three regions: thigh-region, the localized region over the QF (QF-region), and the localized region over the hamstrings (Ham-region). ECW changes were analyzed using two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance, and Pearson's correlation analyses were performed to examine relationships between ECW and MT changes. ECW increased significantly only in the QF-region under both load conditions (+8.6% and +13.4%, respectively). Main effects indicated greater ECW changes under 80% than 30% 1RM (mean difference, 2.32 percentage points) and in the QF-region than the thigh- and Ham-regions. ECW changes were significantly and positively correlated with MT changes in the QF-region under both the 30% and 80% 1RM conditions (r = 0.708 and 0.667, respectively). Localized ECW assessment over the QF revealed region-specific changes following RE that were associated with MT changes. These findings suggest that localized ECW assessment using S-BIS may provide a region-specific measure of exercise-induced fluid changes associated with muscle swelling.

articles.title: Effect of Catechin Supplementation on Muscle Fatigue and Physical Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
articles.authors: Dandara B Bonifácio, Pedro H V Mendes, Gabriela M Fraiz et al.
articles.abstract: CONTEXT: The antioxidant properties of catechins are well established; however, whether these biological effects translate into meaningful improvements in muscle fatigue and physical performance remains uncertain. OBJECTIVE: To systematically evaluate the effects of acute and chronic catechin supplementation on muscle fatigue and physical performance in humans. DATA SOURCES: A literature search was conducted in the MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials databases to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining the effects of catechin supplementation on muscle fatigue and physical performance outcomes. DATA EXTRACTION: The search strategy was defined according to the PICOS framework (ie, participants, intervention, comparison, outcomes, and study design) and conducted in September 2025. Risk of bias was independently assessed using the JBI critical appraisal tool. DATA ANALYSIS: Of the 771 records identified, 7 RCTs met the inclusion criteria, reflecting the still emerging evidence base available in this field. Catechin supplementation was associated with improvements in aerobic performance and reductions in perceived exertion in selected intervention settings; however, these findings varied across studies and outcomes. Additionally, no significant improvements were observed for aerobic and anaerobic performance, functional exercise capacity, or physiological responses to exercise. Meta-analytic synthesis showed no significant overall effects of catechin supplementation on performance-related outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: Catechin supplementation does not appear to enhance muscle fatigue and physical performance. Although potential effects on aerobic performance and perceived exertion were observed under specific intervention conditions, the current evidence remains limited and does not support a clear ergogenic effect. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO registration no. CRD42024605740.

articles.title: Genetic and Epigenetic Determinants of Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviors: A Systematic Review.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Layan Mendis, Lianne de Vries, Floris Huider et al.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION/PURPOSE: A better understanding of the determinants of physical activity (PA) and sedentary behavior (SB) is needed to counter increasing inactivity. Twin and family studies indicate that these behaviors are shaped by biological factors, including genetic and epigenetic mechanisms. The number of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) on PA and SB that try to elucidate these mechanisms has been increasing, motivating a review on whether their findings point to overlapping or distinct biological mechanisms. METHODS: In this preregistered systematic review, we synthesize GWAS and EWAS findings on PA and SB and identify replicated loci across studies. RESULTS: We included nine GWAS reporting 414 unique lead SNPs and seven EWAS reporting 437 significant CpG sites associated with PA and/or SB. Across all findings, 51 genomic loci and 93 SNPs met our replication criteria, defined as support from at least two different GWAS or EWAS studies. Five genomic loci (1p36.23, 1p13.3, 1q21.3, 6p22.2, and 6p21.31) including six lead SNPs (rs301799, rs8450, rs4845364, rs2393593, rs10947452, and rs6457816), showed convergence between PA/SB-associated GWAS variants and mQTLs for PA/SB-associated CpG sites, highlighting candidate regions for future functional follow-up. Functional annotation indicated that these loci are mostly enriched in genic and transcript-associated regions. Gene mapping and enrichment analyses highlighted biological pathways across neurobiological systems involved in motivation and exercise liking, as well as peripheral systems related to movement, exercise capacity, energy metabolism, and cardiometabolic functioning. PA/SB-associated SNPs also overlapped with variants linked to body composition, cardiometabolic markers, educational attainment, cognitive ability, and brain-size traits. CONCLUSIONS: Overall, PA and SB appear to be influenced by a complex, highly polygenic architecture, with consistent genetic influences but limited convergence yet in epigenetic influences. Further large-scale, multi-ancestry studies integrating genomic and epigenomic data with harmonized PA/SB measures are needed to inform functional genetic studies.

articles.title: Does Increased Maximal Sprint Speed Alter Pacing Distribution in the 400-m Race Among Male 400-m Sprinters? A Longitudinal Study.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Kentaro Sato, Takaya Yoshimoto, Yoshihiro Chiba et al.
articles.abstract: Sato, K, Yoshimoto, T, Chiba, Y, Ohnuma, H, Iso, S, Tsuchiya, J, and Takai, Y. Does increased maximal sprint speed alter pacing distribution in the 400-m race among male 400-m sprinters? A longitudinal study. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Performance in the 400-m sprint is influenced not only by short sprint ability but also by pacing strategy during a race. However, the effects of changes in short sprint ability on pacing characteristics remain unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to clarify the effects of changes in maximal sprint speed (MSS) on 400-m sprint performance and segmental running speed in competitive 400-m sprinters. Twenty-three male 400-m sprinters (age: 20.04 ± 1.76 years, height: 1.75 ± 0.06 m, body mass: 66.93 ± 6.93 kg, 400-m personal best: 49.03 ± 1.56 seconds; range: 45.58-52.70 seconds) performed 400-m and 60-m sprint tests on 2 occasions separated by 1 year. Maximal sprint speed was defined as the highest mean running speed among the 10-m segments during a 60-m sprint. In the 400-m sprint, the relative running speed for each 50-m segment (%MSS) was calculated as the mean running speed divided by the MSS, and the percentage of the 400-m time spent in each 50-m segment (%ST) was determined. Sprinters who exhibited greater increases in MSS demonstrated greater improvements in 400-m sprint performance. Furthermore, increases in MSS were significantly associated with improvements in running speed during the 0-250-m segments of the 400-m sprint. These findings indicate that increases in MSS may contribute to improvements in 400-m sprint performance, particularly through enhanced running speed during the first half of the race.

articles.title: The Relationship Between Muscle Cross-Sectional Area and Joint Torque of Trunk and Hip Generating Swing Rotation Around the Vertical Axis in Baseball Batting.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Takuya Yanaka, Yoshitaka Morishita
articles.abstract: Yanaka, T and Morishita, Y. The relationship between muscle cross-sectional area and joint torque of trunk and hip generating swing rotation around the vertical axis in baseball batting. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-In baseball batting, the bat is accelerated mainly by rotation around the vertical axis. The main joint motions responsible for generating this rotation are believed to be hip flexion of the lead-side leg, hip extension of the pivot-side leg, and trunk rotation. This study investigated the relationship between muscle cross-sectional area (CSA) and joint torques contributing to swing rotation around the vertical axis in 27 baseball batters, using magnetic resonance imaging and inverse dynamics. Initial analysis confirmed significant correlations between bat-head speed and peak pivot hip torque (r = 0.59) and peak trunk rotational torque (r = 0.62). The lead hip torque correlated significantly with the CSA of psoas major (r = -0.50) and rectus femoris r (r = -0.60). The pivot hip torque correlated significantly with the CSA of gluteus maximus r (r = 0.73) and hamstrings r (r = 0.73). Similarly, trunk rotational torque was correlated with the CSAs of the pivot-side external oblique (r = 0.50) and lead-side internal oblique (r = 0.50). By contrast, all correlations involving both hip joint torques and trunk joint torque (with bat-head speed and muscle CSAs) disappeared after controlling for body mass in the partial correlation analysis. These results indicated that both hip torques and trunk torque generation are strongly dependent on muscle size and body size in baseball batters. This study suggested that hypertrophying muscles in the hips and trunk is important for generating large torque to improve bat-head speed in baseball batting.

articles.title: Comparative Effects of Resistance Training and High-Intensity Interval Training on Body Composition, Metabolic Health, and Functional Strength in Overweight and Obese Adults: A 12-Week Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Cristina Petisco-Rodríguez, Álvaro Barroso-Hernández, Ignacio Bartolomé-Sánchez et al.
articles.abstract: Petisco-Rodríguez, C, Barroso-Hernández, Á, Bartolomé-Sánchez, I, and Crego, A. Comparative effects of resistance training and high-intensity interval training on body composition, metabolic health, and functional strength in overweight and obese adults: A 12-week randomized controlled trial. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to compare the effects of 2 training programs on anthropometric and physiological variables in overweight and obese adults. Ninety subjects (age = 39.9 ± 10.4 years; body mass index (BMI) = 31.0 ± 4.3 kg·m-2) were randomly assigned to a resistance training group (RG; n = 30), a high-intensity interval training (HIIT) group (HG; n = 30), or a nontraining control group (CG; n = 30). Both the RG and HG performed 2 weekly sessions for 12 weeks. The RG completed 8 upper-body and lower-body resistance exercises at 70% of 1 repetition maximum, while the HG performed high-intensity intervals at 80% of the maximum heart rate. A 3 (group: CG, RG, HG) × 2 (time: pre, post) mixed ANOVA revealed significant effects on the BMI, body fat, and fasting glucose. Both training groups showed similar improvements in all measures from preintervention to postintervention. Compared with CG, RG and HG had reduced body fat and BMI, while RG demonstrated greater gains in muscle mass, fasting glucose, and grip strength. Paired t-tests confirmed significant within-group improvements in BMI, body fat, grip strength, and fasting glucose in the RG and HG. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.017 after the Bonferroni correction. These findings suggest that both resistance training and HIIT enhance the body composition of overweight and obese adults. However, resistance training may provide additional benefits in muscular fitness and glycemic control, supporting its role as a practical strategy for improving metabolic health in this population.

articles.title: Activity level strongly affects extremity, but not cheek, temperature and heat loss during cold wind exposure.
articles.authors: Pim Scheiberlich, Lisa Klous, Elsa Rijpstra et al.
articles.abstract: Background: The wind chill temperature index (WCTI) estimates frostbite risk from air temperature and wind speed, but is based on exposed cheek skin during walking at a fixed speed. This may limit its applicability across activity levels and body sites, particularly because frostbite frequently occurs at the extremities. This study investigated whether activity level affects skin temperature and heat flux responses at the cheek, finger, and toe during cold wind exposure, hypothesizing that higher activity levels would increase body temperature, resulting in higher skin temperatures, altered heat fluxes, and reduced cold injury risk. Methods: Thirteen healthy male participants completed three experimental conditions in a climate chamber at -10°C with wind exposure. Activity level was varied between standing still (LOW), walking at 4.8 km·h⁻¹ on a level treadmill (MED), and walking at 4.8 km·h⁻¹ with a 5% incline (HIGH). Skin temperature and heat flux were measured continuously at the cheek, finger, and toe. Results: Cheek skin temperature was slightly higher in HIGH (14.8 ± 2.1°C) than in LOW (12.2 ± 1.9°C, P = 0.013) and MED (12.6 ± 1.2°C, P < 0.001), whereas cheek heat flux did not differ among conditions (P = 0.512). Finger skin temperature increased from 8.5 ± 1.6°C in LOW to 23.1 ± 9.2°C in MED and 31.5 ± 1.8°C in HIGH, while toe skin temperature increased from 12.8 ± 2.1°C to 24.5 ± 8.4°C and 31.4 ± 5.0°C, respectively. All pairwise differences in finger and toe skin temperature were significant (P ≤ 0.001). Finger and toe heat flux also increased with activity level, with significant overall condition effects at both sites (P < 0.001). Conclusion: Under the environmental conditions tested, activity level had limited relevance for WCTI-based assessment of exposed cheek cooling, supporting the validity of the current WCTI assumptions for the cheek. However, activity level strongly affected thermal responses at the finger and toe, indicating that cold injury risk assessment may benefit from adjustments for both anatomical location and activity level.

articles.title: Isocapnic breathing mitigates cerebral blood flow reductions after ketone monoester supplementation.
articles.authors: Claudia M S Yong, Aedan J Rourke, Geoff B Coombs et al.
articles.abstract: Ketone monoester (KME) ingestion lowers cerebral blood flow (CBF), likely due to reduced arterial carbon dioxide (PaCO2). We tested the hypothesis that maintaining end-tidal CO2 (PETCO2; surrogate for PaCO2) following KME ingestion would prevent reductions in CBF and improve cerebrovascular reactivity (CVR) to CO2 compared to free-breathing. In a single-blinded randomized crossover design, twenty-three adults (age=22±2 yrs) ingested 0.6 g·kg-1 KME and breathed either room air (poikilocapnia) or a gas mixture that clamped PETCO2 at baseline (isocapnia) for 60 min. CVR to CO2 was assessed at targeted PETCO2 of +3, +6, and +9 mmHg above baseline. CBF was assessed using duplex ultrasound of extracranial arteries and transcranial Doppler ultrasound of the middle cerebral artery. Venous β-hydroxybutyrate, pH, and bicarbonate were measured. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, 45-, and 60-min post-supplementation. PETCO2 was higher during isocapnia at 45 min (3.9±3.8 mmHg; P<0.001) and 60 min (4.4±3.8 mmHg; P<0.001) post-supplementation corresponding with 15% higher CBF compared to poikilocapnia (P<0.001). Blood pH was reduced during isocapnia (P<0.001), whereas it was unchanged in poikilocapnia (P=0.246), suggesting that the ventilatory response to KME ingestion effectively buffered metabolic acidosis in poikilocapnia. CVR to CO2 was reduced following KME ingestion regardless of condition (P<0.001). Exploratory analyses demonstrated that biological sex did not alter cerebrovascular responses to KME ingestion. This work confirms that reductions in CBF and CVR to CO2 following KME ingestion are due to reduced PaCO2 in response to metabolic acidosis. Strategies that buffer metabolic acidosis likely will mitigate CBF reductions following acute KME ingestion.

articles.title: Assessing Skeletal Muscle Reactive Hyperemia with Intramuscular Doppler Ultrasound: Insights from Exercise-Trained and Untrained Adults.
articles.authors: Olavo João Frederico Ramos Junior, Maria Clara Ramos Souza Rodrigues, Paola Quevedo da Costa et al.
articles.abstract: Power Doppler ultrasound can detect low-velocity blood-flow signals within skeletal muscle, providing a spatially localized, semiquantitative index of intramuscular blood flow (IMBF). Whether this signal can characterize post-occlusive reactive hyperemia (RH), distinguish populations with different vascular responsiveness, and correlate with established indices of RH is unknown. We examined whether power Doppler-derived IMBF can be used to evaluate skeletal muscle RH following arterial occlusion, distinguish hyperemic responses between resistance-trained and untrained adults, and correlate with near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS)-derived total hemoglobin ([tHb]) and tissue oxygen saturation (StO2) reperfusion slopes and brachial artery RH blood flow. Forty-four adults (24 trained, 20 untrained) underwent a vascular occlusion test with simultaneous power Doppler IMBF, NIRS, and brachial artery Doppler assessments. IMBF was quantified as the percentage of Doppler-positive pixels within a standardized region of interest in the extensor carpi radialis muscle. RH-IMBF0-60 and RH-IMBF0-TTP were defined as the area under the IMBF curve from cuff deflation to 60s and to the individual time-to-peak (TTP), respectively. RH-IMBF0-TTP and RH-IMBF0-60 were greater in trained individuals (P<0.001), as were the [tHb] and StO2 reperfusion slopes (both P<0.001), RH-blood flow, and peak blood flow (both P=0.001). RH-IMBF0-60 correlated with the [tHb] slope (r=0.624), StO2 slope (r=0.535), and RH-blood flow (r=0.597) (all P<0.001). These findings demonstrate that Power Doppler-derived IMBF is sensitive to post-occlusion reperfusion, distinguishes hyperemic responses between trained and untrained adults, and correlates with established indices of RH, providing proof-of-principle evidence for its application as an accessible, spatially localized, complementary approach for assessing skeletal muscle vascular reactivity.

articles.title: HIV proteins disrupt a network of phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate binding sites on the dopamine transporter to regulate amphetamine behaviours.
articles.authors: Yanqi Zhu, Diksha Parwana, Heinrich J G Matthies et al.
articles.abstract: Amphetamine (AMPH) use has been linked to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) transmission because HIV can spread through unprotected sex that is associated with AMPH use disorder (AUD). Thus, AUD and HIV have been termed a double epidemic. In this bidirectional relationship, the role played by AUD in HIV-dependent neuropathogenesis is well documented. By contrast, how HIV infection regulates the development of AUD remains elusive. In rodents, expression of HIV viral proteins, such as the trans-activator of transcription (Tat), enhances AMPH escalation (i.e. a progressive intensification of drug use), a Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) criteria for addiction. In humans, HIV infection increases AMPH frequency of use, as well as the total amount used. Thus, it is possible that HIV/HIV proteins promote the progression of AUD. AMPH-associated behaviours stem, at least in part, from the ability of AMPH to reverse the dopamine (DA) transporter (DAT) function, causing non-vesicular DA release (NVDR) and an increase in extracellular DA. Previously, we provided the first evidence that specific domains of DAT engage in direct association with the plasma membrane lipid, phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2). These interactions are essential for AMPH-induced NVDR and specific behaviours. HIV Tat is a protein that binds PIP2 through its basic domain. We demonstrate that Tat impairs NVDR by disrupting the network of PIP2 binding sites on DAT. Our study provides an atomic scale mechanistic description on how Tat disrupts human DAT/PIP2 association and blunts AMPH-induced NVDR. Using Drosophila as an animal model, we show that Tat by blunting NVDR in the setting of AUD promotes AMPH escalation. KEY POINTS: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) trans-activator of transcription (Tat) impairs non-vesicular dopamine (DA) release (NVDR) by disrupting the network of PIP2 binding sites on human Da transporter (DAT). Our study provides an atomic scale mechanistic description on how Tat disrupts human DAT/phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate association and blunts amphetamine (AMPH)-induced NVDR. We associate Tat blunting of NVDR to the ability of Tat to foster AMPH escalation, using Drosophila as an animal model.

articles.title: Immediate transcranial magnetic stimulation-evoked potentials reveal short-latency intracortical inhibition.
articles.authors: Lasse Christiansen, Yufei Song, Ditte Haagerup et al.
articles.abstract: Short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI) is the most widely used neurophysiological index of GABAergic inhibition in the human cortex. However, it is an indirect measure, inferring synaptic inhibition from suppression of peripherally recorded motor-evoked potentials (MEPs) elicited by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). In the standard protocol, a subthreshold conditioning pulse suppresses the MEP evoked by a suprathreshold test pulse delivered 1-5 ms later. Interpretation is further complicated by temporal overlap with short-interval intracortical facilitation (SICF), reflecting excitatory interactions at interstimulus intervals of ∼1.5 and 2.7 ms. To overcome these limitations, we recorded immediate TMS-evoked EEG potentials (iTEPs; 1-10 ms post-stimulus) as a more direct measure of motor cortical activity in 16 healthy volunteers (20-35 years; seven male). The conventional SICI protocol suppressed only later components of the iTEP, probably corresponding to late corticospinal volleys previously identified in epidural spinal recordings after suprathreshold TMS, while the earliest iTEP component was unaffected. Importantly, later iTEPs were suppressed to a similar extent whether conditioning-test intervals coincided with SICF peaks or troughs, and the magnitude of iTEP suppression correlated with concurrently recorded paired-pulse MEP suppression. SICI also reduced an early TEP component (N15; 10-20 ms), but paired-pulse N15 suppression showed a different dependence on stimulus intensity and did not correlate with MEP suppression. These findings demonstrate that SICI measured via MEPs does not reflect a global index of cortical GABAergic motor cortical inhibition but instead reflects inhibition within specific cortical circuits that can be investigated more directly with iTEPs. KEY POINTS: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over the primary motor cortex evokes high-frequency activity in the corticospinal tract, which can be measured directly with invasive, epidural recordings or indirectly as a time-locked, compound EMG response [i.e. motor evoked potential (MEP)]. GABAergic intracortical inhibition can be indexed as the MEP suppression caused by a subthreshold TMS pulse preceding the suprathreshold pulse by 1-5 ms. Combining TMS with artifact-minimized EEG allows the assessment of paired-pulse inhibition of immediate and early peaks of TMS-evoked EEG potential (TEP). Both immediate TEP (iTEP) and early TEP peaks display paired-pulse inhibition but only iTEP suppression relates to MEP suppression. iTEPs enable investigations of intracortical interactions non-invasively at the cortical level, which enables assessment of cortical and corticospinal physiology with TMS even in the absence of MEPs.

articles.title: Allostatic load is not associated with augmented vasoconstrictive response to cold pressor test or functional sympatholysis in Black emerging adults.
articles.authors: Emily F Blake, Lauren E Eagan, Cynthia M Weiner et al.
articles.abstract: Black individuals are disproportionately affected by hypertension (HTN), even after controlling for conventional risk factors (i.e., obesity, smoking, physical fitness). Emerging evidence implicates chronic psychosocial stress, including discrimination/race-related events, in HTN development. Allostatic load (AL) reflects the cumulative adverse impact of repeated activation of compensatory physiological responses to psychosocial stressors. We assessed the associations between AL and disruptions in vascular parameters that may indicate heightened HTN risk in Black emerging adults. Forearm blood flow (FBF) and vascular conductance (FVC) were measured during sympathoexcitation (cold pressor test; CPT), alone and with handgrip exercise, (EX + CPT) in 35 Black undergraduate students (24F/11M, 20 ± 1 years). AL was determined using both clinical cutoffs (AL-CC) and individual z-scores (AL-z) from nine biomarkers (heart rate, systolic blood pressure (BP), diastolic BP, C-reactive protein, glucose, creatinine, total cholesterol/HDL-C ratio, cortisol, %body fat). Higher scores reflected greater AL burden. AL scores were overall low (AL-z: 0.003 ± 3.9; AL-CC: 1.6 ± 1.2). Reductions in FBF and FVC during EX + CPT (∆FBF: -3.58% ± 3.14%; ∆FVC: -12.56% ± 6.77%) were significantly attenuated (P < 0.001) as compared to CPT alone (∆FBF: -24.15% ± 7.95%; ∆FVC: -35.54% ± 9.20%). AL was not correlated with CPT-FBF, -FVC or with functional sympatholysis magnitude (%); however, blunted diurnal cortisol slope correlated with larger reductions in CPT-FBF (r = -0.55, P = 0.00328), and increased FBF- (r = 0.49, P = 0.00957) and FVC- (r = 0.43, P = 0.0283) lysis. These findings suggest hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysregulation in Black emerging adults may elicit exaggerated vasoreactivity to sympathoexcitatory stress.

articles.title: Revisiting Tandler's model: Developmental anatomy of the gastrointestinal arteries and the embryological basis of human variants.
articles.authors: Daniel Gondorf, George Triantafyllou, Maria Piagkou
articles.abstract: The arterial supply of the foregut, midgut, and hindgut is commonly interpreted through the classical Tandler-Felix model, in which ventral splanchnic roots and a longitudinal anastomotic channel undergo selective persistence, regression, and remodeling. Although this framework is widely used to explain adult coeliac, mesenteric, and hepatic arterial variants, the evidence for individual developmental mechanisms remains uneven. This critical narrative review re-examines the classical model against historical primary observations, contemporary human embryological and early fetal studies, adult anatomical and radiological series, and recent meta-analyses of arterial variation. This review emphasizes separating directly observed human developmental events from comparative evidence and retrospective interpretations based on adult morphology. Modern serial histology and three-dimensional reconstruction demonstrate marked variability during superior mesenteric artery and intestinal-branch formation, underscoring that definitive adult branching patterns emerge through dynamic remodeling rather than a rigid predetermined sequence. Coeliac-mesenteric common trunks, hepatic arteries of mesenteric origin, and the arc of Bühler are anatomically compatible with persistence or altered interruption of classical connections, but most specific mechanisms remain inferential. Retropancreatic topography can support developmental homology but cannot prove it on its own, and primitive longitudinal superior-inferior mesenteric arteries continuity is less directly documented than is often implied. An evidence-graded developmental framework is therefore proposed to integrate embryology, adult variation, and clinical anatomy while avoiding overstatement of historical models.

articles.title: Natural-abundance carbon isotope profiling of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid supplement incorporation in extremely preterm infants: a sub-study of the Mega Donna Mega randomized clinical trial.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Chuck T Chen, Ulrika Sjöbom, Mats X Andersson et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Extremely preterm infants are deprived of most third-trimester long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid accretion. In the Mega Donna Mega trial, enteral arachidonic acid (ARA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) supplementation reduced severe retinopathy of prematurity despite modest early changes in circulating levels. OBJECTIVE: We investigated whether natural-abundance carbon isotope ratio (δ13C) profiling detects early entry of supplemented ARA and DHA into circulating phospholipids in extremely preterm infants. METHODS: This sub-study of the randomized Mega Donna Mega trial included 25 infants born before 25+2 weeks' gestation who received standard-of-care nutrition (SOC, n=12) or enteral ARA+DHA supplementation (intervention, n=13; 100 and 50 mg/kg/day, respectively) from ≤3 days after birth until 40 weeks' postmenstrual age. Serum phospholipid fatty acid composition and δ13C values were determined at Day 0-3, 10-16, 34-47, and 75-87. Group differences were assessed with mixed models of treatment group by sampling window. RESULTS: Between-group differences in ARA and DHA weight percent (wt%) emerged late in the intervention (Day 75-87, mean [SD]: ARA 10.1 [2.0] versus 6.9 [1.4]; DHA 3.3 [1.0] versus 2.3 [0.7]). ARA and DHA δ13C were similar between groups at Day 0-3 and higher in supplemented infants from Day 10-16 (difference [95% CI]: ARA 1.9 [0.9, 2.8] mUr; DHA 2.0 [0.3, 3.6] mUr). The group-by-window interaction was significant for ARA δ13C (p=0.007) but not for DHA δ13C (p=0.11; p=0.005 after excluding one infant with necrotizing enterocolitis and low compliance). CONCLUSIONS: Natural-abundance δ13C profiling showed that supplemented ARA and DHA were bioavailable and entered circulating phospholipids within two weeks of birth, before clear separation in fatty acid composition. Concentration-based biomarkers may underestimate early exposure to supplemented fatty acids in extremely preterm infants. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03201588, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03201588.

articles.title: Effects of Moderate Weight Loss on the Thermic Effect of Food and Postprandial Substrate Oxidation in Healthy Normal-Weight Adults.
articles.journal: Applied physiology, nutrition, and metabolism = Physiologie appliquee, nutrition et metabolisme
articles.authors: Noémie Beauregard, Léna Pélissier, Ines Ramos et al.
articles.abstract: While most weight-loss research focuses on individuals with obesity, normal-weight individuals also frequently attempt to lose weight through dietary restriction. However, the effects of weight loss on the thermic effect of food, a less well-studied component of total energy expenditure, remain poorly documented in this population. Normal-weight adults (age = 23.3 ± 3.8 years, BMI = 22.8 ± 1.9 kg.m-2) achieved 3% (n = 32, 23 females) and 6% (n = 18, 11 females) reductions in initial body weight. Postprandial energy expenditure and substrate oxidation were assessed following consumption of a standardized breakfast. Compared with baseline, TEF slightly increased after 3% weight loss (β = 0.05 kcal·min⁻¹, 95% CI 0.018-0.084; p = 0.002) but did not differ from baseline after 6% weight loss. Total postprandial fat oxidation increased at both 3% and 6% weight loss compared with baseline, whereas total carbohydrate oxidation decreased at both time points. Future studies should determine whether larger magnitudes of weight loss, longer-term energy restriction, or weight loss achieved through increased energy expenditure, elicit changes in TEF and how such changes may influence long-term energy balance.

articles.title: 24-hour Movement Guideline Adherence and Cardiometabolic Health among Adults with Disabilities: Analysis of NHANES 2013-2018.
articles.journal: Applied physiology, nutrition, and metabolism = Physiologie appliquee, nutrition et metabolisme
articles.authors: Yahan Liang, Xihe Zhu, Justin Haegele
articles.abstract: A growing body of evidence has examined the association between adherence to the 24-hour movement guidelines and cardiometabolic health outcomes. However, it remains unclear whether these associations extend to adults with disabilities, a population experiencing substantial health disparities. Therefore, this study examined the association between adherence to the 24-hour movement guidelines and cardiometabolic health among adults with disabilities. This cross-sectional study used data from the 2013-2018 cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). A nationally representative sample of U.S. adults with disabilities (n = 4,985) was included. Survey-weighted logistic regression models with multiple imputation were used to examine associations between guideline adherence and cardiometabolic health. Subgroup analyses were conducted across cardiometabolic outcomes and functional disability types. The results showed that participants meeting three guidelines had higher odds of being free from cardiovascular disease (AOR = 2.05, 95% CI: 1.42-2.94), obesity (AOR = 1.99, 95% CI: 1.44-2.75), hypertension (AOR = 1.75, 95% CI: 1.22-2.50) and type 2 diabetes (AOR = 1.60, 95% CI: 1.14-2.24), than those meeting none of the guidelines. Meeting two guidelines was associated with higher odds of being free from hypertension and obesity. Associations between guideline adherence and cardiometabolic health varied across functional disability subgroups. These findings suggest that adherence to a greater number of movement guidelines is associated with having more favorable cardiometabolic health profiles for adults with disabilities. Exploratory subgroup analyses showed variation in the associations across disability types, further research is needed to determine whether associations differ across functional impairment groups and whether movement recommendations should be tailored accordingly.

articles.title: A single bout of intermittent hypoxia provides an inhibitory control benefit across the continuum of low- to high-fit young adults.
articles.authors: Antonio Mendes, Nasimi A Guluzade, Emma D F X Miller et al.
articles.abstract: Exposure to brief alternating intervals of hypoxic and normoxic breathing (i.e., intermittent hypoxia: IH) increases cerebral blood flow (CBF) and is a change linked to a post-intervention executive function (EF) benefit. It is, however, unknown whether cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) influences the benefit. This is a salient question because individuals with higher CRF show increased CBF and more efficient dynamic cerebral autoregulation in response to environmental stressors - a change that may potentiate post-IH EF benefits. Here, healthy young adults classified as high-fit (n = 18: V ̇ O 2 peak range: 42-75 mL/kg/min) and low-fit (n = 18: V ̇ O 2 peak range: 13-35 mL/kg/min) completed a 60-min IH condition involving alternating 5-min intervals of hypoxic ( P ET O 2 = 50 mmHg) and normoxic (room air: P ET O 2 ≈ 90-95 mmHg) breathing (IH condition), and on a separate day completed a same duration normoxic control condition. During both conditions, participants' end-tidal carbon dioxide was maintained at a baseline level (i.e., normocapnic). Near-infrared spectroscopy and transcranial Doppler ultrasound measured cortical haemodynamics, and the antisaccade task was used to assess EF at baseline (T0), and at immediate (T1), and 30-min post-intervention (T2) timepoints. Results showed that high- and low-fit individuals produced an equivalent magnitude reduction in cortical oxygenation and increase in middle cerebral artery velocity (MCAv) during hypoxic intervals. Both groups produced an equivalent magnitude reduction in antisaccade reaction times at T2, and this benefit was unrelated to changes in cortical oxygenation or MCAv. Thus, a single bout of IH confers a delayed EF benefit across low- to high-fit individuals, potentially reflecting multiple interacting (neuro)physiological changes.

articles.title: Identifying Players' Performance Profiles in Elite Men and Women 3 × 3 Basketball: Evidence From the Olympic Games.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Shaoliang Zhang, Lorenzo Gasperi, Miguel-Angel Gomez-Ruano et al.
articles.abstract: Zhang, S, Gasperi, L, Gomez-Ruano, M-A, Conte, D, and Sansone, P. Identifying player's performance profiles in elite men and women 3×3 basketball: Evidence from the Olympic Games. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to cluster the performance profiles of elite male and female 3 × 3 basketball players according to their stature. Data from the 2021 and 2024 Olympic Games were retrieved, involving 128 players (64 per sex). The players' stature was noted, alongside the game-related statistics (GRS) for all tournament games. Two-step cluster analyses classified male and female players according to their stature, whereas comparisons of GRS across clusters were performed using independent samples t test, Mann-Whitney U test, or 1-way ANOVA. For men, 2 clusters were identified: perimeter and internal. The analyses of performance profiles showed how perimeter players registered more 2-point shots made, 2-point shots attempted, key assists, and drives than internal players (all p < 0.05, effect size [ES]: small-moderate), whereas internal players had more 1-point shots made, 1-point shots attempted, free-throws attempted, and blocked shots than perimeter players (all p < 0.05, ES: small-moderate). For women, 3 clusters were identified: perimeter, all around, and internal. Perimeter players achieved more 2-point shots made, 2-point shots attempted, and drives than internal players (all p < 0.05, ES: moderate-large). All-around players only differed from internal players in their lower 1-point shots attempted (p = 0.043, ES: moderate). Internal players recorded more 1-point shots made than both perimeter and all-around players (all p < 0.05, ES: moderate) and more defensive rebounds than perimeter players (p = 0.010, ES: moderate). Current results provide initial information on the positional performance profile of elite male and female 3 × 3 basketball players, which can inform player selection, talent identification, strength and conditioning practices, and technical-tactical strategies.

articles.title: Effect of Interrepetition Rest Set Structures on Total Volume, Velocity Loss, and Rating of Perceived Exertion Accuracy.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Caitlyn M Meehan, Timothy B Davies, Jake A Ridenoure et al.
articles.abstract: Meehan, CM, Davies, TB, Ridenoure, JA, Gotla, TX, Thompson, BK, Walpole, KJ, Watson, BA, and Colquhoun, RJ. Effect of interrepetition rest set structures on total volume, velocity loss, and rating of perceived exertion accuracy. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The purpose of this study was to examine differences between traditional sets (TS) and 2 different interrepetition rest (IRR) set structures on the amount of volume able to be performed, velocity loss (VL), and rating of perceived exertion (RPE) accuracy across sets to a fixed RPE in the back squat. Twenty (10 males and 10 females) healthy, resistance-trained subjects reported to the laboratory for a 1 repetition maximum visit and 3 experimental visits in the back squat, where subjects were randomized into a different protocol for each visit. The 3 experimental visits consisted of a set to an 8 and 10+ RPE in the following conditions: (a) TS that involved 0 seconds of intraset rest and 180 seconds of interset rest (TS); (b) IRR that involved 40 seconds of intraset rest and 180 seconds of interset rest (IRR-180); and (c) IRR that involved 40 seconds of intraset rest and 40 seconds of interset rest (IRR-40). Our results indicate that the number of repetitions completed was significantly greater in IRR-180 and IRR-40 when compared with TS (p < 0.001-0.030). In addition, despite greater volume completed in IRR-180 and IRR-40, VL was significantly lower in these conditions (-17.7% ± 4.6% and -18.1% ± 4.5%, respectively) when compared with TS (-24.7 ± 8.6%; p = 0.019). Finally, RPE accuracy was significantly greater in TS when compared with both IRR-180 and IRR-40 (p < 0.001). The present data suggest that IRR set structures allow for additional volume to be performed compared with TS when exertion is held constant, without increasing mechanical fatigue.

articles.title: 3D Biomechanics of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries in Football: What We Have Learned in the Last Five Years.
articles.authors: Matteo Zago, Francesco Della Villa
articles.abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture is among the most impacting injuries in professional football. Understanding these injuries in their environment, and their biomechanical mechanism, is the bottleneck between injury surveillance and effective mechanism-informed prevention and rehabilitation. We reconstructed the three-dimensional kinematics of 33 cases of ACL injury sustained by elite male football players during official matches. The Model-Based Image-Matching technique was leveraged to obtain quantitative, detailed estimates of three-dimensional joint kinematics, thereby overcoming the limitations of traditional bidimensional video analyses. This paper reviews and interprets findings derived from over five years of research on the topic from a novel perspective. At the knee level, ACL injury mechanics involved a sequence of multiplanar joint rotations; on the sagittal plane, knee flexion increased from initial contact to injury frame; on the frontal plane, a knee abduction (valgus) shift emerged; on the transverse plane, following ground contact, we observed a sequence of internal and then external rotation of the femur, relative to the tibia, occurring during loading acceptance. Expanding the analysis on total-body kinematics, marked inter-individual variability was observed across the studied cohort; while ACL failure exhibits consistent kinematic features at the knee level, the sequence of whole-body postures leading to injury appears to be context-dependent. Finally, we propose biomechanically informed approaches to injury mitigation, emphasizing the integration of sport-specific contextual determinants, perceptual and decision-making processes, challenging the traditional separation between technical coaching and injury prevention.

articles.title: Individualized Amplitude-Time Models of Post-activation Performance Enhancement Using the Velocity-Loss Method in Trained Populations: A Systematic Review and Individual Participant Data Meta-analysis.
articles.authors: Jun Li, Kai Xu, Yuming Zhong et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Five study-level models describe post-activation performance enhancement (PAPE) amplitude-time characteristics: (i) nil or fluctuating, (ii) immediate enhancement, (iii) inverted-U enhancement, (iv) skewed or delayed inverted-U enhancement, and (v) performance impairment. However, the moderators of these models at the individual level remain unclear. Velocity-loss (VL) approaches, which reflect neuromuscular fatigue, may provide a useful framework to better understand these amplitude-time characteristics. OBJECTIVES: The aims of this study were (i) to establish an individualized PAPE amplitude-time model using VL-based conditioning activities (CAs); (ii) to examine how relative maximal strength (RMS) affects performance changes across recovery times at the individual level; and (iii) to investigate how VL methods influence study-level PAPE amplitude-time characteristics through within- and between-study analyses. METHODS: Three databases were systematically searched. Studies were included if CA involved squats or bench presses prescribed using the VL method and reported performance outcomes reflecting PAPE magnitude. Individual performance-recovery relationships were modeled using linear and nonlinear regression. A generalized linear mixed-effects model was applied to analyze the one-stage (individual participant data) effects of RMS on performance changes, while a three-level (multilevel) model was used for two-stage (study-level) meta-analysis. Multivariate linear and nonlinear models tested moderators including recovery time, sex, CA type, VL threshold, %1-repetition maximum (RM), and number of sets. RESULTS: Fifteen studies were included, with individual data from nine studies (248 participants: 224 males, 24 females). Individual performance-recovery responses generally matched the five established study-level PAPE amplitude-time patterns, though random deviations were observed. One-stage analyses revealed that individuals with low RMS (< ~ 1.5, unstable estimates) exhibited early enhancement followed by decline, whereas those with high RMS (> ~ 1.5) showed early decrements followed by an inverted-U response. Greater RMS was linked to smaller peak improvements (β = - 2.65) but was unrelated to minimum values (β = - 0.86). In females, maximal improvements occurred at RMS ~ 1.00-1.25, with lowest minimum values at ~ 1.25-1.50. Two-stage analyses indicated that VL alone did not significantly improve performance (standardized mean change = 0.11), but yielded greater improvements than control conditions (rest or traditional CA; standardized mean difference = 0.35). Recovery time, %1-RM, and VL threshold emerged as key moderators. CONCLUSIONS: Individual PAPE amplitude-time models exhibited random deviations from, but generally reflected, study-level patterns. Strength level influenced individual responses, with distinct PAPE profiles observed across participants. At the study level, 5% VL, 10% VL, and 60-90% 1-RM CAs appeared most effective for inducing peak PAPE responses. However, at the individual level, there was no single 'optimal' prescription, only a 'most suitable' one. PROTOCOL REGISTRATION: The original protocol was prospectively registered ( osf.io/hf6px ) with the Open Science Framework.

articles.title: A comprehensive review of craniomandibular morphometric indices in carnivora: Anatomical basis, functional significance, and comparative applications.
articles.authors: Babak Rasouli
articles.abstract: The skull of carnivorans represents a highly integrated anatomical structure shaped by selective pressures associated with feeding ecology, sensory specialization, locomotion, and phylogenetic history. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of craniomandibular morphometric indices in the order Carnivora, integrating their anatomical definitions, morphometric foundations, and functional significance. Standardized cranial and mandibular measurements are reviewed together with 11 widely used proportional indices, including the Cranial Index (CI), Skull Index (SI), Facial Index (FI), Facial Length Index (FLI), Cranial Length Index (CLI), Cranial Height Index (CHI), Orbital Index (OI), Palatal Index (PI), Foramen Magnum Index (FMI), Mandibular Body Index (MBI), and Mandibular Ramus Index (MRI). The review highlights the biomechanical and evolutionary relevance of these indices by examining their relationships with bite performance, craniofacial organization, sensory adaptations, feeding ecology, and morphological diversification among carnivoran families. In addition to summarizing published morphometric indices, several proportional indices that have rarely been reported as independent variables are derived from previously published linear craniometric measurements, providing standardized quantitative descriptors for comparative analyses across species. By compiling anatomical landmarks, measurement protocols, functional interpretations, and comparative data within a unified framework, this review identifies current knowledge gaps and promotes greater methodological consistency in future studies. Although some proportional indices were calculated from published measurements rather than directly reported in the original literature, they provide valuable complementary metrics for evaluating cranial and mandibular morphology. Overall, the integration of these 11 morphometric indices offers a comprehensive approach for investigating craniofacial evolution, functional morphology, feeding adaptations, and taxonomic diversity in both extant and fossil carnivorans. This review provides a practical reference for researchers in comparative anatomy, evolutionary biology, paleontology, and veterinary morphology.
