articles.title: Silent Teachers in Anatomical Education: A Historical Review of Paradigm Shifts in Human Cadaver Procurement Since Ancient Persia.
articles.authors: Seyed Behnamedin Jameie, Setareh Nejadrostam, Melika Jameie et al.
articles.abstract: Human cadaveric dissection has played an important role in the development of anatomical knowledge and remains an established component of medical education. The availability of human bodies for anatomical study has varied across historical periods, reflecting changes in educational institutions, procurement practices, and ethical and sociocultural considerations. This narrative review examines the historical development of human dissection and cadaver procurement, with particular emphasis on Iran. Relevant literature was identified through searches of MEDLINE via PubMed and supplemented by historical publications, scholarly sources, locally sourced literature and contextual information, reference-list screening, and citation tracking. The literature was synthesized chronologically and thematically to examine the development of anatomical knowledge, the emergence of modern anatomy education in Iran, and reported changes in cadaver procurement practices. The historical literature documents a long tradition of medical scholarship and anatomical knowledge in Iran, followed by the gradual development of formal anatomy education through modern medical institutions. Reported sources of cadavers for anatomical education in Iran have included unclaimed bodies, imported cadavers, and voluntary body donation. However, the available evidence is insufficient to establish a comprehensive chronology of these practices or to determine their relative contributions across institutions and historical periods. The increasing recognition of voluntary body donation represents an important development in contemporary anatomical education, alongside continuing ethical and sociocultural considerations concerning informed consent, respect for human remains, and public acceptance. Cadaveric dissection continues to be used alongside alternative teaching approaches, including anatomical models and digital technologies. The historical development of cadaver procurement in Iran reflects broader changes in anatomical education and institutional practice. Further research based on historical records and institutional documentation is needed to clarify the chronology of procurement practices and their implications for contemporary anatomical education and ethical governance.

articles.title: Paleontological and paleoenvironmental analyses of the Barro Alto site: A window to the mid Permian of western Gondwana.
articles.authors: Douglas da Silva Strattmann, Amanda Goulart Rodrigues, Pedro Lucas de Barros Pruciano et al.
articles.abstract: The Barro Alto fossil site (Rio Grande do Sul State, Brazil) is considered a prolific place for understanding the Guadalupian (Wordian) vertebrate diversity, especially for tetrapods and cartilaginous fishes. However, its paleoenvironmental context has not been deeply discussed in the literature. The present work aims to integrate previous and new paleontological data for this fossiliferous site and provide the depositional context for the Permian fauna of the Rio do Rasto Formation (Paraná Basin) at the Barro Alto site. The stratigraphic columnar profile is divided into six sedimentary facies grouped into two facies associations, which were integrated with paleontological and petrological data. The association of facies suggests that the paleoenvironmental context for the Barro Alto fossil site consists of a lacustrine paleoenvironment with seasonal variations in water levels and sediment influx, being eventually invaded by river channels. Furthermore, it contained a remarkable diversity of vertebrate remains, with bony (both Actinopterygii and Sarcopterygii) and cartilaginous fishes, terrestrial tetrapods from different groups such as anomodont synapsids, archosauromorphs, and temnospondyls, besides coprolites and plant remains. Additionally, recent paleontological studies involving the Karoo basin in South Africa may suggest a geochronological repositioning of the Barro Alto site to the Wordian due to biostratigraphic relationships between South African and Brazilian taxa.

articles.title: Mechanistic investigation of central, coronary, and arterial hemodynamics during lower body negative pressure using a validated 0D-1D cardiovascular model.
articles.authors: Francesco Tripoli, Luca Ridolfi, Jerry J Batzel et al.
articles.abstract: Lower body negative pressure (LBNP) is used in physiological and space medicine research as a tool to simulate central hypovolemia and orthostatic loading. Despite its extensive application, hemodynamic characterization is fragmented due to limitations in current acquisition methodologies and substantial inter-individual variability in LBNP-induced cardiovascular responses. This study presents an advanced multiscale 0D-1D cardiovascular model to investigate the hemodynamic response to graded LBNP (0 to -50 mmHg). The model combines a 1D representation of the arterial and coronary trees with a 0D description of the peripheral, venous, cardiopulmonary, coronary, and cerebro-ocular circulations. The model accounts for short-term regulatory mechanisms (i.e., baroreflex, cardiopulmonary reflex, and cerebral autoregulation) and includes transcapillary fluid exchange and lymphatic return to the heart. Model outcomes were validated against in vivo measurements obtained during a previously published graded LBNP experimental study. Once validated, the model enabled a detailed investigation of cardiac and arterial hemodynamics, including ventricular mechano-energetic and oxygen consumption parameters, coronary circulation, and pressure wave propagation throughout the arterial tree. The simulations revealed a greater mechano-energetic vulnerability of the right ventricle compared with the left ventricle, whereas coronary blood flow remained nearly constant despite the increase in rate-pressure product at higher LBNP levels. Wave propagation analysis revealed variations limited to the lower-limb arteries due to elevated transmural pressure and arterial stiffening. The proposed in silico - in vivo framework provides a comprehensive description of cardiovascular responses to LBNP, offering mechanistic insights that are difficult to obtain experimentally.

articles.title: Plasma Amino Acid Responses to an Oral Glucose Challenge Relate More Strongly to Obesity Than to Insulin Resistance.
articles.journal: American journal of physiology. Endocrinology and metabolism
articles.authors: Eduardo D S Freitas, Kailin A Johnson, Matthew Buras et al.
articles.abstract: The coexistence of obesity and insulin resistance is associated with elevated plasma amino acid concentrations. However, it remains unclear whether obesity or insulin resistance is more strongly associated with plasma amino acid dysregulation. Twenty-one adults were studied spanning a broad range of obesity and insulin resistance, and who underwent an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). Insulin resistance was assessed in the basal state using the homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) and during the OGTT from the OGTT-derived plasma glucose and insulin responses, using the Matsuda insulin sensitivity index (Matsuda-ISI). Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed greater clustering of amino acid responses according to obesity-related measures (body mass index, body fat, body fat percentage, and waist circumference), as well as HOMA-IR and Matsuda-ISI, during the OGTT-stimulated state compared with the fasting state. Regression analyses showed statistically significant models (P < 0.05) only for branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) in both the fasting and OGTT-stimulated states. The models explained 59% and 67% of the variance in BCAA outcomes in the fasting and OGTT-stimulated states, respectively. A composite obesity score, derived from the obesity-related measures, was a significant predictor of BCAAs in both states, whereas indices of insulin resistance/sensitivity were not. In conclusion, these exploratory findings show that plasma amino acids, specifically BCAAs, are more closely related to obesity than to insulin resistance, with these differences in plasma amino acid profiles becoming more evident during an OGTT-stimulated state than in the fasting state.

articles.title: Modeling intersegmental mechanics to reproduce physiologic coordination patterns of multi-joint finger movements.
articles.authors: Orooluwa D Emmanuel, Quang D Tran, Derek G Kamper et al.
articles.abstract: Biomechanical models of the hand are important for understanding the functional roles of individual muscles to facilitate rehabilitation planning or prediction of surgical outcomes. Interpreting the contributions of specific hand muscles is challenging, however, because of the complex anatomy of the hand, including multiarticular muscles, distributed tendon insertions, and soft tissue structures. Most existing biomechanical models estimate joint torques based primarily on geometric moment arms and therefore rely on a kinematic representation of muscle action. In this study, we developed a dynamic biomechanical model of the index finger that incorporates intersegmental mechanical interactions arising from tendon pathways, adhesions, and ligamentous constraints (model 1: 'intersegmental mechanics model'), enabling more accurate prediction of multi-joint coordination patterns produced by individual musculotendons. The performance of the proposed model was compared with that of a conventional kinematic model (model 2: 'individual joint moment-arm model'). Both models were used to simulate index finger movements driven by individual muscle forces. Predicted joint coordination patterns were compared with experimental data collected from in vitro and in vivo studies. Model 1 reproduced multi-joint coordination patterns more accurately than Model 2, producing lower RMSE values in 26 of 27 submovements. This advantage was most evident for intrinsic plus and intrinsic minus movements, suggesting that intersegmental mechanical interactions are important for reproducing intrinsic muscle-driven coordination patterns relevant to hand function. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating intersegmental dynamics into finger modeling and suggest that the proposed framework may provide a useful tool for studying hand function and its impairment.

articles.title: The effect of prosthetic alignment and multiplanar deformation of a single prosthetic foot on musculoskeletal model predictions in unilateral transtibial prosthesis users.
articles.authors: Jannis Hill, Cleveland T Barnett, Paul J Felton
articles.abstract: Prosthetic design and alignment are optimised to benefit prostheses users. Computer simulations can help to explain how prosthetic changes affect prosthesis users' bodies but often neglect some prosthetic design characteristics. This study explores how including non-sagittal plane deformation of the prosthetic foot and prosthetic foot to socket alignment affect prosthetic limb joint angles and joint moments. A lower-body musculoskeletal model using kinematic and kinetic data of overground running from unilateral transtibial prostheses users. The model incorporated a prosthetic foot scaled to each participant for four model variations (1) two to account for individual prosthetic alignment and (2) two to account for non-sagittal internal deformation of the prosthetic foot. Comparisons were made between prosthetic limb joint angles and normalised joint moment time histories and peaks. Correlations between prosthetic foot to socket offsets and peaks were also assessed. Prosthetic alignment changes caused small variations in angle and moment comparisons, but medio-lateral alignment correlated strongly with non-sagittal angles and moments (r > 0.80). Allowing for three-dimensional deformation in the model of the prosthetic foot resulted in generally small variations in joint angles and moments but were highest in non-sagittal planes. These were more pronounced during a run with a higher degree of non-sagittal plane loading. Therefore, accounting for individual alignment of transtibial prostheses users in inverse simulations may not be necessary, but care is warranted with greater medio-lateral offsets. Also, modelling non-sagittal prosthetic intersegmental movement may impact non-sagittal kinematics and kinetics during movements with high non-sagittal plane loading.

articles.title: Normative values of spatiotemporal parameters and three-dimensional gait kinematics in 500 healthy Korean individuals: Age- and sex-stratified reference data.
articles.authors: Woo Sub Kim, Moon Seok Park, Ki Hyuk Sung
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Normative gait kinematic data are essential for interpreting pathological gait and evaluating treatment outcomes, but Korean population-specific reference data covering both age strata and sex remain limited. RESEARCH QUESTION: What are the age- and sex-stratified normative values of spatiotemporal parameters and three-dimensional lower-extremity gait kinematics in healthy Korean adolescents and adults? METHODS: Five hundred healthy Korean volunteers (254 male, 246 female; aged 13-75 years) in four age strata underwent three-dimensional gait analysis during barefoot walking at a self-selected speed. Dimensionless spatiotemporal parameters and pelvis, hip, knee, and ankle kinematics in three planes were compared across age strata (ANOVA with Tukey testing) and between sexes (t-tests) with false discovery rate correction. Full waveforms were compared using statistical parametric mapping (SPM), and side-to-side asymmetry and stride-to-stride variability were quantified. RESULTS: Throughout the gait cycle, women showed greater hip adduction (maximum 9.1° vs 4.8°), less external hip rotation (mean -0.7° vs -5.9°), and less out-toeing (foot progression -7.7° vs -12.1°) than men, together with greater knee flexion in stance and swing, whereas men showed greater knee varus. Despite similar walking speeds, women took shorter steps at a higher cadence. Across increasing age strata, anterior pelvic tilt (3.9° to 6.1°) and peak hip and knee flexion increased and swing-phase plantarflexion decreased. The shorter steps and slower speed of the 51-75-year stratum were no longer significant after dimensionless normalization. SPM showed broadly concordant patterns (sex differences up to 8°, age differences up to 5°). Side-to-side differences were small and stride-to-stride variability was low. SIGNIFICANCE: This population-based, age- and sex-stratified dataset provides reference values and upper reference limits of asymmetry and variability for Korean adolescents and adults, indicates that coronal- and transverse-plane hip variables warrant sex-specific reference values, and can serve as a normative basis for gait indices in Korean clinical populations.

articles.title: Propulsion-related gait characteristics in individuals using hip disarticulation prostheses.
articles.authors: Tsukasa Kawaguchi, Nami Shida, Takumi Yamada
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: People using hip disarticulation prostheses walk with substantial mechanical constraints; however, limb-specific propulsion-related gait mechanics remain unclear. It is also unknown whether gait strategies differ between unaided and cane-assisted walkers. This study examined the propulsion-related gait characteristics of these users. We hypothesized that propulsive and braking impulses, ankle work, and ankle power would be lower on the prosthetic side. METHODS: Three-dimensional gait analysis and ground reaction force measurements were obtained from seven adults during self-selected walking (four unaided, three cane-assisted). Propulsive and braking impulses, positive ankle and hip work, peak joint power, and spatiotemporal parameters were calculated. RESULTS: Compared with the non-prosthetic side, the prosthetic side showed lower propulsive and braking impulses and lower peak anterior-posterior ground reaction forces (all p = 0.016). Prosthetic-side ankle positive work and peak ankle power were lower (p = 0.031 and p = 0.016, respectively). Positive hip work did not differ between the limbs (p = 0.688), although peak hip power was lower on the prosthetic side (p = 0.016). Single-limb support was shorter and double-limb support was longer on the prosthetic side (both p = 0.016). Unaided walkers had higher median walking speed (1.06 vs 0.68 m/s) and cadence than cane-assisted walkers, whereas cane-assisted walkers had longer double-limb support. CONCLUSIONS: The non-prosthetic side exhibited greater propulsive and braking impulses, ankle work and peak ankle joint power. Differences between unaided and cane-assisted walkers may be associated with walking speed, non-prosthetic ankle power, cadence, step time, prosthetic-side step length, and individual compensatory movements.

articles.title: Sound-limb propulsive impulse after lower-limb amputation increases with amputation level but is not driven by peak ankle power.
articles.authors: Darlan Martins Ribeiro, Ruth Losada de Menezes, Flávia Martins Gervásio et al.
articles.abstract: Individuals with lower-limb amputation are thought to compensate for reduced prosthetic push-off by generating additional propulsion in the sound limb, but whether this originates at the ankle remains unclear. We compared propulsive impulse (PI), peak ankle power generation (A2), ankle positive work (APW) and related variables in 87 participants: 31 unimpaired controls, 30 with transfemoral amputation (TFA) and 26 with transtibial amputation (TTA), all fitted with prostheses through Brazil's public health system under a standardised protocol. Three-dimensional gait analysis provided ground reaction forces, ankle kinetics and spatiotemporal parameters. PI increased monotonically from Control to TTA to TFA and remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons and after adjustment for gait speed. In contrast, A2 was lower in both amputee groups than in Control; this reduction persisted after adjustment for gait speed only in TFA. APW, a time-integrated measure more directly comparable to PI, likewise did not follow the PI gradient. PI and A2 remained moderately correlated within every group, and the greater PI was attributable mainly to a longer propulsive phase rather than greater propulsive force. These findings indicate that the greater sound-limb propulsive impulse is not accompanied by increased peak ankle power generation or ankle positive work, although some ankle contribution cannot be excluded; whether it involves redistribution of mechanical output to more proximal joints remains a plausible hypothesis for future work. Prosthetic and rehabilitation strategies focused narrowly on restoring ankle push-off power may therefore not, by themselves, normalise sound-limb loading, particularly after transfemoral amputation.

articles.title: Head impact exposure is associated with altered medio-lateral trunk dynamics during field-based walking in collegiate football athletes.
articles.authors: Abdullah Zafar, Samuel Guay, Matthias Krüll et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Trunk-worn inertial sensors can measure medio-lateral trunk dynamics during naturalistic walking. This study examined whether head impact exposure (HIE) during Canadian varsity football games was associated with differences in these dynamics. METHODS: Sixty-eight unique male collegiate football athletes were monitored across multiple competitive seasons using instrumented mouthguards for head impact detection and chest-worn inertial measurement units for walking analysis. HIE was quantified at play-level and game-level temporal scales. Linear mixed-effects models assessed associations between HIE and root-mean-square lateral trunk acceleration (ACC) and trunk roll angular velocity (ROLL) extracted from walking bouts, adjusting for baseline dynamics, cadence and game exposure, with additional workload adjustment at play level. RESULTS: The analyzed sample comprised 13,956 walking bouts across 386 paired athlete-games, including 2106 post-impact bouts. Play-level HIE was associated with higher ROLL (β = 0.06, p < 0.001) after adjustment for recent physical workload. Game-level HIE was associated with higher baseline-adjusted post-game ROLL (β = 0.11, p = 0.016). ACC associations were not statistically significant at either the play level (β = 0.03, p = 0.149) or game level (β = 0.09, p = 0.055). Sensitivity analyses most consistently supported play-level ROLL; game-level ROLL estimates remained positive but were more sensitive to sampling window and team composition. CONCLUSION: HIE was associated with measurable differences in medio-lateral trunk dynamics during field-based walking, particularly trunk roll angular velocity. Continuous trunk-worn inertial sensing may provide a field-based approach for investigating locomotor dynamics associated with head impact exposure in football athletes.

articles.title: Neural Profiles of Pistol Shooting Performance Across Skill Levels in Hearing and Deaf Shooters: Insights into Cognitive-Motor Processes.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Ting-Yu Chueh, Jia-Hao Wu, Tsung-Min Hung et al.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Precision sport performance requires optimal motor preparation supported by efficient neural processing. While the psychomotor efficiency framework has been used to explain expertise-related neural patterns, it remains unclear whether such neural signatures generalize across individuals with different sensory experiences. The present study aimed to examine expertise-related neural oscillations during motor preparation in 10-m air-pistol shooting by comparing skilled and novice performers in hearing and deaf populations. METHODS: Study 1 included 37 hearing participants (skilled: n = 19; novice: n = 18), whereas Study 2 included 43 deaf participants (skilled: n = 19; novice: n = 24). Electroencephalography (EEG) was used to assess temporal alpha asymmetry (T4 minus T3), parietal alpha, occipital alpha, frontocentral alpha, sensorimotor rhythm (SMR), and frontal midline theta during the 4 s preceding trigger pull. RESULTS: In Study 1, skilled hearing shooters showed lower temporal alpha asymmetry, reflecting relatively greater left temporal alpha power. They also exhibited higher posterior and frontocentral alpha power, a time-specific increase in SMR, and higher frontal midline theta power relative to novice shooters. In contrast, Study 2 revealed a distinct neural profile in deaf shooters. Deaf novices showed a time-dependent decrease in temporal alpha asymmetry as the trigger pull approached, whereas skilled deaf shooters remained relatively stable. In addition, skilled deaf performers showed reduced frontocentral alpha and SMR power relative to novices, indicating greater sensorimotor cortical engagement during motor preparation. CONCLUSIONA: These findings highlight population specificity in expertise-related neural profiles, indicating that neural markers of expertise may not generalize across sensory contexts. Rather than reflecting a universal pattern of psychomotor efficiency, the observed neural profiles may vary across populations with different sensory experiences. Overall, the present study highlights the importance of considering sensory experience when examining neural optimization and provides insights into the cognitive-motor processes underlying skilled performance across diverse athletic populations in precision sports.

articles.title: Biomechanical, Anthropometric, Body Composition, Psychological, and Training-Related Correlates of Barbell Deadlift Strength.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Adam E Mohan, Alec Piñero, Dan Montenegro et al.
articles.abstract: Mohan, AE, Piñero, A, Montenegro, D, Rivera, O, Van Every, DW, Larsen, S, Androulakis Korakakis, P, Swinton, PA, and Schoenfeld, BJ. Biomechanical, anthropometric, body composition, psychological, and training-related correlates of barbell deadlift strength. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-To examine the relative contributions of biomechanical, body composition, anthropometric, psychological, and training-related variables to maximal barbell deadlift strength in resistance-trained individuals, 21 well-trained subjects (17 men, 4 women) completed assessments of body composition, anthropometry, motion capture, isometric dynamometry, psychological characteristics, and 1 repetition maximum (1RM) deadlift performance. Given the number of candidate predictors relative to the sample size, analyses were framed as theory-informed and exploratory rather than tests of causal determinants. Bayesian correlation and regression analyses, including bootstrap LASSO and Bayesian grouped-shrinkage models, were used to identify variables associated with deadlift strength. Body composition variables demonstrated the strongest associations with deadlift 1RM, particularly fat-free mass and lean mass. After adjustment for height and body mass, lean mass retained positive associations with performance, whereas fat mass showed negative associations. Relative arm length was also positively associated with deadlift strength. Bootstrap LASSO analyses identified arm lean mass as the most consistently retained predictor (67% of models), followed by isometric knee net joint moment (54%). Neck circumference, ankle width, and handgrip strength showed weaker and less consistent associations. In the Bayesian grouped-shrinkage model, body composition exhibited the strongest domain-level signal (τ = 0.31, 95% CrI: 0.08-0.92) and the highest probability of being the most influential predictor domain (0.53), exceeding anthropometric, biomechanical, training, psychological, and demographic domains. Body size and body composition, particularly lean mass, appear to provide the strongest and most consistent signal for maximal deadlift performance, whereas psychological characteristics contribute comparatively little in resistance-trained individuals.

articles.title: Recombinant type III collagen: a promising ingredient for enhancing skin repair post UVB exposure.
articles.authors: Qian Wang, Guodong Li, Fei Liu et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Skin damage is accelerated by UVB exposures. Therefore, it is essential to develop skin repair ingredients to protect the skin from damage caused by UVB exposures. This study was performed to evaluate the efficacy of recombinant type III collagen (RC-III) in alleviating damage induced by UVB exposure, and to elucidate its underlying mechanisms, using the normal human epidermal keratinocytes (NHEKs) and 3D epidermal models (EpiKutis®). METHODS: The MTT assay and cell morphology observations were used to assess the cytotoxicity of RC-III. The skin repair potential of RC-III was evaluated on NHEKs and EpiKutis® models by immunofluorescence (IF) staining, Reverse Transcription Quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), wound closure assay and ultra-high performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometer (UHPLC-MS/MS). RESULTS: RC‑III showed no cytotoxicity against NHEKs at a concentration of 2 mg/mL. In the UVB‑damaged models, RC‑III displayed prominent antioxidant effect and anti‑inflammatory property while also modulating the expression of barrier‑related proteins and lipids. Specifically, RC-III could reduce the levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), increase superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity, decrease the gene and protein expression of inflammatory factors and reduce the protein expression of NF-κB p65, promote the protein expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) and its downstream proteins, and restore the levels of skin lipids. CONCLUSIONS: All findings reported here are derived exclusively from in vitro systems. RC-III showed remarkable skin repair potential, effectively alleviating damage induced by UVB exposure in NHEKs and EpiKutis® models. Our study provided more scientific evidence for the application of RC-III.

articles.title: Dynamic responsivity of heart rate variability metrics to changing exercise intensity.
articles.authors: Matias Kanniainen, Johannes Mämmelä, Agnese Sbrollini et al.
articles.abstract: Heart rate variability (HRV) provides a non-invasive measure of autonomic regulation during exercise. Here, we examine the dynamic responsiveness of conventional and non-linear HRV metrics, with particular focus on dynamical detrended fluctuation analysis (DDFA), to changes in running intensity. Ten healthy runners completed a multi-phase outdoor protocol comprising flat, uphill, downhill and recovery segments, with RR intervals recorded via chest-worn ECG. HRV indices included RMSSD, SDRR, LF/HF, SD1/SD2, DFA α1 and the DDFA exponent α ∼ ( t ) . Phase-averaged non-linear metrics showed very strong Spearman correlations (|ρ| = 0.99, P = 0.000309) with a phase-dependent intensity index, Ik. DFA α1 and SDRR showed strong correlations (|ρ| = 0.93, P = 0.00767), LF/HF moderate non-significant association (|ρ| = 0.70, P = 0.125), and RMSSD virtually none (|ρ| = 0.06, P = 0.913). Time-lagged windowed cross-correlation analysis revealed that conventional metrics lost coupling with heart rate during sustained exertion, whereas SD1/SD2, DFA α1 and, especially, DDFA α ∼ ( t ) maintained clear intensity-dependent modulation. During recovery, DDFA α ∼ ( t ) returned rapidly towards baseline, consistent with parasympathetic reactivation. DDFA more effectively tracks rapid changes in exercise intensity than conventional HRV measures.

articles.title: Does succinic acid treatment improve metabolic health in a male murine model of early ageing?
articles.authors: Stephen J Ives, Kendall S Zaleski, Cheyanne Slocum et al.
articles.abstract: Ageing associates with obesity, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired glucose homeostasis. Previously, we documented that succinic acid (SA) treatment improves mitochondrial function and adiposity; however, the effects on ageing are unknown. Therefore, we determined the effect of SA treatment on metabolic health in 19 aged male mice (Age; 16 months), randomized to receive vehicle (Veh, n = 8) or SA (n = 11) and compared to young controls (Young; 6 months) (n = 24). After 6 weeks of treatment, insulin tolerance (IT), glucose tolerance (GT), pyruvate tolerance (PT) and physical activity (PA) were assessed. Body mass (BM), epididymal white adipose tissue (EWAT) and heart mass (HM) were measured at study end. Soleus muscle and EWAT underwent mitochondrial respirometry. Mice in the Age group had higher HM and EWAT (both P < 0.001). Blood glucose levels were higher in the Age group during the PT test (25470 ± 1206 vs. 31884 ± 4348 area under the curve (AUC), P = 0.014, Young vs. Age, respectively), though GT and IT were not affected (P > 0.05). PA was ∼50% lower in the Age group (8778 ± 5774 vs. 4132 ± 1523 rev/day), though Age-SA had 48% higher PA (Age-SA 6118 ± 2203 rev/day). SA treatment did not affect BM (37.8 ± 2.7 vs. 37.7 ± 3.2 g), EWAT (1.4 ± 0.4 vs. 1.3 ± 0.4 g) or HM (0.17 ± 0.01 vs. 0.19 ± 0.04 g, Age-Veh vs. Age-SA, all P > 0.05, respectively). GT AUC differed by group (P = 0.019), with Age-SA having lower AUC (Young 47120 ± 8751 vs. Age-SA 37180 ± 5383 AUC, P < 0.018), but not IT or PT (both P > 0.22). SA reversed the age-associated reduction in complex I+II-driven respiration in adipose (P < 0.05). Ageing elevated adiposity, impaired pyruvate tolerance and reduced adipose mitochondrial function, though SA was partially restorative in mitigating these age-associated effects, warranting further study.

articles.title: Carbohydrate quality and progression trajectories of cardiometabolic multimorbidity: a prospective cohort study with multi-omics analyses.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Mingrui Chen, Huan Liu, Chenhui Zhang et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Carbohydrate quality is associated with cardiometabolic health, but its relationships with cardiometabolic multimorbidity (CMM) progression and molecular and genetic characteristics remain unclear. OBJECTIVE: To investigate associations of carbohydrate quality with CMM progression and explore potential multi-omics signatures, pathways, and genetic effect modification. METHODS: We included 177,763 UK Biobank participants free of baseline cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs). Carbohydrate quality was assessed using correlation and principal component analyses. Multivariable Cox and multi-state models evaluated CMD incidence and CMM progression. Carbohydrate-associated proteomic and metabolomic signatures were derived for exploratory mediation analyses, and genomic data were used for gene-environment-wide interaction study (GEWIS). RESULTS: During a median 12.56-year follow-up, 37,527, 5,751, and 650 participants developed first, double, and triple CMDs, respectively. High- and low-quality carbohydrates showed opposing associations with CMM accumulation, strongest for ≥3 CMDs [HRs (95% CIs): 0.92 (0.86, 0.98) and 1.11 (1.05, 1.19), respectively]. In multi-state analyses, associations were particularly evident for progression from hypertension to comorbid T2D [HRs (95% CIs): 0.98 (0.96, 0.99) and 1.05 (1.03, 1.06), respectively]. Exploratory multi-omics mediation analyses yielded statistical mediation signals, with estimated pathway-level mediation proportions for T2D of 40.1% for PPAR signalling with high-quality carbohydrates and 36.2% and 36.4% for PI3K-Akt and MAPK signalling with low-quality carbohydrates. GEWIS identified candidate interaction loci with genotype-dependent differences in carbohydrate-CMD associations. High-quality carbohydrates were inversely associated with CHD onset among rs17589271 TT carriers but positively associated among GT/GG carriers [HRs (95% CIs): 0.95 (0.93, 0.98) and 1.22 (1.10, 1.35), respectively]. Low-quality carbohydrates showed a stronger association with progression from prior CMDs to comorbid T2D among rs144465069 AG/AA carriers [HR (95% CI): 2.09 (1.57, 2.78)]. CONCLUSIONS: Carbohydrate quality was differentially associated with CMM progression. Exploratory multi-omics and genetic analyses highlighted potential pathways and genotype-specific associations. These findings may inform future research on personalised nutritional strategies for cardiometabolic prevention.

articles.title: Watermelon supplementation lowers blood pressure: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.authors: Yunzhen Lei, Jiaying Diao, Ming Xu et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Watermelon contains L-citrulline, polyphenols, lycopene, and other bioactive compounds that may influence vascular function and blood pressure regulation. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the effects of watermelon supplementation on blood pressure, arterial stiffness-related indices, autonomic function, lipid metabolism, and anthropometric parameters. METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to May 13, 2026. Randomized controlled trials comparing watermelon, watermelon juice, or watermelon extract with non-watermelon control interventions were included. Methodological quality was assessed using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool, and evidence certainty was evaluated using the GRADE framework. Continuous outcomes were synthesized using mean differences with 95% confidence intervals. Crossover trials were analyzed as paired data, with each participant counted once; when paired variance information was unavailable, a within-participant correlation coefficient of 0.50 was assumed. Primary analyses used post-intervention values, and analyses based on change-from-baseline values were conducted as supplementary analyses. Heterogeneity was explored using subgroup analysis, meta-regression, restricted cubic spline analysis, and leave-one-out sensitivity analysis. Trial sequential analysis was conducted using unique participant counts. RESULTS: Sixteen randomized controlled trials were included. Five trials were judged to have a low risk of bias, eight had some concerns, and three had a high risk of bias. In the post-intervention primary analysis, watermelon supplementation was associated with lower systolic blood pressure (SBP; 12 studies; WMD, -5.53 mmHg; 95% CI, -8.99 to -2.06; P=0.002; I2=89.7%) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP; 12 studies; WMD, -2.55 mmHg; 95% CI, -3.77 to -1.33; P<0.001; I2=57.1%). Significant pooled reductions were observed for first systolic peak pressure and pulse pressure, whereas second systolic peak pressure, mean arterial pressure, reflection time, heart rate, pulse-wave velocity, augmentation index, and anthropometric and lipid outcomes were not statistically significant. Among autonomic outcomes, RMSSD and high-frequency power increased, whereas SDNN, low-frequency power, and the LF/HF ratio did not show statistically significant changes; these outcomes were each informed by two studies. Exploratory subgroup and study-level meta-regression analyses showed nominal differences across study characteristics, but these analyses were based on sparse, potentially confounded evidence and were not adjusted for multiple comparisons. Restricted cubic spline analyses found no evidence of nonlinearity. In the TSA analysis, 236 unique participants represented 15.9% and 28.9% of the required information sizes for SBP and DBP, respectively, and neither cumulative Z-curve crossed the trial sequential monitoring boundary. Potential small-study effects could not be excluded. According to the current GRADE profile, certainty was very low for SBP and low for DBP. CONCLUSIONS: Watermelon supplementation was associated with lower SBP and DBP, but substantial heterogeneity, limited accrued information, and low certainty of evidence restrict confidence in the estimated effects. Evidence for haemodynamic, autonomic, arterial-stiffness, lipid, and anthropometric outcomes was inconsistent and was usually based on few studies. The subgroup and meta-regression findings are exploratory study-level observations and do not establish patient-level effect modification or an optimal intervention regimen. Larger, well-designed randomized controlled trials with prespecified analyses are needed.

articles.title: Presynaptic GluN2D containing NMDARs on CA1 Shaffer collateral terminals control the release of glutamate onto pyramidal cells.
articles.authors: Tue G Banke, Jean-Francois Pare, Viktor J Olah et al.
articles.abstract: NMDA receptors (NMDARs) are expressed throughout the brain and, in addition to their central role in synaptic transmission, are essential mediators of many forms of synaptic plasticity. Given their widespread expression, it is not surprising that NMDAR dysfunction has been implicated in numerous neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders, including epilepsy, autism spectrum disorders and depression. NMDARs are localized at both pre- and postsynaptic sites, but presynaptic NMDARs are poorly understood. Here, by combining the use of wild-type and NMDAR subunit-specific knockout mice, a series of highly selective subunit-specific pharmacological modulators, and electron microscopy analysis of immunostained brain sections, we describe GluN2D-containing NMDARs located presynaptically on CA3 pyramidal neuron axon terminals. We show that presynaptic NMDARs at the Schaffer collateral terminals control the probability of glutamate release onto connecting CA1 pyramidal neurons, but not Schaffer innervation of radiatum interneurons. Thus, GluN2D-containing NMDARs could be involved in various forms of plasticity. KEY POINTS: Functional presynaptic NMDA receptors (NMDARs) are present on CA3 pyramidal cell presynaptic terminals synapsing onto pyramidal cells Presynaptic NMDARs contain GluN2D and GluN2B subunits Activation of presynaptic GluN2D-containing NMDARs enhances the probability of vesicular release of glutamate Presynaptic GluN2D-containing NMDARs regulate short-term plasticity.

articles.title: Load Range During Isokinetic Knee Extension and Flexion Exercise in Strength-Matched Male and Female Collegiate Athletes.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Tianyi Lu, Marvin Powell, B Christine Green et al.
articles.abstract: Lu, T, Powell, M, Green, BC, Brown, LE, and Jones, MT. Load range during isokinetic knee extension and flexion exercise in strength-matched men and women collegiate athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Isokinetic testing is a quantitative and objective measure of muscular strength. Despite its accurate nature, mistakes may occur in interpretation of test results when not accounting for load range. The aim of this study was to quantify acceleration, deceleration, and load range across a velocity spectrum during concentric knee extension and flexion exercises on an isokinetic dynamometer and to investigate sex differences in these components among strength-matched male and female collegiate athletes. Thirty male (n = 15) and female (n = 15) collegiate track and field athletes performed maximal knee extension and flexion exercise at constant angular velocities of 60, 120, 180, 300, 350, and 400 deg·s-1. Load range is defined as the range during which the athlete's legs moved over 90% of the preset velocity. Repeated measures analysis of variance was applied to evaluate differences in acceleration, deceleration, and load range across angular velocities and sex. There was a significant main effect of angular velocity on all ranges in both knee extension and flexion (p < 0.001). Men exhibited smaller acceleration range at all conditions except for the knee extension at 120 deg·s-1 (p = 0.228, d = 0.28) and a larger load range at all conditions except for the knee extension at 120 deg·s-1 (p = 0.065, d = 0.57). Results suggest that despite being matched in relative strength, male athletes required less time to accelerate the limb to a desired velocity. Practitioners are recommended to use different protocols for male and female athletes when performing isokinetic training and testing.

articles.title: How Often Should Volume Increase? Effects of Different Volume-Progression Frequencies on Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations in Women.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Alysson Enes, Ana Carolina G Macedo, Guilherme Nass et al.
articles.abstract: Enes, A, Macedo, ACG, Nass, G, Costa-Rodrigues, J, Alves-Marques, F, Santana, C, Dell'Avanzi, FG, Rodrigues, BG, Alves, RC, De Souza, EO, and Souza-Junior, TP. How often should volume increase? Effects of different volume-progression frequencies on strength and hypertrophy adaptations in females. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Resistance training (RT) volume is an important programming variable for strength and hypertrophy. However, how frequently RT volume should be progressed remains unclear. Thus, we investigated the effects of progressively increasing RT volume by 2 weekly sets targeting the quadriceps femoris every 2 weeks (2 W) or every 4 weeks (4 W) over a 12-week period in recreationally trained women. Using a within-subject design and accounting for previous RT volume, 21 subjects (age 23.3 ± 3.9 years; RT experience 1.1 ± 0.7 years) had their limbs assigned to one of the 2 conditions: 2 weeks (2 W) or 4 weeks (4 W). 45° leg-press 1-repetition maximum (1RM) and the sum of muscle thickness (∑MT) of the proximal (30%), middle (50%), and distal (70%) portions of the lateral thigh were assessed at baseline and after 12 weeks. Our mixed-model analysis indicated a main effect of time for 1RM (p < 0.0001), with no difference between the 2 and 4 W conditions (p = 0.317). Similarly, regarding the ∑MT, the analysis indicated a main effect of time (p < 0.001), with no difference between the conditions (p = 0.616). Within the relatively high training volumes examined, progressing the RT volume by 2 weekly sets every 2 or 4 weeks did not elicit detectable differences in strength and hypertrophy adaptations over 12 weeks in recreationally trained women.

articles.title: Dumbbell Bench Press and Dumbbell Fly Elicit Similar Pectoralis Major Muscle Hypertrophy in Recreationally Trained Men.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Filipi G Dell'Avanzi, Alysson Enes, Felipe Alves-Marques et al.
articles.abstract: Dell'Avanzi, FG, Enes, A, Alves-Marques, F, Costa-Rodrigues, J, Bello, G, Seima, G, Nass, G, Moreira, NF, Santana, C, Mohan, AE, Piñero, A, Schoenfeld, BJ, and Souza-Junior, TP. Dumbbell bench press and dumbbell fly elicit similar pectoralis major muscle hypertrophy in recreationally trained men. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Exercise selection is one of the main resistance training (RT) variables for eliciting inhomogeneous muscle growth. Whether exercises that differ in resistance moment arm elicit whole- and nonuniform hypertrophy of the pectoralis major remains unclear. This study investigated the effects of the dumbbell bench press (DBP) and dumbbell fly (DFLY) on pectoralis major muscle thickness (MT). Twenty-six young healthy men (RT experience 3.3 ± 3.1 years) were allocated to DBP or DFLY groups, training twice a week over a 10-week period. The weekly set number was individualized according to subjects' previous RT pectoralis major volume. Pectoralis major MT was assessed by ultrasound imaging at medial (30%), intermediate (50%), and lateral (70%) sites at baseline and postintervention. Our mixed-model analysis indicated a main effect for time (p < 0.05) but no time-by-group interaction for the medial site (p = 0.500), intermediate site (p = 0.864), lateral site (p = 0.720), and the sum of the MT across sites (p = 0.985). Therefore, both exercises elicited similar general and regional hypertrophy on pectoralis major MT in recreationally trained individuals. Coaches and practitioners can select DBP or DFLY when targeting pectoralis major muscle development in recreationally trained men based on personal preference and goals within the RT program.

articles.title: Effect of Different Plyometric Training Protocols on Physical Fitness in Trained Youth Soccer Players.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Raouf Hammami, Abdelkader Mahmoudi, Wajdi Dardouri et al.
articles.abstract: Hammami, R, Mahmoudi, A, Dardouri, W, and van den Tillaar, R. Effect of different plyometric training protocols on physical fitness in trained youth soccer players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study examined the effects of bilateral and unilateral plyometric training, performed at different volumes, on physical performance in trained youth male soccer players. Thirty-two subjects were randomly assigned to one of three 8-week plyometric training groups: bilateral (4 × 8 reps), high-volume unilateral (4 × 8 reps per leg), and low-volume unilateral (4 × 4 reps per leg). All groups completed 2 supervised sessions per week, with intensity increases adjusted according to individual readiness. Pre- and postintervention assessments included dynamic balance, maximal lower-limb strength (bilateral and unilateral 1 repetition maximum half squat), lower-limb power (five-jump test), linear sprint speed (10 and 30 m), and change-of-direction (CoD) ability. Significant improvements were observed over time for all performance measures (p ≤ 0.001, η2 ≥ 0.41). Unilateral plyometric training was associated with greater improvements in both bilateral and unilateral strength, and five-jump performance, compared with the bilateral condition, whereas CoD, sprint, and balance performance improved similarly across all groups, with no significant differences between training modalities. In addition, no differences were observed between the low- and high-volume unilateral protocols for any measured variables, suggesting that training volume within the tested range did not differentially affect outcomes. The findings indicate that incorporating plyometric training alongside regular soccer practice is associated with improvements in multiple aspects of physical performance in youth players. Within this context, unilateral plyometric training was associated with greater improvements in strength and power outcomes compared with bilateral training, whereas changes in sprint, CoD, and balance performance were similar across training modalities, suggesting that these capacities were not differentially influenced.

articles.title: Aqua Steps: A Feasibility Study of a new Aquatic Exercise Therapy Intervention for Falls Prevention in Older Adults.
articles.authors: Stelios G Psycharakis, Linda Linton, John Norrie et al.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: One-third of people ≥65 years old fall at least once each year. Falls cause major deteriorations in physical and mental health and have high economic costs. Aquatic exercise may reduce falls, but research on older adults at high falls risk is sparse. OBJECTIVE: The objective was to assess the feasibility and acceptability of a new aquatic exercise intervention (Aqua Steps) and explore preliminary evidence on its effectiveness for older adults at high falls risk. DESIGN: A feasibility study for the Aqua Steps intervention, with secondary outcome assessments at baseline, end of intervention, and 6 months after end of intervention. A second group undertook an established pre-existing land-based program for falls prevention (Steady Steps). SETTING: The settings were swimming pools and exercise halls. PARTICIPANTS: Participants were 101 older adults at high falls risk. INTERVENTIONS: Both the aquatic and land-based group participants undertook 60 minutes of supervised exercise therapy per week, for 16 weeks. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Primary outcomes, based on Aqua Steps feasibility, included recruitment, retention, and adverse events. The following secondary outcomes were also explored to identify preliminary evidence of improvements: falls; functional, strength, and balance tests; and patient-reported outcomes. RESULTS: The Aqua Steps intervention exceeded comfortably all feasibility targets set for progression to a large-scale trial; recruitment took 1 month, the program had 88% retention and 90% adherence, and there were no accidents or severe adverse events. After the intervention, falls, fallers, and frequent fallers were reduced by 38%, 36%, and 58%, respectively. There were statistically significant improvements, which were maintained at follow-up, on all functional (22%-70%) and strength (10%-80%) tests, falls efficacy (11%), and balance confidence (8%). In the Steady Steps group, there was a reduction in falls and fallers/frequent fallers (29%-35%) and significant improvements in functional tests (8%-30%) and falls efficacy (7%). CONCLUSIONS: Aqua Steps had very high feasibility and acceptability and was popular and safe. There was preliminary evidence for improvements in falls and risk factors for falls. RELEVANCE: Such positive effects could have a significant impact on people's lives. The findings can inform the design of a large-scale follow-up definitive trial to confirm and generalize findings and to shape future policy on exercise for falls prevention.

articles.title: Midlife Cardiorespiratory Fitness and Site-Specific Cancer Outcomes in Men.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Clare Meernik, David Leonard, Kerem Shuval et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Higher cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) is associated with a lower risk of cancer and mortality after diagnosis. However, mortality data are generally not specific to cancer sites or causes of death, limiting insights into the underlying mechanisms and opportunities for targeted prevention and survivorship strategies. This study aimed to examine the association between CRF and site-specific cancer incidence and mortality after diagnosis in men. METHODS: This cohort study used data from the Cooper Center Longitudinal Study (1971-2018) linked to Medicare claims (1999-2019). CRF was estimated using a maximal treadmill test. The associations between CRF and site-specific cancer incidence and death after cancer for the leading cancer sites in men (colorectal, lung, and prostate) were estimated using multivariable illness-death models and proportional hazards regression with Gompertz baseline hazards. RESULTS: Among 28,612 men with a mean Medicare follow-up of 7.9 years to cancer incidence, 4,998 colorectal, lung, and prostate cancers were identified. Higher CRF was associated with a lower risk of colorectal (HR: 0.91 per metabolic equivalent of task [MET]; 95% CI: 0.87, 0.96) and lung cancer (HR: 0.81 per MET; 95% CI: 0.77, 0.85), but not prostate cancer. During a mean follow-up of 7.1 years to death after diagnosis of colorectal, lung, or prostate cancer, 1,549 deaths were identified. High- (vs. low-) fit men with colorectal, lung, or prostate cancer had a 33-41% lower likelihood of all-cause mortality, including a generally lower risk of death from cardiovascular disease and other non-cancer causes. CONCLUSIONS: Achieving higher CRF levels may contribute to cancer prevention and longer survival after diagnosis. Interventions that increase CRF through physical activity may improve health across the cancer control continuum.

articles.title: Understanding the conceptual layers of 'sympathetic': Implications for autonomic neuroscience.
articles.authors: Thomas J M Verlinden

articles.title: Do Putative Human Reticulospinal Tract Properties Adapt Following Short-Term Isometric Resistance Training?
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Khai Abu-Talip, Jakob Škarabot, Danyang Wei et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: The primary purpose of this study was to investigate whether isometric resistance training (RT) leads to reticulospinal tract (RST) adaptations. METHODS: A "RT group" of 30 healthy adults completed 4 weeks (15 sessions) of volume-matched unilateral elbow flexion RT involving high (32 repetitions/session at 70% maximal voluntary torque [MVT]) or low (64 repetitions/session at 35%MVT) loads. An additional 15 participants served as controls (CON group). Pre- and post-test MVT, RST properties (RST gain ratio derived from the StartReact assessment; startling auditory stimulus-conditioned/control motor evoked potential [MEP] ratio; and startling stimulus-conditioned/control cervicomedullary MEP [CMEP] ratio), CST excitability and intracortical inhibition properties (in response to transcranial magnetic stimulation) were assessed. RESULTS: MVT increased more in the RT group (+12.8%; n = 30) vs. CON group (-4.3%; n = 15; group (2) × time (2), p = 0.001). However, changes in RST properties assessed using a series of indirect measures did not differ between the RT group (-1.4% to 6.6%; n = 30) and CON group (-4.5% to 10.5%; n = 15; group (2) × time (2), 0.352 ≤ p ≤ 0.834). CONCLUSIONS: RST adaptations within a sample of healthy young men and women, assessed using various indirect measurement approaches, did not occur following only 4 weeks of isometric elbow flexion RT. These findings add to the currently limited scientific evidence from short-term human RT intervention studies available to inform the use of RT for healthy individuals or patients primarily targeting the development of RST function.

articles.title: Effect Of Joint-Angle Configuration on Hamstring Torque-Duration Relationship Parameters and the Etiology of Motor Performance Fatigue.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Baptiste Corcelle, Gregory M Blain, Pierre Demeusoy et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This study examined how hamstring muscle-tendon unit length influences critical torque (CT), work capacity above CT (W'), and the mechanisms of motor performance fatigue during and after repeated maximal voluntary contractions. METHODS: Twelve healthy men (25 ± 4 years) performed, on separate days, two fatiguing protocols consisting of fifty 3-s maximal isometric knee flexions (2-s rest) at joint-angle configurations expected to produce relatively long (LL) and short (SL) hamstring muscle-tendon unit lengths. Neuromuscular assessments were conducted before, during, and up to 15 min post-exercise. CT and W' were determined from the torque-duration relationship. Peripheral fatigue was evaluated using peak evoked torques (T100), and central fatigue using voluntary activation (VA) derived from the twitch interpolation technique. Linear mixed-effects models and paired t-tests assessed the effects of time and joint-angle configuration. RESULTS: CT did not differ between LL and SL (p = 0.65), whereas W' was significantly lower at SL than LL (p < 0.001, d = 0.96). MVC torque decreased by ~45% after fatiguing protocols (p < 0.001, η 2p = 0.84), accompanied by reductions in T100 (-22%) and VA (-17). During recovery, VA returned to baseline within 3 min, while T100 remained depressed throughout recovery (p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: In the knee flexors, short muscle-tendon unit length reduces the capacity to perform work above CT without altering CT or the magnitude and etiology of fatigue. The rapid recovery of voluntary activation alongside persistent peripheral impairment extends current knowledge of recovery kinetics specifically for repeated maximal knee-flexion exercise.

articles.title: Low-Intensity Resistance Training Improves Irisin-Associated Endothelial Function in Aging.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Sosuke Yasunaga, Shumpei Fujie, Reita Ito et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Low-intensity resistance training (LRT) may be suitable for both muscle and cardiovascular health of older adults. However, its effects and mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to examine whether LRT improves endothelial function in adult senescence-accelerated mouse prone 1 (SAMP1) mice, a model of accelerated aging, and whether this response is accompanied by changes in circulating irisin, arterial protein kinase B (Akt)/endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) signaling, and nitric oxide (NO) levels. METHODS: Adult (38-week-old) SAMP1 mice were randomized to three groups: LRT (climbing a ladder at 40% maximal carrying capacity, 3 days/week for 12 weeks), high-intensity resistance training (80%), or sedentary control, with assessment at 50 weeks of age. Young (13-week-old) SAMP1 mice were used as a sedentary-control group. In the human study, 17 healthy middle-aged and older adults were allocated to an LRT or control group in a randomized controlled trial. LRT participants performed an elastic band-based resistance training program for 45 min, three times per week, for 8 weeks. RESULTS: In adult mice, aging was associated with reduced circulating irisin levels and muscle fibronectin type III domain-containing protein 5 (FNDC5) expression, accompanied by impaired endothelial function, diminished arterial NO production, and attenuated Akt/eNOS signaling. These age-related impairments were improved by LRT. Consistent with these findings in mice, LRT in middle-aged and older adults increased circulating nitrate/nitrite (NOx) and irisin concentrations, accompanied by improvements in endothelial function. CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that LRT-induced enhancement of circulating irisin secretion in adult SAMP1 mice and middle-aged and older adults may be involved in the improvement of endothelial function accompanied by increased NO production and the activation of the arterial Akt/eNOS signaling pathway.

articles.title: Three separate pancreatic acinar cell receptors employ different combinations of intracellular pathways to Ca2+ signalling.
articles.authors: Muhanad Salih, Julia V Gerasimenko, Oleg V Gerasimenko et al.
articles.abstract: Cytosolic Ca2+ spiking in pancreatic acinar cells, elicited by low concentrations of ACh, cholecystokinin (CCK) and gastrin-releasing peptide (GRP), controls the secretion of digestive enzymes, whereas high-intensity stimulation induces sustained Ca2+ elevation initiating acute pancreatitis. Since the discovery of the Ca2+-releasing function of inositol 1,4,5-trisphophate (IP3), it has been assumed that Ca2+ signalling relies on the phospholipase C-IP3 pathway. We have now compared the mechanisms of action of the three physiological stimulants acting on three different receptors. Each pathway to Ca2+ signalling depends on functional IP3 receptors. However, low physiological concentrations of CCK and GRP, unlike ACh, cannot elicit Ca2+ signals without co-operation of an additional intracellular mechanism. CCK-elicited Ca2+ signalling has an absolute requirement for functional intracellular receptors for nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NAADP) but, surprisingly, does not depend on the activity of CD38, the enzyme involved in the synthesis of both NAADP and cyclic ADP ribose (cADPR). Thus, physiological CCK-evoked Ca2+ signalling requires functional NAADP and IP3 receptors, but not necessarily an increase in the production of these messengers. In contrast, GRP-elicited Ca2+ signal generation does not require functional NAADP receptors but does depend on the operation of CD38, indicating a requirement for increased cADPR production. Even Ca2+ signals elicited by ACh are partially dependent on CD38 but not on functional NAADP receptors. It is the engagement of non-IP3 pathways that allows low concentrations of secretagogues to elicit safe Ca2+ spiking and therefore secretion, obviating the need for potentially toxic high levels of agonists. KEY POINTS: Three different agonists acting on three different receptors, on the same normal pancreatic acinar cell, employ different combinations of intracellular pathways to generate cytosolic Ca2+ signals. Activation of IP3 receptors is always required for Ca2+ signal generation but is insufficient alone. At least two separate intracellular pathways and intracellular receptors are required for physiological Ca2+ signalling. Although functional IP3 receptors are always required, the second parallel pathway, and its relative importance, differs for the different agonists. The exceptionally high sensitivity of pancreatic acinar cells to physiological, low pico-molar, cholecystokinin (CCK) concentrations appears to be due to sensitization of IP3 and nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NAADP) receptors to resting messenger levels.

articles.title: A 6-month randomized clinical trial to test the effect of different dietary interventions on abdominal fat components and cardiometabolic profile in overweight adults.
articles.authors: Isa Galvão Rodrigues, Gabriela Maria Pereira Floro Arcoverde, Camila Lima Chagas do Nascimento et al.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Abdominal obesity is strongly associated with cardiometabolic risk and can be modified through nutritional interventions, yet there is still no consensus on the dietary strategy capable of producing the best outcomes. This study examined the effects of different dietary interventions, with macronutrient management, on abdominal fat components and cardiometabolic parameters in overweight adults. METHODS: A randomized clinical trial was conducted with three individualized dietary interventions involving caloric restriction combined with balanced macronutrient management (BALANCED), carbohydrate reduction (LOWCARB), and fat reduction (LOWFAT), in addition to a control group that received qualitative and group-based counseling (CONTROL). Participants were followed for six months, with assessments at baseline, three, and six months. Visceral adipose tissue (VAT) and subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) were evaluated by ultrasound, along with body weight, biochemical parameters, and blood pressure. RESULTS: Body weight and VAT decreased significantly over time, with no significant time × group interactions, indicating comparable trajectories across the intervention groups. The average weight reduction was ~3%. Significant changes over time were also observed for total cholesterol, glucose, HbA1c, and blood pressure, with no significant time × group interactions for cardiometabolic parameters. CONCLUSION: After six months of dietary intervention, without changes in physical activity level, modest but significant reductions in body weight and VAT were observed over time, with no significant differences in their trajectories among the intervention groups. No evidence of a differential effect of macronutrient composition on these outcomes was observed.

articles.title: Reduced Erythropoietic Signalling may be responsible for anemia without iron deficiency among Indian Pregnant Women: findings from a cross-sectional study.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Ravindranadh Palika, Monica Chilumula, Teena Dasi et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: A substantial proportion of anemia is not associated with iron deficiency (ID), particularly in India. However, the aetiology of anemia without ID remains elusive. OBJECTIVE: To compare erythropoietic activity markers (erythropoietin, erythroferrone), micronutrient profiles, and inflammatory markers across four mutually exclusive groups of anemia and iron deficiency (ID) status: anemia with ID, anemia without ID, no-anemia with ID, and no-anemia and no-ID, to identify the factors associated with anemia without ID. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, pregnant women in their third trimester (n=687) were screened for complete blood count including hemoglobin, plasma ferritin (PF), soluble transferrin-receptor (sTfR), high-sensitive C-reactive protein (hsCRP) and Alpha-1-Acid Glycoprotein (AGP), vitamins B12, A, D and red blood cell-folate and in a sub-sample hepcidin, erythropoietin (EPO) and erythroferrone (EFRE) levels were measured. Anemia was defined when Hemoglobin <11g/dL and ID was defined when inflammation adjusted PF levels <20μg/L. RESULTS: The prevalence of anemia with ID, anemia without ID, no-anemia with ID and no-anemia and no ID were 26%, 21%, 11%, 42%, respectively. The anemia with ID group exhibited significantly lower mean Hb (9.32g/dL; 95% CI: 9.1, 9.5 Vs 10.08g/dL 95%CI: 9.9, 10.2), EFRE (0.55ng/mL, 95%CI: 0.5, 0.7 Vs 0.19ng/mL 95%CI: 0.1, 0.3) and higher median EPO (28.18mIU/mL; IQRs: 22.7, 41.0 Vs 22.00mIU/mL; IQRs: 20.8, 24.5) compared to anemia without ID group. Furthermore, despite lower hemoglobin, median EPO in anemia without ID was comparable to non-anemic groups. Micronutrient or Inflammatory markers were either similar or did not show consistent trends across the four groups. Further, hemoglobin levels showed significant negative correlation with EPO (r=-0.55, p<0.001) in anemia with ID group, but not in anemia without ID group (r=0.11, p=0.438). CONCLUSION: Our study findings suggest that reduced erythropoietic signalling may underly anemia without ID, which is not explained by inflammation or micronutrient deficiencies. Thus, diagnosing ID is vital for effective iron treatment.

articles.title: Effects of a multisectoral household agricultural and livelihood intervention on nutrition, development, and morbidity among HIV-affected children 6 to 36 months of age in Western Kenya: A cluster-randomized trial.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Lisa M Butler, Phelgona Otieno, Bezawit E Kase et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Food insecurity and HIV are interconnected, potentially increasing nutritional and health-related risks. OBJECTIVE: The Pediatric Shamba Maisha study evaluated the effects of an agricultural and livelihood intervention on growth, development, and common morbidities among children in HIV-affected households in Kenya. METHODS: The Pediatric Shamba Maisha study was a parallel-arm cluster-randomised controlled trial nested within a multisectoral agriculture and livelihood intervention trial among food-insecure adults living with HIV in rural Kenya. The Pediatric Study enrolled children aged 6 to 36 months from participating households. Anthropometric and clinical data were collected every 6 months for 24 months. RESULTS: Of the 359 children enrolled (intervention arm=173, control arm=186), 334 (90%) completed the 24-month visit. In 215 children aged 6 to <24 months at enrolment, height/length increased more in the intervention arm than in the control arm (βheight: 1.18 cm, p=0.004, 95% confidence interval (CI) = (0.390,1.98); βheight-for-age z-score: 0.390, p=0.007, 95% CI = (0.109,0.670)). Weight change of children enrolled at aged 6 to <24 months was similar between study arms across 24 months (βweight: -0.126 kg, p=0.299, 95% CI = (-0.3647,0.113); βweight-for-age z-score: -0.099, p=0.279, 95% CI = (-0.278,0.080)). In 142 children aged 24 to 36 months at enrolment, changes in height and weight over time did not differ between arms. For the intervention compared to control, younger children had lower prevalence of cough (β: -0.790 log-odds, p = 0.037, 95% CI = (-1.57,-0.047)), and older children had lower prevalence of diarrhoea (β: -1.66 log-odds, p = 0.017, 95% CI = (-3.03,-0.296)). Neurobehavioral development outcomes did not differ between study arms. CONCLUSIONS: The intervention improved growth and health of children aged 6 to <24 months at enrolment, underscoring the importance of early-life interventions. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifiers: NCT02815579, NCT03170986https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02815579?term=NCT02815579&rank=1https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03170986?term=NCT03170986&rank=1.

articles.title: Assessing dietary intake in infants through fecal sample analysis in the LLNEXT Cohort.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Jurate Gumbaragyte, Caroline Rivera, Anna Bauer et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Accurate diet tracing is fundamental to diet-health association studies, yet it remains challenging. This is particularly the case for early life studies, which rely on parental recall. Fecal sample analysis offers a non-invasive method for assessing those dietary components that have sufficient quantities of DNA remaining in stool, and are able to be taxonomically distinguished by marker gene sequence. OBJECTIVE: We aimed to determine whether a fecal DNA-based approach can be used to characterize infant dietary history. METHODS: We detected food-derived DNA in fecal samples from 73 infants at 9 and 12 months of age (139 samples total) and 25 mothers (25 samples) in the Dutch Lifelines NEXT cohort using FoodSeq, a novel fecal DNA-based tool. We compared FoodSeq data with infant food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) data using logistic mixed-effects models. We also evaluated the coherence of matching FoodSeq/FFQ in relation to the gut microbiome. RESULTS: Infant fecal samples demonstrated a lower diversity in food groups than observed in the mothers. We identified nine significant associations between matching DNA-detected and FFQ-reported food items including nuts (OR = 1.89 [1.24-2.89], q = 0.035), potatoes (OR = 2.16 [1.94-3.91], q = 0.064), dairy (OR = 2.28 [1.20-4.33], q = 0.061), formula feeding (OR = 3.96 [1.58-9.94], q = 0.055), and pork (OR = 2.44 [1.27-4.67], q = 0.063). Matched FFQ/FoodSeq pairs showed significantly stronger associations than unmatched ones (p = 1.6x10-12). Stronger associations of FFQs to gut microbiome taxa showed higher direction concordance with matching FoodSeq items. CONCLUSIONS: Fecal DNA-based diet identification showed evidence for concordance with several caregiver-reported FFQ categories (i.e., potatoes and nuts) in early life, supporting further development and validation of the FoodSeq tool for infant diet assessment up to 12 months of age.

articles.title: Corrigendum to 'Dietary guidelines adherence and pregnancy exposure to 10 classes of priority chemicals: an observational study in the Environmental influences on Child Health Outcomes Cohort' Am J Clin Nutr. 2026; volume: 124(2) 101393.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Diana C Pacyga, Xiaoshuang Xun, Deborah H Bennett et al.
